They called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel. The council is the Sanhedrin. “Senate” (gerousia): council of elders. A full, formal session.

And sent to the prison to have them brought. The comic irony begins.

In a sentence. They went into the temple at dawn and began teaching, while the high priest called a full session of the council and sent to the prison to have them brought.

For worship. The council assembled to judge the apostles, who were already free and preaching. God laughs at those who oppose him (Psalm 2:4).
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, “We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.”

We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside. Locked doors, guards in place, cells empty. Like the empty tomb, with guards and seal. No human explanation.

In a sentence. The officers didn’t find them in the prison, and reported that it was securely locked with the guards at the doors, but no one was inside.

On a Tuesday. No locked door can keep in those God wants out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”

They were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. “Perplexed” (diēporoun): at a total loss. They have lost control.

The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people. Back at work, a few hundred yards away.

In a sentence. The captain and chief priests were completely baffled, wondering where this would lead, until someone told them the men they had jailed were in the temple teaching the people.

For worship. The gospel keeps breaking out. Opposition only spreads it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.

But not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. The apostles come willingly. The authorities fear the people.

They set them before the council. The apostles could have resisted with the crowd’s help. They didn’t. They submit to arrest, and then refuse to submit on the question of preaching.

In a sentence. The captain and his officers brought them without force, fearing the people would stone them, and set them before the council.

On a Tuesday. Christians don’t use mob power to resist authorities. They submit where they can, and obey God where they must.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest questioned them, saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.”

We strictly charged you not to teach in this name. Again he avoids saying the name of Jesus.

Yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching. An unintended compliment.

And you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us. Key words. The irony: at Jesus’ trial, the crowd cried, “His blood be on us and on our children” (Matthew 27:25). Now the leaders are afraid of being held responsible. But the apostles offer the very blood they fear as the means of forgiveness (Hebrews 12:24).

In a sentence. The high priest said they had been strictly ordered not to teach in this name, yet had filled Jerusalem with their teaching and intended to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood.

For worship. The blood they feared is the blood that cleanses. Plead it for yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.

We must obey God rather than men. Key words. The principle of 4:19, now stated as a short, clear rule. “Must” (dei): it is necessary. When a human command conflicts with God’s, God wins. The motto of martyrs through the centuries.

The God of our fathers raised Jesus. Not a foreign God, but Israel’s God.

Whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The leaders meant to show Jesus was cursed by God. The apostles show that he bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24).

In a sentence. Peter and the apostles answered that they must obey God rather than men, and that the God of their fathers raised Jesus, whom the leaders had killed by hanging him on a tree.

For worship. Christ hung on the tree under the curse, so that the curse would never fall on you.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.

God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior. Key words. “Leader” (archēgon): prince, pioneer, author (3:15). “Savior” (sōtēra): rescuer. Titles that the Old Testament gives to God (Isaiah 43:11).

To give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. Key words. Christ gives repentance. Not only forgiveness, but repentance itself is his gift (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). We cannot produce it on our own. And yet we are commanded to repent (3:19). Both are true.

And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit. Two witnesses: the apostles and the Spirit (John 15:26–27). The Spirit bears witness through the signs and through the change in believers.

Whom God has given to those who obey him. “Obey” here means obey the gospel, believe (6:7; Romans 1:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8). Not that the Spirit is earned by obedience, but that he is given to those who submit to God’s call to repent and believe.

In a sentence. God exalted Jesus to his right hand as Leader and Saviour to give Israel repentance and forgiveness, and the apostles and the Holy Spirit, given to those who obey God, are witnesses.

On a Tuesday. Ask Christ for repentance. It is his gift to give.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.

They were enraged and wanted to kill them. “Enraged” (dieprionto): literally sawn through, cut to the quick. Contrast those “cut to the heart” at Pentecost (2:37), who repented. The same word can produce repentance or rage.

But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel. Setting and background. Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, grandson of the great rabbi Hillel, and Paul’s teacher (22:3). The Mishnah says that when he died, the glory of the law ceased. The Pharisees were a minority in the council, but popular with the people.

And gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. A private discussion.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they were furious and wanted to kill them, but Gamaliel, a Pharisee teacher of the law honoured by all the people, stood up and ordered the men to be put outside for a while.

For worship. God can raise up an unexpected voice to protect his people. He rules over councils.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing.

Take care what you are about to do with these men. A call to caution.

For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody. Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a Theudas who led a revolt about AD 45, about ten years after this speech. Either Gamaliel refers to an earlier Theudas, a common name, or Josephus is mistaken in his dating. There were many such rebels in those years; Josephus says the land was full of them. There is no reason to doubt Luke’s accuracy, which has been confirmed many times elsewhere.

He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. His movement died with him.

In a sentence. Gamaliel told them to be careful what they did, for Theudas had once claimed to be somebody and gathered about four hundred followers, but he was killed and his movement came to nothing.

On a Tuesday. Many movements claiming to be from God die with their leaders. Christ’s did not, because he rose.
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;

After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6 (Josephus confirms it), teaching that paying taxes to Rome was slavery and that God alone was king. His movement fed the later Zealots.

He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. Another failed messiah.

Keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail. Key words. Gamaliel’s principle: time will tell. Human movements fail.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said Judas the Galilean also rose up at the time of the census and led people away, but he died and his followers scattered, so they should leave these men alone, for if this plan was of human origin it would fail.

For worship. Human plans fail. God’s purpose stands for ever (Isaiah 46:10).
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice.

But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. True, and Luke’s whole book proves it.

You might even be found opposing God! “Opposing God” (theomachoi): fighters against God. Gamaliel’s own pupil, Saul, would soon do exactly that, and discover it (26:14).

Where Christians differ: is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some treat it as a sure rule: if something succeeds, it is from God. Verdict: it is wise caution, and true in the long run, but not a full test. False religions have lasted centuries, and God’s work can look as if it is failing for a time. The true test is Scripture and Christ (1 John 4:1–3). Gamaliel’s advice was sensible, but it was neutrality, not faith. Neutrality towards Christ is not enough.

So they took his advice. For now.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said that if it was of God they could not overthrow them, and might even find themselves fighting against God, and the council accepted his advice.

On a Tuesday. Waiting to see whether Christ is real is not enough. He is. Decide.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

They beat them. The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3; 2 Corinthians 11:24), a brutal flogging. Jesus had warned them: they will flog you in their synagogues (Matthew 10:17).

And charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The same command as before. It will have the same effect.

In a sentence. They called the apostles in, had them flogged, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.

For worship. The first apostles bled for the name. Honour them by speaking it.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.

Rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. Key words. Joy after a flogging. Not because pain is good, but because suffering for Christ is an honour (Matthew 5:11–12; 1 Peter 4:13–16; Philippians 1:29). “The name”: no need to say whose. Within a few years Christians spoke of “the name” as a title for Jesus (3 John 7).

And every day, in the temple and from house to house. Public and private: in the temple courts and in homes. The pattern of ministry (20:20).

They did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus. “Preaching” (euangelizomenoi): proclaiming the good news. The heart of it: the Messiah is Jesus.

In a sentence. They left the council rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name, and every day in the temple and in homes they kept teaching and proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked for Christ today, count it an honour. Then keep speaking of him.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church only weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; a few verses later we are told that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The growing church faces a problem from within. It now contained two groups of Jewish believers: “Hebrews”, who spoke Aramaic and were rooted in the land, and “Hellenists”, Greek-speaking Jews, many born abroad, who had settled in Jerusalem. Many Hellenists were elderly couples who had come to Jerusalem to die near the temple, which left a large number of widows without family support. The church shared food daily with widows in need, and the Hellenists complained that their widows were being overlooked. Prejudice between language groups was threatening the unity of chapter 4.

The apostles do not ignore the problem or try to handle it themselves. They tell the church to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of the distribution, so that the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. All seven have Greek names, so the church entrusts the matter to the very group that complained. The apostles pray and lay hands on them, and the word of God spreads, even many priests becoming believers. Then Luke turns to one of the seven, Stephen, full of grace and power, who works wonders and debates with Greek-speaking Jews from the Synagogue of the Freedmen. When they cannot answer his wisdom, they bring false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law, and he is brought before the council, where those staring at him see that his face is like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the number of disciples grew, the Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained against the Aramaic-speaking ones that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food. So the Twelve gathered all the disciples and said it would not be right for them to neglect the ministry of God’s word to wait on tables. The believers should choose seven men from among them who were known to be full of the Spirit and wisdom, and the apostles would put them in charge of this task, while giving their own attention to prayer and the ministry of the word. The proposal pleased everyone. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch. They presented these men to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. So God’s word spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about vocation, not about dignity, and the passage guards against the misreading in the very next sentence: the men appointed to the tables must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower bar. The whole argument turns on a single Greek root that appears on both sides of it — the apostles will not abandon the service of the word in order to serve tables. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, one menial and one spiritual. They are two forms of one thing, and the only question is which form a particular man is called to. Nor are the Seven junior figures: Stephen is preaching within a paragraph and dead within a chapter, and Philip is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. What the passage protects is not the apostles' status but the church's food supply — a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked has already stopped believing what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows were very likely the kind of women Luke described in chapter 2 — Diaspora Jews, some of whom had come home to Jerusalem to end their days near the temple. Their husbands died, and the widows were left in a city where they had no land, no clan and no relatives, and could not follow the conversation at the distribution. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone. It is who is currently being looked past — the people whose absence nobody notices, because they were never in the middle of the room to begin with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables.

Meaning first. Acts 6 shows a third threat to the church: division. A practical problem, the neglect of some widows, threatens to split Greek-speaking and Aramaic-speaking believers. The apostles solve it by appointing seven men to oversee the care, so that they can keep to prayer and the word. The result: the word spreads further. Then one of the seven, Stephen, becomes the first great witness to suffer death, and his story leads the gospel out of Jerusalem.

When the disciples were increasing in number. Growth brings new problems.

A complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews. Setting and background. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside Israel, who had settled in Jerusalem, perhaps to die in the holy city. The Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews of the land. There were cultural tensions between them. “Complaint” (gongysmos): grumbling, the word used of Israel in the wilderness.

Because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. Widows had no social security; the church fed them daily. Widows of Hellenists, perhaps without local family, were being overlooked. Probably oversight, not malice, but it was real.

It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. Key words. Not that serving tables is beneath them, but that their calling is the word. If they did everything, the word would suffer. A matter of priority, not of dignity.

In a sentence. As the disciples grew in number, the Greek-speaking Jews complained that their widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution, and the Twelve gathered all the disciples and said it was not right for them to neglect the word of God to serve tables.

On a Tuesday. Growth brings problems. Deal with complaints honestly and quickly before they divide.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside the land; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic. Widows without family depended on the community’s daily food distribution.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.

Pick out from among you seven men. The congregation chooses; the apostles appoint. Shared responsibility.

Of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom. Key words. The qualifications for a practical task are spiritual. Good reputation, filled with the Spirit, wise. Paul’s qualifications for deacons are similar (1 Timothy 3:8–13). Handling money and caring for people requires character.

Whom we will appoint to this duty. “Duty” (chreias): need, task.

But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. Key words. The priorities of pastoral ministry: prayer and the word. Both are labour. A minister who neglects them for administration fails his flock. “Ministry” (diakonia): service. Serving tables and serving the word are both service.

Where Christians differ: were the seven the first deacons? They are not called deacons here, though the verb “serve” (diakonein) and noun (diakonia) are used. Verdict: many rightly see here the pattern for the office of deacon, which appears formally later (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13): men set apart to oversee practical care so that elders can give themselves to the word and prayer. The two offices, elders and deacons, are the New Testament pattern for church leadership.

In a sentence. The apostles told the believers to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to put in charge of this, while they gave themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.

For worship. Pray for your pastors to be free for prayer and the word. And serve, so that they can.

parallels.desc: Jethro advises Moses to share the load

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.

And what they said pleased the whole gathering. Unity restored.

And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. Stephen stands out. He will be the first martyr (chapter 7).

And Philip. Later “the evangelist” (21:8), who takes the gospel to Samaria and the Ethiopian (chapter 8).

And Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas. Otherwise unknown.

And Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. A Gentile convert to Judaism, then to Christ. Antioch will become the great Gentile mission centre (11:19–26).

All seven have Greek names. All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. The majority gave the care of the neglected group to leaders from that group. Generous and wise.

And they prayed and laid their hands on them. Key words. Laying on of hands: a sign of commissioning and blessing, as Moses did for Joshua (Numbers 27:18–23). Not a magical transfer of power, but a public setting apart, with prayer (13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14).

In a sentence. The whole group agreed and chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, along with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch, and presented them to the apostles, who prayed and laid hands on them.

On a Tuesday. When people feel overlooked, give them a voice and a share in leadership. It heals division.
verseByVerse.note: All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. Laying on hands marked commissioning for a task.

parallels.desc: Moses lays hands on Joshua

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.

And the word of God continued to increase. Key words. One of Luke’s progress reports (9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:31). The word grows, like a living thing (Isaiah 55:10–11). Solving the problem freed the apostles, and the word spread.

And the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem. Steady growth.

And a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation at the temple (Luke 1:8–9), distinct from the chief priests. They were often poor, and not part of the Sadducee aristocracy. “Obedient to the faith”: believing the gospel is obedience to God’s call (Romans 1:5).

In a sentence. The word of God kept spreading, the number of disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly, and many priests became obedient to the faith.

For worship. The word of God grows. Even priests of the old order bowed to Christ. Pray for unlikely conversions.
verseByVerse.note: There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen, full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. Opposition arose from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, as it was called, Jews from Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia, who began to argue with him. But they could not stand up against his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke. So they secretly persuaded some men to say they had heard Stephen speak blasphemy against Moses and God. They stirred up the people, the elders and the teachers of the law, seized Stephen and brought him before the council. They produced false witnesses, who said that this man never stopped speaking against the holy place and the law, and that they had heard him say Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down. Everyone in the council looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest follows the shape of his master's with a precision Luke's first readers cannot have missed: suborned witnesses, a charge concerning the temple and the law, a council, a verdict of blasphemy. The accusation that Matthew and Mark record against Jesus (Matthew 26:61; Mark 14:58) is in fact the accusation Luke records against Stephen — the servant is handed the master's charge sheet. Reformed theology has read this as more than a coincidence of circumstance. Where the gospel genuinely threatens entrenched religious power it meets the same resistance in the same order, because the objection is never finally to the argument — the argument had already been lost at verse 10 — but to what conceding it would cost. What Stephen's case adds to the pattern is the sober detail that winning the argument and losing your life are entirely compatible, and that Luke plainly did not consider the second to be a reversal of the first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they changed the subject to blasphemy and found men who would swear to it. The gospel does not always win in the short term; sometimes the first thing it wins is a grave. Now: The promise attached to moments of that kind is more modest, and more useful, than it is usually made out to be. A believer put on the spot is promised a mouth, not a result — that he will not be left standing there with nothing to say. Whether he is believed, and what it costs him, are God's business.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.

And Stephen, full of grace and power. Key words. Stephen is described as “full” four times: of the Spirit and wisdom (v. 3), of faith and the Spirit (v. 5), of grace and power (here), and of the Spirit (7:55). A man filled with God.

Was doing great wonders and signs among the people. The first non-apostle in Acts to do signs, after the apostles laid hands on him (v. 6). Signs went with the apostles and those they commissioned (8:6, 18).

In a sentence. Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.

On a Tuesday. A man appointed to serve tables became a mighty witness. Faithfulness in small tasks prepares for great ones.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.

The synagogue of the Freedmen. Setting and background. The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, probably taken to Rome by Pompey in 63 BC. An inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built for Greek-speaking Jews from abroad. There may have been one synagogue, or several, for these groups.

And of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia. Greek-speaking Jews from North Africa and Asia Minor. Cilicia’s capital was Tarsus, Saul’s home city (21:39). Saul may well have been among those who argued with Stephen.

Rose up and disputed with Stephen. Stephen, a Hellenist himself, debates in the Hellenist synagogues.

In a sentence. Members of the so-called Synagogue of the Freedmen, with Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, began to argue with Stephen.

For worship. Witness in your own circles. Stephen went to those he knew best.
verseByVerse.note: The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps taken captive to Rome. Cilicia, in south-east Asia Minor, was Paul’s home province.

parallels.desc: Tarsus in Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.

But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. Key words. The promise of Jesus kept: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (Luke 21:15). They lost the argument. And when you can’t win the argument, you can attack the man.

In a sentence. But they could not stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.

On a Tuesday. Ask for the Spirit’s wisdom in conversations about Christ. He gives it.

parallels.desc: a mouth and wisdom none can withstand

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,

Then they secretly instigated men. “Instigated” (hypebalon): put up, bribed, planted. They used false accusers, as against Jesus (Mark 14:55–59).

We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God. A charge carrying the death penalty.

And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes. For the first time, the people turn against the church. Until now, the people had been on their side (5:13, 26).

And brought him before the council. The council is the Sanhedrin.

In a sentence. They secretly got men to claim they had heard him blaspheme Moses and God, stirred up the people, elders and scribes, seized him and brought him before the council.

For worship. Christ’s servants are often falsely accused, as he was. Entrust yourself to the one who judges justly.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: false witnesses against Naboth

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.”

This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law. Two charges: against the temple, and against the law.

For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place. Key words. A twisted version of Jesus’ words (John 2:19; Mark 14:58). Jesus did foretell the temple’s destruction (Luke 21:6). Stephen probably taught that Jesus is the true temple, and that God does not live in buildings made by hands (7:48). The false witnesses twist the truth into a lie.

And will change the customs that Moses delivered to us. Stephen probably taught that the law is fulfilled in Christ (Matthew 5:17), and that its ceremonies were shadows (Hebrews 10:1). Not against the law, but beyond its shadows to its substance.

In a sentence. They produced false witnesses who said he never stopped speaking against the temple and the law, and that he had said Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses.

On a Tuesday. Half-truths are the most dangerous lies. Be careful how you report what others say.

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

All who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel. Key words. A face shining with God’s glory, like Moses’ face after speaking with God on Sinai (Exodus 34:29–35). The irony: the man accused of speaking against Moses shines with Moses’ glory. Calm, radiant, unafraid. God visibly vindicates his servant before he speaks a word.

In a sentence. Everyone in the council stared at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

For worship. The peace of God can shine on a face in the worst moment. Ask him for it.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

6.theology: Word and Deed, Order and Spirit. Acts 6 is the New Testament’s foundational text on church structure. It establishes that the body has different members with different callings; that no one person can or should do everything; that the criterion for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and that when ministry is rightly ordered, the Word — not the institution, not the ministers — is what grows. This is not a management manual; it is a theology of the church as the body of Christ, each member functioning according to its calling, all of it in service of the one mission: that the Word of God would run and be glorified.
6.examples:
Then: A rapidly growing Jerusalem church discovering that love without structure produces injustice — the widows being neglected are real women with real needs — and that structure without love produces dead religion. The seven are the church’s solution: Spirit-filled servants who bring both.

Now: Every growing church faces the tension of Acts 6: how do we care well for people without the leaders becoming so consumed with management that the Word is starved? The answer is not to choose between pastoral care and proclamation; it is to raise up men and women of Spirit and wisdom to share the load — and then to watch what God does with a church that is both devoted to the Word and devoted to its neighbours.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built a house for him. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts. Accused of speaking against the temple and the law, he answers by retelling Israel’s history, and two threads run through it. First, God has never been confined to one land or one building: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, met Moses in the desert at the burning bush, and was worshipped in a portable tent; Solomon built him a house, but, as the prophets said, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. Second, Israel has repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed aside, the people turned to idols in the wilderness and persecuted the prophets. The pattern ends where Stephen’s hearers stand: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One.

Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament and some Jewish traditions of his day, which explains a few details that differ from the Hebrew text, such as seventy-five rather than seventy members of Jacob’s family. His conclusion is a direct charge: they are stiff-necked and resist the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did. Enraged, the council rushes at him. Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees heaven open and Jesus, the Son of Man, standing at God’s right hand. They drag him out of the city and stone him, laying their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen dies as his Lord did, committing his spirit to Jesus and praying that this sin not be held against them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest asked whether the charges were true. Stephen began with Abraham: the God of glory appeared to him in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran, and told him to leave his country for a land God would show him. So Abraham moved to Haran and then, after his father’s death, to Canaan, though God gave him no inheritance there, not even a foot of ground, only a promise that his descendants would possess it, when as yet he had no child. God warned that his descendants would be foreigners, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but God would judge their oppressors and they would come out and worship him. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and the line ran through Isaac, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs. The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt, but God was with him, rescued him and gave him wisdom and favour with Pharaoh, who made him ruler over Egypt. In a famine Jacob sent the patriarchs to buy grain; on their second visit Joseph revealed himself, and he brought his whole family, seventy-five people, to Egypt. Jacob and the patriarchs died there and were buried in Shechem. As the time of the promise drew near, the people grew in Egypt until a new king arose who did not know Joseph. He oppressed them and forced them to abandon their babies. Moses was born then, a fine child, raised for three months in his father’s house and then adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. He was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt and was powerful in speech and action. At forty he visited his fellow Israelites, defended one who was being mistreated and killed the Egyptian, thinking his people would realise that God was using him to rescue them; but they did not. The next day he tried to reconcile two Israelites who were fighting, and the one in the wrong pushed him aside, asking who had made him ruler and judge, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian. Moses fled to Midian and had two sons there. After forty years an angel appeared to him in the flames of a burning bush near Mount Sinai. The Lord’s voice said he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled. God told him to take off his sandals, for the place was holy ground. God had seen his people’s oppression and heard their groaning, and was sending Moses to Egypt. This Moses, whom they rejected, God sent as ruler and deliverer through the angel in the bush. He led them out with wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. He told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from their own people. He was with the congregation in the wilderness, with the angel at Sinai and with their ancestors, and he received living words to pass on. But their ancestors refused to obey him; in their hearts they turned back to Egypt and asked Aaron to make them gods. They made a calf, sacrificed to it and celebrated what their hands had made. So God gave them over to worship the stars, as the prophet Amos says: they did not bring sacrifices to God in the wilderness but carried the shrine of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, and so God would send them into exile beyond Babylon. Their ancestors had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, made to the pattern Moses was shown, and brought it in with Joshua when they took the land, until the time of David. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling for him, but it was Solomon who built him a house. Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is his throne and earth his footstool; what house could anyone build for him, or where would his resting place be? Did his hand not make all these things?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Temple and the Transcendence of God

Stephen's climax — the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48) — is not an outsider's attack on the temple. It is the temple's own prophetic self-criticism, read back to the men who ran it. Solomon said it himself on the day he dedicated the building: the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27). Isaiah said it within sight of the same building. God had said it to David before a stone was laid, pointing out that since the exodus he had never once asked anybody for a house of cedar. The problem was never the temple; it was the reduction of God to a location — the belief that having the building in Jerusalem meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Reformed theology has read Stephen's argument as the permanent warning against every arrangement in which the sign is kept and the reality quietly replaced by it. And the warning has teeth precisely because Stephen is not against the sign: God designed the tent, God filled the temple, and God was the one who said he would not be confined to either.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Every institution Stephen's accusers trusted came after the God who made it. Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is not whether it values its building, its tradition or its structures — Stephen valued the tabernacle and said God designed it. It is whether it could lose them and still know where to find God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest said, “Are these things so?”

Meaning first. Acts 7 is Stephen’s defence, the longest speech in Acts, and his martyrdom. Charged with speaking against the temple and the law (6:13–14), he retells Israel’s history. He makes two points. First, God was never confined to the land or the temple: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, spoke to Moses in Midian. Second, Israel always rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph, Moses, the prophets, and now Jesus. Then Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, and dies forgiving his killers. A young man named Saul watches.

Are these things so? The high priest, probably Caiaphas, invites Stephen to answer the charges. The formal opening of a trial.

In a sentence. The high priest asked Stephen whether these charges were true.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked about your faith, answer with the whole story of God’s dealings, as Stephen did.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’

Brothers and fathers, hear me. Respectful. He is a Jew among Jews.

The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia. Key words. Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building. The God of glory, as the psalmist calls him (Psalm 29). He appeared to Abraham far from the promised land, in pagan Mesopotamia, in Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 11:31; 15:7). God’s presence is not tied to a holy place.

Before he lived in Haran. Genesis 12:1 records the call in Haran; Stephen follows Genesis 15:7 and Nehemiah 9:7, which say God brought Abraham from Ur. God called him twice, or the call began in Ur.

Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you. Genesis 12:1. The life of faith begins with leaving.

In a sentence. Stephen began by recalling that the God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran, and told him to leave his land and family for the land God would show him.

For worship. The God of glory is not confined to buildings. He meets his people wherever they are.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building, and that Israel repeatedly rejected his messengers.

parallels.desc: go to the land that I will show you

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.

Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. Haran, in northern Mesopotamia.

And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land. Genesis 11:26, 32 suggest Terah lived on after Abraham left. Stephen may follow a tradition (also found in Philo), or may mean that Terah was spiritually dead, an idolater (Joshua 24:2). It doesn’t affect his point.

Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length. Key words. Abraham lived in the land as a stranger (Hebrews 11:9). The only land he ever owned was a burial plot. God’s promises were not exhausted by the land.

But promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. Faith in a promise, without seeing it. Abraham had no land and no child, only God’s word.

In a sentence. Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran, and after his father died God brought him to this land, though he gave him none of it, not even a foot, but promised it to him and his descendants, though he had no child.

On a Tuesday. Live by God’s promise even when you have nothing to show for it. Abraham did.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. ‘But I will judge the nation that they serve,’ said God, ‘and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’

That his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. Genesis 15:13–14. Four hundred is a round number; Exodus 12:40 says 430.

But I will judge the nation that they serve. The plagues on Egypt.

And after that they shall come out and worship me in this place. Key words. Stephen blends Genesis 15:14 with Exodus 3:12, where “this place” was Mount Sinai. Notice: the first worship God promised was at Sinai, outside the land. Worship, not land, was the goal of the exodus.

In a sentence. God told Abraham his descendants would be strangers in another land, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but God would judge that nation, and they would come out and worship him.

For worship. God redeems his people so that they will worship him. That is why he saved you.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. Genesis 17:9–14. Given before the law, before the temple. Stephen honours it: he is not against Moses or the covenant.

Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day. God kept his promise of a son.

And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. The heads of the twelve tribes. The family grows.

In a sentence. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and he became the father of Isaac, whom he circumcised on the eighth day, and Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises across generations. Trust him for your children and grandchildren.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.

And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. Key words. The first rejection. The fathers of Israel rejected the one God had chosen to save them, out of jealousy, the same motive as the leaders who handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10; Acts 5:17). Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s pictures of Jesus.

But God was with him. In Egypt, outside the land. God’s presence went with him.

And rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh. God exalted the rejected one.

Who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. The rejected one became the saviour of his brothers (Genesis 45:5–8; 50:20).

In a sentence. The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, but God was with him, rescued him from all his troubles, and gave him favour and wisdom before Pharaoh, who made him ruler over Egypt and his household.

For worship. Joseph points to Jesus: rejected by his brothers, exalted by God, the saviour of those who sold him.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit.

Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan. Genesis 41:54–57.

And our fathers could find no food. The brothers who rejected Joseph are in desperate need.

He sent out our fathers on their first visit. On the first visit they didn’t recognise Joseph (Genesis 42:8). Like Israel, at Christ’s first coming.

In a sentence. A famine came over Egypt and Canaan, and their fathers could find no food, so when Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he sent them on their first visit.

On a Tuesday. God uses hunger to bring people to the one they rejected. Your need may be his call.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all.

And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers. Key words. Only on the second visit did they recognise him (Genesis 45:1–4). Some see a hint: Israel did not recognise Jesus the first time, and Stephen is calling them to recognise him now.

Seventy-five persons in all. Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text has seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). The Greek counts some of Joseph’s grandsons. A difference in counting, not an error.

In a sentence. On the second visit Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, Pharaoh learned about his family, and Joseph sent for Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people.

For worship. The one they rejected welcomed them and fed them. That is what Christ does for sinners.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers. They all died outside the promised land.

And they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought. Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron (Genesis 23), and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19), where Joseph was buried (Joshua 24:32). Jacob was buried at Hebron (Genesis 50:13). Stephen telescopes the stories, as speakers often did, to make his point: the patriarchs were buried in Samaria, at Shechem, the region despised by Jerusalem Jews.

In a sentence. Jacob went down to Egypt and died there, as did their fathers, and they were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb bought from the sons of Hamor.

On a Tuesday. The patriarchs died in faith, not having received what was promised (Hebrews 11:13). So may we.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph.

But as the time of the promise drew near. God’s clock was moving.

The people increased and multiplied in Egypt. Exodus 1:7. Outside the land, God blessed them.

Until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. Exodus 1:8. A new dynasty, with no memory of Joseph’s service.

In a sentence. As the time drew near for God to fulfil his promise to Abraham, the people grew in Egypt until a new king came to power who did not know Joseph.

For worship. God’s promises ripen in his time. Wait for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house,

He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants. Exodus 1:10, 22. “Expose”: abandon to die, a common practice in the ancient world, which Christians later opposed by rescuing abandoned babies.

At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. Exodus 2:2. “Beautiful in God’s sight”: a Hebrew way of saying exceptionally fine, or pleasing to God. God had his hand on him.

He was brought up for three months in his father’s house. Hidden by his parents, in faith (Hebrews 11:23).

In a sentence. The king dealt cunningly with them and forced them to abandon their babies, and at that time Moses was born, a beautiful child before God, cared for three months at home.

On a Tuesday. God saw and valued an infant marked for death. Every child is precious to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds.

When he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him. Exodus 2:5–10. Rescued by the enemy’s own household.

And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education: writing, mathematics, astronomy, law, administration. Philo and Josephus describe it. God prepared him in a pagan court.

And he was mighty in his words and deeds. Moses said he was not eloquent (Exodus 4:10), but his words carried power. Luke uses the same phrase of Jesus (Luke 24:19).

In a sentence. When he was abandoned, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and raised him as her son, and Moses was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt and was powerful in words and deeds.

For worship. God prepares his servants in unlikely places. Your training may be his preparation.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.

When he was forty years old. Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties: forty in Egypt, forty in Midian (v. 30), forty in the wilderness (v. 36; Deuteronomy 34:7).

It came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. He chose to identify with his oppressed people (Hebrews 11:24–26).

And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. Exodus 2:11–12.

In a sentence. At forty, Moses decided to visit his fellow Israelites, and seeing one being mistreated, he defended him and avenged him by killing the Egyptian.

On a Tuesday. Moses chose God’s suffering people over Egypt’s comforts. What will you choose?
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’

He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. Key words. Stephen’s point. Israel didn’t recognise its deliverer. “Salvation” (sōtērian): rescue. The same pattern as with Jesus: God sends a saviour, and his own don’t understand (John 1:11).

He appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them. A peacemaker.

Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other? A plea for unity.

In a sentence. Moses thought his brothers would realise God was saving them through him, but they didn’t, and the next day he came upon two of them fighting and tried to reconcile them, asking why brothers would wrong each other.

For worship. Christ came to save his own, and many did not understand. Pray that your eyes would be opened to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’

But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside. “Thrust aside” (apōsato): pushed away, rejected. The key word: Israel thrust Moses away (v. 39). The guilty one rejects the peacemaker.

Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Key words. Exodus 2:14. The question Israel always asks of God’s deliverers, and asked of Jesus (Matthew 21:23). Stephen will answer it: God did (v. 35).

Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? A threat.

In a sentence. The man in the wrong pushed Moses aside, asking who made him ruler and judge over them, and whether he meant to kill him as he killed the Egyptian.

On a Tuesday. When the guilty resist correction, don’t be surprised. Moses was rejected for trying to make peace.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?
