verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.

At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian. Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in north-west Arabia. “Exile” (paroikos): a sojourner, a resident alien, like Abraham.

Where he became the father of two sons. Gershom and Eliezer (Exodus 2:22; 18:3–4). Life went on outside the land.

In a sentence. When he heard this, Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in Midian, where he had two sons.

For worship. God’s servant was rejected and lived in exile for forty years. God was still preparing him.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:

When forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai. Exodus 3:1–2. The angel of the Lord, whom Exodus identifies with God himself (Exodus 3:4–6).

In a flame of fire in a bush. In the wilderness, outside the land, far from any temple. God revealed his name there.

There came the voice of the Lord. God speaks.

In a sentence. After forty years an angel appeared to Moses in the wilderness of Mount Sinai in a flame of fire in a bush, and as Moses went closer to look, the Lord’s voice came.

On a Tuesday. God can meet you in the wilderness, in the most ordinary place. Stop and look.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’

I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob. Exodus 3:6. The covenant God.

And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Holy fear.

Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. Key words. Exodus 3:5. The point for Stephen’s hearers: holy ground in the wilderness, far from Jerusalem. Wherever God is, the ground is holy. The temple has no monopoly on God’s presence.

In a sentence. God said he was the God of their fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled and didn’t dare look, and the Lord told him to take off his sandals, for he stood on holy ground.

For worship. Wherever God meets you is holy ground. Worship him with reverence.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’

I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. Exodus 3:7. God sees and hears the suffering of his people.

And I have come down to deliver them. God himself comes down to save, as he did in the incarnation.

And now come, I will send you to Egypt. God sends the one his people had rejected.

In a sentence. God said he had seen his people’s suffering in Egypt and heard their groaning, and had come down to rescue them, and he was sending Moses to Egypt.

On a Tuesday. God sees your affliction and hears your groaning. He comes down to deliver.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

This Moses, whom they rejected. Key words. The heart of Stephen’s speech. Notice the repeated “this” (vv. 35, 36, 37, 38): this man, this one. Stephen is drawing a portrait of Jesus.

This man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. The answer to their question: God made him ruler. And more: redeemer (lytrōtēn), deliverer, ransomer. The man they rejected was the one God sent to save them. So with Jesus (2:36; 4:11).

This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. Signs confirmed him, as they confirmed Jesus (2:22).

In a sentence. This Moses, whom they rejected by asking who made him ruler and judge, God sent as ruler and redeemer through the angel in the bush, and he led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

For worship. The rejected one is the redeemer. That is the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us.

This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, “God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.” Key words. Deuteronomy 18:15, the verse Peter used (3:22). Moses himself pointed beyond himself, to Jesus. To honour Moses is to listen to Jesus.

This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness. “The congregation” is the same word as “church” (ekklēsia). Israel in the wilderness was God’s assembly, the church of the old covenant.

With the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai. The law was given through angels (v. 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2).

He received living oracles to give to us. Stephen calls the law “living oracles,” life-giving words of God. He honours the law. He is not against Moses. The charge was false.

In a sentence. This is the Moses who told Israel God would raise up a prophet like him, who was with the congregation in the wilderness and with the angel at Sinai, and received living words to give them.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is living. Read it as such.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’

Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside. Key words. The second rejection of Moses, the same word as v. 27. They had the living oracles, and refused them.

And in their hearts they turned to Egypt. The heart turned back before the feet did (Numbers 14:3–4).

Make for us gods who will go before us. Exodus 32:1. Idolatry: wanting a god you can see and control.

As for this Moses... we do not know what has become of him. Contempt.

In a sentence. Their fathers refused to obey Moses and pushed him aside, turning back to Egypt in their hearts and asking Aaron to make them gods to lead them, since they didn’t know what had happened to Moses.

For worship. Idolatry begins in the heart. Guard yours.

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?

And they made a calf in those days. The golden calf (Exodus 32:4).

And were rejoicing in the works of their hands. Key words. “The works of their hands”: idolatry is worshipping what we make. Stephen will soon say the temple is “made by hands” (v. 48). The same phrase. Even a God-given building can become an idol when it takes God’s place.

But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven. “Gave them over”: the terrible judgment of being given what you want (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). “The host of heaven”: the stars, worshipped as gods.

Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness? From Amos 5:25. Their sacrifices in the wilderness were not truly offered to God.

In a sentence. They made a calf, sacrificed to the idol and celebrated what they had made, so God turned away and gave them over to worship the stars, as Amos wrote, asking whether they had really offered sacrifices to him in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. What have your hands made that you are tempted to worship: career, home, reputation? Turn from it.

parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan. Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was a god worshipped with child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10), and Rephan probably an astral deity, linked with Saturn. Amos 5:26. Instead of carrying God’s tent of witness, they carried pagan shrines.

The images that you made to worship. Again, made.

And I will send you into exile beyond Babylon. Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” applying it to the later exile. The end of persistent idolatry: exile from the land. The land did not protect them.

In a sentence. Amos said they carried the shrine of Moloch and the star of Rephan, idols they made to worship, and so God would exile them beyond Babylon.

For worship. Persistent idolatry leads to judgment. Worship God alone.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,

Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness. Key words. The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the law, the testimony (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). A contrast: the fathers carried the tent of Moloch; God gave them the tent of witness. And it was a tent: portable, moving with the people. God was not fixed to a place.

Just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. The tabernacle was a copy of heavenly realities (Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5). It pointed beyond itself.

Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua. “Joshua” in Greek is “Jesus” (Iēsou). The irony is plain to Greek readers.

So it was until the days of David. For centuries Israel worshipped God in a tent.

In a sentence. Their fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, made to God’s pattern shown to Moses, and they brought it into the land with Joshua when God drove out the nations, and it stayed until David’s time.

On a Tuesday. God moved with his people in a tent. He still goes with you wherever you go.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him.

Who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. Psalm 132:5. David wanted to build a house for God (2 Samuel 7:2).

But it was Solomon who built a house for him. Key words. God said no to David, and promised instead to build David a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11–13). Solomon built the temple. Stephen doesn’t condemn it. But even at its dedication Solomon prayed: heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27).

In a sentence. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling for the God of Jacob, but Solomon built the house.

For worship. God builds his house, his people, through David’s greater Son. You are part of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?

Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Key words. The climax of Stephen’s argument. “Made by hands” (cheiropoiētois): the word used for idols in the Greek Old Testament. A shocking phrase to use of the temple. Not that the temple was wrong, but that treating it as the place where God was contained was idolatry. Paul says the same in Athens (17:24).

Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. From Isaiah 66:1. God is too great for any building.

What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? No house can hold him. Now he dwells in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), and in his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

In a sentence. The Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is my throne and earth my footstool, so what house could you build me, or where is my resting place?

On a Tuesday. Church buildings are useful, but God does not live in them. He lives in his people. Be his temple.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Did not my hand make all these things?’

Did not my hand make all these things? Isaiah 66:2. The contrast: houses made by human hands, and the universe made by God’s hand. The Creator cannot be confined by what creatures make. Isaiah goes on: but this is the one to whom I will look, he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. God’s dwelling is with the humble.

In a sentence. God asks whether his hand did not make all these things.

For worship. God made everything. He doesn’t need our buildings, but he seeks our humble hearts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen turned the charge back on his accusers: they were stubborn, with hearts and ears uncircumcised, always resisting the Holy Spirit just as their ancestors did. Their ancestors persecuted every prophet and killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, and now they had betrayed and murdered him. They had received the law through angels and had not kept it. Hearing this, they were furious and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said he could see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. At this they covered their ears, shouted, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” With that he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it did not come to mean somebody killed for the faith until enough witnesses had been. Stephen is where the shift begins, and the shape of his death is the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Reformed theology has been careful about what this is and is not. It is not heroism and it is not an achievement that earns anything — Luke states plainly that Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit at the moment he looked up, which is to say that the courage and the vision and the forgiveness were all supplied to him. What this passage exhibits is not a strong man but a sustained one. And it should be added, because the church has periodically forgotten it, that martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for this. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: Nobody watching that morning could have identified what was actually happening. The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.

You stiff-necked people. Key words. God’s own words about Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5). Stubborn, like an ox that won’t bend to the yoke.

Uncircumcised in heart and ears. “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for those who will not listen to God (Jeremiah 4:4; 6:10; 9:26; Deuteronomy 10:16). Outwardly circumcised, inwardly pagan. The worst insult a Jew could receive. True circumcision is of the heart (Romans 2:28–29).

You always resist the Holy Spirit. The Spirit who spoke through the prophets (Isaiah 63:10).

As your fathers did, so do you. The pattern Stephen has traced: rejecting Joseph, rejecting Moses, worshipping idols, and now rejecting Jesus.

In a sentence. Stephen said they were stubborn people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, who always resisted the Holy Spirit, just as their fathers did.

On a Tuesday. Is there a word of God you are resisting? Soften your neck and listen.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.

Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? Jesus said the same (Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 11:47–51). Jeremiah was imprisoned, Isaiah traditionally sawn in two, Zechariah stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21).

And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One. “The Righteous One”: Jesus, the sinless one (3:14; Isaiah 53:11).

Whom you have now betrayed and murdered. The climax of the pattern.

You who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law (Deuteronomy 33:2; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). The charge turns round: they accused Stephen of speaking against the law; he says they are the ones who broke it.

In a sentence. Stephen asked which prophet their fathers had not persecuted, for they killed those who foretold the Righteous One, whom they had now betrayed and murdered, though they had received the law through angels and not kept it.

For worship. The Righteous One was betrayed and murdered, and by his death he makes the unrighteous righteous.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

They were enraged. The same word as 5:33: cut to the quick.

And they ground their teeth at him. Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury (Psalm 35:16; 37:12). Jesus uses it of the lost in hell (Matthew 8:12).

But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven. Key words. While they look at him with hatred, he looks up.

And saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham (v. 2) now appears to Stephen. And Jesus is at his right hand, the place of honour and power.

In a sentence. When they heard this they were furious and ground their teeth at him, but Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand.

On a Tuesday. When the world grinds its teeth at you, look up. Jesus is there.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

Behold, I see the heavens opened. As at Jesus’ baptism (Luke 3:21).

And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Key words. The only time outside the Gospels that anyone calls Jesus “the Son of Man.” Jesus told this same council: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). Stephen says: I see him. He confirms the very claim for which they condemned Jesus. Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he is standing. Why? Perhaps to welcome his servant home; or as a witness standing to testify for him in the heavenly court, as Stephen testifies for him on earth (Luke 12:8); or as a judge rising to pass sentence. All may be true.

In a sentence. Stephen said he saw heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.

For worship. Jesus stands for those who stand for him. He will welcome you home.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.

parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears. To them, it was blasphemy. They would not hear it.

And rushed together at him. “With one accord” (homothymadon): the word used of the church’s unity (1:14; 2:46), now of a mob’s rage.

Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones (Leviticus 24:14; Deuteronomy 17:7). It was probably a lynching rather than a legal execution, since Rome reserved capital punishment (John 18:31). Like Jesus, he dies outside the city (Hebrews 13:12).

And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Key words. Saul enters the story. A “young man” (neanias): perhaps in his twenties or thirties. He minded the coats, and approved (8:1; 22:20). He never forgot it. God was about to make the persecutor a preacher.

In a sentence. They shouted, covered their ears, rushed at him together, dragged him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

For worship. The young man holding the coats would become the apostle to the Gentiles. No one is beyond God’s grace.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Key words. Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). But Stephen prays to Jesus, as one prays to God. The first Christian martyr dies praying to Jesus as Lord. And he expects his spirit to go at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Like Jesus: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34). Stephen loves his enemies to the last. Augustine said: if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul.

And when he had said this, he fell asleep. “Fell asleep” is the New Testament’s gentle word for the death of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20). Amid the stones, a quiet word. For the Christian, death is sleep, from which we wake in resurrection.

In a sentence. As they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” and kneeling, cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them,” and having said this, he fell asleep.

On a Tuesday. Learn to forgive like Stephen, who learned it from Jesus. And learn to die like him, commending your spirit to the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Stephen’s death sets off the first great persecution, led by Saul, who goes from house to house dragging believers to prison. The church in Jerusalem is scattered, except the apostles, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. So the second stage of Jesus’ plan in 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria. The Samaritans were descendants of northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest; they accepted only the five books of Moses, worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and were despised by Jews, and the feeling was mutual (John 4:9). Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ there with signs, and many believe, including a famous magician named Simon. The apostles send Peter and John, and only when they pray and lay hands on the Samaritans do they receive the Spirit, a sign to everyone that Samaritans and Jews are one church. Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter sternly rebukes him.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where he meets a high official of the queen of Ethiopia, the kingdom of Meroë on the Nile far south of Egypt. The man is a eunuch who had come to worship in Jerusalem, and he is reading aloud from Isaiah 53 about the lamb led to the slaughter. Philip explains that the passage is about Jesus, and when they come to water the Ethiopian asks to be baptised. Philip is then taken away by the Spirit, and the Ethiopian goes home rejoicing, the gospel already heading towards the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered through Judea and Samaria. Devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. Saul set out to destroy the church, entering house after house and dragging men and women off to prison. Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. When the crowds heard Philip and saw his signs they all paid close attention: impure spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many paralysed and lame people were healed, so there was great joy in that city. A man named Simon had practised sorcery there for some time and amazed the Samaritans, claiming to be someone great; everyone, high and low, called him the great power of God, because he had astonished them with his magic for so long. But when they believed Philip’s good news of God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptised. Simon himself believed and was baptised, and followed Philip everywhere, astonished by the signs and miracles. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had simply been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John laid hands on them and they received the Spirit. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money to give him the same power. Peter told him to take his money to destruction with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift; he had no share in this ministry, because his heart was not right before God. He must repent and pray that the Lord would perhaps forgive him for such a thought, for Peter could see he was full of bitterness and captive to sin. Simon asked them to pray for him that none of this would happen to him. After testifying and proclaiming the Lord’s word, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology has read Acts 8 as the clearest narrative demonstration that God's purposes are not merely undamaged by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.

Meaning first. Acts 8 is the turning point when the gospel leaves Jerusalem. Persecution scatters the church, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, where many believe, a sorcerer is exposed, and the apostles confirm the work. Then Philip meets an Ethiopian official on a desert road and leads him to Christ from Isaiah 53. The gospel is moving outward, as Jesus said (1:8): to the half-Jewish Samaritans, and to a Gentile from the ends of the earth.

And Saul approved of his execution. “Approved” (syneudokōn): consented, was pleased. He later confessed it with shame (22:20).

A great persecution against the church in Jerusalem. The first general persecution.

They were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Key words. The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria. The church hadn’t left Jerusalem by choice; God used persecution to push them out. “Scattered” (diesparēsan): sown, like seed. The apostles stayed, perhaps to hold the centre. Probably the Hellenists, Stephen’s circle, were the main targets.

Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. Brave, at such a time. Public mourning for an executed man was forbidden; they defied it.

In a sentence. Saul approved of Stephen’s killing, and that day a great persecution broke out against the Jerusalem church, scattering everyone except the apostles through Judea and Samaria, while devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply.

On a Tuesday. God can use what looks like disaster to spread his word. Trust him in your scattering.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.

But Saul was ravaging the church. Key words. “Ravaging” (elymaineto): destroying, like a wild animal mauling its prey. Used in the Greek Old Testament of a boar tearing up a vineyard (Psalm 80:13). Saul later admitted it (22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13; 1 Timothy 1:13).

Entering house after house. The churches met in homes. He went to the house churches.

He dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. Women too. He spared no one.

In a sentence. But Saul was trying to destroy the church, going from house to house, dragging off men and women and putting them in prison.

For worship. The worst persecutor of the church became its greatest apostle. Never stop praying for the enemies of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.

Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Key words. Not the apostles, but ordinary believers. “Preaching” (euangelizomenoi): telling the good news. Every believer a witness. The scattering became sowing.

Philip went down to the city of Samaria. This Philip is one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle. Samaritans were descendants of Israelites who intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim. Jews and Samaritans hated each other (John 4:9). For a Jewish believer to preach Christ there was a breakthrough.

And proclaimed to them the Christ. The Samaritans expected a Messiah too, the Taheb, the restorer (John 4:25).

In a sentence. Those who were scattered went everywhere preaching the word, and Philip went to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ there.

On a Tuesday. Wherever life scatters you, take the gospel with you.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

The crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip. Unity of attention.

When they heard him and saw the signs that he did. Word and signs together, confirming each other.

For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them. As in Jesus’ ministry (Mark 1:26).

And many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. The kingdom’s power at work.

In a sentence. The crowds listened intently to Philip as they heard him and saw his signs, for unclean spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many paralysed and lame people were healed.

For worship. Christ’s power over demons and disease was shown in Samaria. His kingdom has come.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.

So there was much joy in that city. Key words. The gospel brings joy (v. 39; 13:52; 16:34).

But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city. Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as the father of heresies, especially Gnosticism. Justin Martyr, himself a Samaritan, wrote that the Samaritans honoured him as the first god. “Practiced magic” (mageuōn): sorcery, occult arts.

And amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. Self-promotion. Compare Philip, who proclaimed Christ.

In a sentence. There was great joy in that city, but a man named Simon had been practising magic there, amazing the Samaritans and claiming to be someone great.

On a Tuesday. Beware of spiritual leaders who proclaim themselves. True servants proclaim Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest. His influence was enormous.

This man is the power of God that is called Great. Key words. They thought he was a divine power, an emanation of God. Pagan religion often spoke of divine powers. Simon was worshipped.

Because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. Real occult power can deceive (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13). Signs alone do not prove truth; the message must be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

In a sentence. Everyone from the least to the greatest followed him, calling him the great power of God, because he had amazed them with his magic for a long time.

For worship. Not every wonder is from God. Test everything by Christ and his word.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.

But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. The gospel content: the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ. The kingdom has come in Jesus.

They were baptized, both men and women. Believers’ baptism: they believed, then were baptised.

Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. Key words. Simon “believed.” But in what sense? The rest of the story shows his faith was not saving: Peter says his heart was not right with God and he was still bound by sin (vv. 21–23). Like those in John 2:23–25, or the seed on rocky ground (Luke 8:13), he believed something, for a time, without new birth. Baptism did not make him a Christian.

And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. The amazer is amazed. He was drawn by power, not by Christ.

In a sentence. When the people believed Philip’s good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptised, and even Simon believed, was baptised, followed Philip, and was amazed by the signs and great miracles.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised and amazed by God’s power is not the same as being born again. Make sure your faith is in Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,

When the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God. News of a breakthrough.

They sent to them Peter and John. John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:52–54). Now he comes to pray for Samaritans to receive the Spirit. Grace changes men.

Who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Prayer, the first thing.

In a sentence. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit.

For worship. The disciple who wanted to burn a Samaritan village came to bless one. Let the gospel soften your hostilities.
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.

For he had not yet fallen on any of them. Unusual. Normally the Spirit comes with faith (2:38; 10:44). Why the delay here?

But they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Their baptism was real.

Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. Key words. The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem. After centuries of hatred and rival temples, there was a danger of two churches: a Jewish one and a Samaritan one. God held back the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritans received the Spirit through Jewish apostles, and the church remained one. Something visible probably happened, since Simon saw it (v. 18).

Where Christians differ: a second blessing, or a sacrament? Pentecostals see a two-stage pattern here: conversion, then Spirit baptism. Roman Catholics and others see the basis for confirmation, a sacrament in which a bishop’s hands confer the Spirit. Verdict: this was a unique moment in salvation history, as the gospel crossed a great barrier, like the Gentiles in chapter 10 and John’s disciples in chapter 19. It was a once-for-all bridging, not the normal pattern. Romans 8:9 says anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, without a second stage or an apostle’s hands.

In a sentence. The Spirit had not yet come on any of them, though they had been baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus, but when the apostles laid hands on them, they received the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his church one. Work for the unity of believers across old hostilities.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”

Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands. He saw an outward effect, perhaps tongues or praise.

He offered them money. Key words. Simon thinks the Spirit is a power to be bought and used, like a magic trick. From this comes the word “simony”: buying or selling church offices or spiritual things, a sin that plagued the medieval church.

Give me this power also. Not “give me the Spirit,” but “give me the power to give the Spirit.” He wanted to be the dispenser, to be somebody great again (v. 9).

In a sentence. When Simon saw that the Spirit came through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money to give him the power to give the Holy Spirit to anyone he laid hands on.

For worship. The Spirit is God, not a power to use. Ask him to use you, not to give you power to use him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.

May your silver perish with you. Key words. Literally “your silver be with you to destruction.” Strong words. J. B. Phillips translated it: to hell with you and your money. Peter is horrified.

Because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! The gift of God is free (2:38; Isaiah 55:1; Romans 6:23). To think you can buy it insults God’s grace.

You have neither part nor lot in this matter. “Part nor lot”: no share at all. Simon has no part in the gospel, nor in the Spirit.

For your heart is not right before God. From Psalm 78:37. Outward faith, inward crookedness.

In a sentence. Peter told him his money could perish with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift, and that he had no part in this, for his heart was not right before God.

On a Tuesday. Grace cannot be bought. Don’t try to purchase God’s favour with gifts or good works. Receive it freely.

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.

Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours. Even for Simon, there is a call to repent. The door is open.

And pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. “If possible”: not doubting God’s mercy, but doubting whether Simon will truly repent. His sin was serious.

For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness. Key words. “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deuteronomy 29:18): a person who turns from God, and spreads poison among God’s people.

And in the bond of iniquity. Still bound by sin, not set free. Not a believer who has slipped, but one who was never released (Isaiah 58:6).

In a sentence. Peter told Simon to repent of his wickedness and pray that the Lord might forgive the intent of his heart, for he saw that Simon was full of bitter poison and chained by sin.

For worship. Christ came to break the bonds of iniquity. If you feel chained, call on him.
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.

Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. Key words. Simon asks Peter to pray, not to repent himself. He fears the consequences, not the sin. Like Pharaoh asking Moses to pray (Exodus 8:8). We hear no more of him in Scripture. Luke leaves him under a question mark.

They returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. The apostles themselves now evangelise Samaritan villages. The barrier has fallen.

In a sentence. Simon asked Peter to pray that nothing he said would happen to him, and the apostles, after testifying and preaching the Lord’s word, returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages.

On a Tuesday. Fear of consequences is not repentance. True repentance hates the sin itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. On the way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a senior official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the man reading Isaiah and asked whether he understood it. He replied that he could not unless someone explained it, and invited Philip to sit with him. He was reading the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whom the prophet meant, himself or someone else. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. As they travelled they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what stood in the way of his being baptised. He ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are usually the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship

Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. From a city revival to a desert road. God sends Philip from crowds to one man.

This is a desert place. Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. The road ran through empty country.

And he rose and went. Immediate obedience, without explanation.

And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch. Key words. “Ethiopia” here is the ancient kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt, in modern Sudan, with its capital at Meroë. To Greeks and Romans, it was the end of the earth. A eunuch: either physically castrated, as many royal officials were, or a title for a high official. If physically a eunuch, he could not enter the assembly of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:1). But Isaiah promised that eunuchs who keep God’s covenant would have a name better than sons and daughters in God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–5).

A court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. “Candace” was a title, like Pharaoh, for the queen mother who ruled Meroë.

Who was in charge of all her treasure. A powerful, wealthy man: the finance minister.

He had come to Jerusalem to worship. A God-fearing Gentile, who travelled perhaps a thousand miles to worship the God of Israel, but was probably barred from the inner courts.

In a sentence. An angel told Philip to go south to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, and he went, and there was an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official in charge of the treasury of the Ethiopian queen, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.

For worship. God sent an evangelist into the desert for one man. He seeks the one, as well as the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.”

Seated in his chariot. A covered carriage, moving slowly, with a driver.

And he was reading the prophet Isaiah. People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession, perhaps bought in Jerusalem. He was seeking.

And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” The angel sent him to the road; the Spirit sends him to the chariot. God arranged the meeting perfectly.

In a sentence. He was returning home in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah, and the Spirit told Philip to go and join the chariot.

On a Tuesday. God is preparing people to hear the gospel. Be ready when he says, “Go over.”
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

So Philip ran to him. Eager obedience.

Do you understand what you are reading? A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?” A simple, direct question. A good way to start a conversation about the Bible.

How can I, unless someone guides me? Key words. Humble honesty. The Bible is clear in its central message, but God uses teachers to explain it (Ephesians 4:11; Nehemiah 8:8). “Guides” (hodēgēsei): leads on the way, the word used of the Spirit guiding into truth (John 16:13).

And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. An open door.

In a sentence. Philip ran up, heard him reading Isaiah, and asked if he understood it, and he replied that he couldn’t unless someone guided him, and invited Philip to sit with him.

For worship. Be willing to admit you need help understanding Scripture. And be ready to help others.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this. Key words. Isaiah 53:7–8, from the fourth Servant Song, the clearest prophecy of Christ’s suffering in the Old Testament. Of all the passages he could have been reading. God’s providence.

Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. The silent, innocent sufferer. Jesus was silent before his accusers (Mark 14:61; 15:5).

In his humiliation justice was denied him. An unjust trial.

Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth. He dies without descendants. Yet Isaiah goes on: he shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10). The eunuch, who could have no children, reads of one who also died childless, yet has countless spiritual children. And just three chapters on, Isaiah promises eunuchs a place in God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–5).

In a sentence. He was reading Isaiah: like a sheep led to slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth; humiliated and denied justice, his life was taken from the earth, and who can speak of his descendants?

For worship. The Lamb was silent before his shearers, for you. He bore your sins in silence.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.

About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else? Key words. The crucial question. Jewish interpreters debated it: the prophet himself? Israel as a nation? Some unknown righteous sufferer? The Messiah?

Then Philip opened his mouth. A solemn phrase for an important speech (10:34; Matthew 5:2).

And beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. Philip begins where the man is and leads him to Jesus. Isaiah 53 is about Jesus: rejected, silent, suffering for the sins of others, dying, and then exalted. It is the gospel in the Old Testament. Jesus himself said it was written of him (Luke 22:37).

In a sentence. The eunuch asked Philip whether the prophet was speaking about himself or someone else, and Philip, starting with this Scripture, told him the good news about Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Start where people are and lead them to Jesus. Every part of Scripture can be a starting point.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” And Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” And he answered and said, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

They came to some water. In a desert, a stream or pool. Providence again.

See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized? Key words. Philip must have explained baptism. “What prevents me?” (ti kōlyei): a eunuch, a Gentile, an outsider, who might have been prevented from much in the temple. Nothing prevents him from Christ.

Textual note: verse 37. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says that if he believes with all his heart he may, and the eunuch confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. It is not in the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added later, perhaps from an early baptismal liturgy, to make the confession explicit. It reflects true early practice, since baptism followed faith, but it was likely not part of what Luke wrote.

In a sentence. On the way they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what prevented him from being baptised, and (in some manuscripts) Philip said he could if he believed with all his heart, and he confessed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.

For worship. Nothing in your past or status prevents you from coming to Christ. Believe, and confess him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.

And they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. Key words. “Went down into” and “came up out of” the water suggest immersion, the meaning of the word baptizō. Baptism pictures burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3–4).

Where Christians differ: the mode and subjects of baptism. Some sprinkle or pour; some baptise infants. Verdict: the pattern here is a believer, confessing faith, baptised by immersion. This is the New Testament norm. Christians who sprinkle or baptise infants hold their views sincerely, and we hold ours with charity, but the credobaptist practice best fits passages like this.

The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away. A sudden removal, like Elijah (1 Kings 18:12; 2 Kings 2:16). Whether miraculous transport or simply a sudden leading, Philip’s work there was done.

And went on his way rejoicing. Key words. Joy again (v. 8). He didn’t need Philip; he had Christ. Tradition says he took the gospel to Ethiopia. The gospel reached the ends of the earth in one man.

In a sentence. He stopped the chariot, they both went down into the water, and Philip baptised him, and when they came up, the Spirit of the Lord took Philip away, and the eunuch went on his way rejoicing.

On a Tuesday. When someone comes to faith, they belong to Christ, not to you. Let them go on their way rejoicing.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

But Philip found himself at Azotus. Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast, about twenty miles north of Gaza, an old Philistine city.

And as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, on the coast. Philip settled there and was living there twenty years later with four daughters who prophesied (21:8–9). Peter will soon preach to Cornelius there (chapter 10). Philip prepared the ground.

In a sentence. Philip turned up at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

For worship. Philip preached in every town he passed through. Make every place you go a place to speak of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
