Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. “Worshiped” (prosekynēsen): bowed down. Perhaps he thought Peter was a divine messenger.

In a sentence. The next day they reached Caesarea, where Cornelius was waiting with relatives and close friends he had invited, and when Peter came in, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in worship.

For worship. Gather your family and friends to hear the gospel. Invite them to church.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” Key words. Peter refuses worship, as Paul and Barnabas will (14:14–15), and the angel in Revelation (19:10; 22:8–9). Worship belongs to God alone. Jesus accepted worship (Matthew 14:33; John 20:28); his apostles refused it. That difference shows who Jesus is.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images. Verdict: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

In a sentence. But Peter raised him up, telling him to stand, for he was only a man.

On a Tuesday. Don’t put any Christian leader on a pedestal. They are only men and women. Worship God.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

He went in. Key words. Into a Gentile house. A huge step for a Jew.

You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation. The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated it as defiling. “Unlawful” (athemiton): taboo, against custom. Strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12).

But God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. Key words. Peter has understood the vision. Not food only, but people. No human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation. The wall of division has come down (Ephesians 2:14).

In a sentence. Talking with Cornelius, Peter went in and found many people gathered, and told them that they knew it was against Jewish custom to associate with or visit a Gentile, but God had shown him not to call anyone impure or unclean.

For worship. In Christ, no one is unclean because of race. Tear down your walls.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.

So when I was sent for, I came without objection. Literally “without saying anything against.” A change from “by no means, Lord” (v. 14).

I ask then why you sent for me. Peter wants to hear Cornelius’s story.

In a sentence. Peter said that when he was sent for he came without objection, and asked why they had sent for him.

On a Tuesday. When God calls you to cross a boundary, go without objection.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.’

Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour. Cornelius retells the story. Luke repeats it to emphasise its importance.

A man stood before me in bright clothing. The angel (v. 3).

Your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. God heard.

In a sentence. Cornelius said that four days earlier at three in the afternoon, while praying at home, a man in bright clothing stood before him and told him his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered by God.

For worship. Tell what God has done for you. Your story can open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.

So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Gratitude.

Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord. Key words. A model congregation. “All here”: they have gathered. “In the presence of God”: they know they are before God. “To hear”: they are ready to listen. “All”: not selectively. “Commanded by the Lord”: they want God’s word, not Peter’s opinions. Every preacher longs for such hearers.

In a sentence. Cornelius said he had sent for Peter at once as the angel told him, thanked him for coming, and said they were all there before God to hear everything the Lord had commanded him.

On a Tuesday. Come to church like this: in God’s presence, ready to hear all he has commanded.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

So Peter opened his mouth. A solemn beginning (8:35).

Truly I understand that God shows no partiality. Key words. “Partiality” (prosōpolēmptēs): literally receiving faces, judging by appearance, favouring one person over another. God doesn’t favour Jews over Gentiles (Deuteronomy 10:17; Romans 2:11). Peter now understands what he had always known in theory.

But in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. Key words. “Acceptable” (dektos): welcome. Nationality is no barrier. God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right in any religion are saved, even without hearing of Christ. Verdict: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, regardless of nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ. Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

In a sentence. Peter began by saying he now truly understood that God shows no favouritism, but welcomes from every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right.

For worship. God shows no partiality. Neither should you.

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),

As for the word that he sent to Israel. The gospel came first to Israel.

Preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ. Key words. “Peace”: with God, and between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–17). Isaiah 52:7: how beautiful are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace.

He is Lord of all. Key words. Peter’s aside is the heart of it. Not Lord of the Jews only, but of all, Jew and Gentile (Romans 10:12). A title the Romans gave to Caesar. Peter gives it to Jesus, in the house of a Roman officer.

In a sentence. Peter said God sent the message to Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.

For worship. Jesus is Lord of all: every nation, every person, every part of your life.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

You yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee. Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel: beginning from Galilee, after John’s baptism, through Jesus’ ministry, to his death and resurrection. Early church tradition says Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching.

How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. Key words. At his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18). “Anointed”: Christ, Messiah, means the anointed one. The Trinity again: God anointed Jesus with the Spirit.

He went about doing good. A beautiful summary of Jesus’ life.

And healing all who were oppressed by the devil. Jesus’ healings were a war against the devil’s tyranny (Luke 13:16; 1 John 3:8).

For God was with him. The explanation of his power. Peter speaks of his true humanity: a man empowered by the Spirit. Elsewhere Peter calls him Lord of all and judge of all (vv. 36, 42).

In a sentence. Peter reminded them of what happened throughout Judea, starting in Galilee after John’s baptism: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.

On a Tuesday. Go about doing good today, as Jesus did.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,

And we are witnesses of all that he did. Eyewitness testimony again.

They put him to death by hanging him on a tree. Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He bore the curse (Galatians 3:13).

But God raised him on the third day. The resurrection, the heart of the gospel.

And made him to appear. Literally “gave him to become visible.” Real appearances.

In a sentence. Peter said the apostles were witnesses of all Jesus did in Judea and Jerusalem, and though they killed him by hanging him on a tree, God raised him on the third day and made him appear.

For worship. He hung on the tree under the curse, and rose on the third day. That is your gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses. Key words. The risen Jesus did not appear to everyone, but to chosen witnesses. Why? Faith comes by hearing their testimony (John 20:29; Romans 10:17). God chose to spread the news by witness, not by spectacle.

Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. Proof of a real, physical resurrection (Luke 24:41–43; John 21:12–13). Ghosts don’t eat.

In a sentence. He appeared not to all the people, but to witnesses God had chosen beforehand, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

On a Tuesday. You believe on the testimony of chosen witnesses. Their word is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. Key words. Jesus is the judge of all (17:31; John 5:22; 2 Timothy 4:1). The gospel includes the warning of judgment. Every person will stand before him.

To him all the prophets bear witness. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27).

That everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Key words. The climax of Peter’s sermon, and the answer to Cornelius’s prayers. “Everyone”: Jew or Gentile. “Who believes in him”: faith alone, not circumcision, not law-keeping, not good works. “Receives forgiveness of sins”: a gift received. “Through his name”: by who he is and what he has done.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments, or faith plus works. Verdict: Peter says forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44). This is justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded them to preach and testify that he is the one God appointed as judge of the living and the dead, and all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

For worship. Everyone who believes in him is forgiven. Everyone. Believe, and rejoice.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.

While Peter was still saying these things. Key words. God interrupts the sermon. Peter hadn’t even finished. As soon as they heard “everyone who believes receives forgiveness,” they believed, and God sealed it.

The Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit with it (Galatians 3:2).

The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed. The six Jewish believers from Joppa.

Because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. “Even on the Gentiles”: unthinkable, but undeniable. God accepted them as they were, uncircumcised.

In a sentence. While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message, and the circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on Gentiles.

For worship. The Spirit is poured out on all who believe, whatever their background. Praise God for the Gentile Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,

For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Key words. The same sign as Pentecost (2:4, 11). Visible, undeniable evidence that God had given the same gift to Gentiles as to Jews (11:15–17). The tongues served as proof, at a turning point in the church’s history. “Extolling” (megalynontōn): magnifying, praising. As at Pentecost, they declared the mighty works of God.

Then Peter declared. He sees what this means.

In a sentence. They heard them speaking in tongues and praising God, and Peter said...

For worship. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise of God. Magnify him today.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.

Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? Key words. “Withhold” (kōlysai): prevent, the same word as the eunuch’s question (8:36). If God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign? “Just as we have”: no second-class Gentile believers.

And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit. The order shows that baptism is not what brings the Spirit or forgiveness; it publicly marks what God has done.

Then they asked him to remain for some days. And Peter stayed, eating with Gentiles (11:3). The wall is truly down.

In a sentence. Peter asked whether anyone could refuse water to baptise these people who had received the Spirit just as they had, and ordered them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ, and they asked him to stay a few days.

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Welcome every believer as a brother or sister.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
News that Gentiles have received the word reaches Jerusalem, and when Peter returns, Jewish believers who insisted on circumcision criticise him: he went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them. Table fellowship meant full acceptance, and that was the offence. Peter tells the whole story step by step, with six witnesses, and ends with the decisive fact: God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Spirit he gave the apostles, so who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and praise God that he has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles.

Meanwhile, believers scattered after Stephen’s death reach Antioch in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, a great trading centre on the Orontes river, with a large Jewish community and a reputation for luxury and loose living. Some of them, from Cyprus and Cyrene, begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and many believe. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who is delighted by what he sees, and fetches Saul from Tarsus to help him; for a whole year they teach the new church, and it is at Antioch that the disciples are first called “Christians”. When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, which came in the reign of the emperor Claudius, the Antioch church sends relief to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul, a first sign of the Gentile churches caring for the mother church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles and believers in Judea heard that the Gentiles had received God’s word. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticised him for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter explained everything in order: the vision at Joppa of the sheet with animals, the voice telling him to eat, his refusal, the voice saying three times not to call unclean what God has made clean, and the arrival at that moment of three men from Caesarea. The Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation, and six brothers went with him into the man’s house. The man told them how an angel had told him to send for Peter, who would bring a message through which he and his household would be saved. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words that John baptised with water but they would be baptised with the Spirit. If God gave them the same gift he gave those who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? When they heard this they had no further objections and praised God, saying that God had granted even the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Reach and the Church's Lag

What this passage shows is not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter at the door were not bigots inventing a rule; they were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, for reasons he himself had given, which had been kept at enormous cost for centuries. Their difficulty was that the boundary had done its work and been retired, and nobody had told them. Reformed theology has taken the episode as the clearest case in Scripture of the Spirit going ahead of the church's understanding — and of how he settles such questions. Not by a decree, not by a text, and not by an apostolic ruling: by doing the thing in public, in front of witnesses who could be cross-examined, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct. The Jerusalem church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council several years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's answer to a hostile hearing was to narrate what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He produced no proof text and pulled no rank. Now: That is still the strongest thing available in a disputed matter, and the rarest. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is very hard to answer — and a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has said nothing anybody can test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,

Meaning first. Acts 11 has two halves. First, Peter defends himself in Jerusalem for eating with Gentiles, and the church accepts that God has given the Gentiles repentance that leads to life. Second, the gospel reaches Gentiles in Antioch, the great city of Syria, where a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles grows under Barnabas and Saul, and where believers are first called Christians. Antioch will become the base for the mission to the world.

The Gentiles also had received the word of God. News travels fast.

The circumcision party criticized him. Key words. The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people (15:1, 5; Galatians 2:12). They were believers, but they had not yet understood that the wall was down. “Criticized” (diekrinonto): disputed, took issue. The same word as “making no distinction” in v. 12: they made the distinction God had removed.

In a sentence. The apostles and believers in Judea heard that Gentiles had received God’s word, and when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticised him.

On a Tuesday. Even true believers can resist what God is doing when it breaks their habits. Be teachable.
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. Key words. Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence. Not that Peter preached to Gentiles, but that he sat at table with them. In the ancient world, sharing a meal meant fellowship. The same objection was made against Jesus: he eats with sinners (Luke 15:2). Paul later had to rebuke Peter himself for drawing back from such meals (Galatians 2:11–14).

In a sentence. They accused him of going to uncircumcised men and eating with them.

For worship. Christ welcomes sinners to his table. Who are you unwilling to eat with?
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter began and explained it to them in order: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me.

But Peter began and explained it to them in order. Key words. “In order” (kathexēs): step by step, the word Luke uses of his own Gospel (Luke 1:3). Peter doesn’t argue or pull rank as an apostle. He simply tells what God did. The best answer to criticism is often a patient, honest account.

I was in the city of Joppa praying. He starts with prayer: it began with God.

Something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. The vision of 10:11.

In a sentence. Peter explained everything to them step by step: while praying in Joppa he saw in a trance a great sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners, right down to him.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised, tell the story patiently and honestly. Let the facts speak.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’

Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. Peter adds “beasts of prey” and “looking closely”: he studied it carefully. All of them unclean by the law.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. The command he resisted.

In a sentence. Looking closely he saw animals, wild beasts, reptiles and birds, and heard a voice telling him to get up, kill and eat.

For worship. God’s commands sometimes cut across our deepest instincts. He knows what he is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’

By no means, Lord. Peter honestly admits he resisted. He was no quicker to accept this than they were.

What God has made clean, do not call common. Key words. The word that changed everything. Peter shows his critics that the change came from heaven, not from him.

In a sentence. Peter said he had refused, since nothing unclean had ever entered his mouth, but the voice from heaven answered that he must not call common what God had made clean.

On a Tuesday. Admitting your own resistance can help others accept what God is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven.

This happened three times. Not a passing dream, but a repeated, deliberate message.

And all was drawn up again into heaven. It came from God and returned to him.

In a sentence. This happened three times, and then everything was pulled back up into heaven.

For worship. God repeats what we are slow to learn. Thank him for his patience.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house.

At that very moment three men arrived. God’s timing confirmed the vision.

And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. Key words. “Making no distinction” (mēden diakrinanta): the very thing his critics had done (v. 2). The Spirit forbade distinction between Jew and Gentile.

These six brothers also accompanied me. Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter. In Roman law, seven seals authenticated an important document. And Jewish law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Peter brought them to Jerusalem: here they are, ask them.

And we entered the man’s house. He doesn’t hide it.

In a sentence. At that moment three men sent from Caesarea arrived, and the Spirit told Peter to go with them without making distinctions, and these six brothers went with him into the man’s house.

For worship. The Spirit makes no distinction among those who believe. Neither should the church.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house. Cornelius’s side of the story.

He will declare to you a message by which you will be saved. Key words. This settles the question of chapter 10. Cornelius, for all his piety, prayers and alms, was not yet saved. He needed the message about Christ. Salvation comes through the gospel (Romans 1:16; 10:14–17).

You and all your household. The whole household heard and believed (10:44). Household salvation in Acts follows household hearing and believing (16:31–34; 18:8).

In a sentence. Cornelius told them an angel had said to send for Simon Peter, who would bring him a message by which he and his whole household would be saved.

On a Tuesday. Good people still need the gospel. Don’t assume your decent friends are fine without Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

As I began to speak. Peter felt he had only just begun.

The Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. Key words. “At the beginning”: Pentecost. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, the start of a new era. The Gentile Pentecost was the same gift.

And I remembered the word of the Lord. Scripture, and Jesus’ words, interpret events.

John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. Jesus’ promise (1:5). It applied to the Gentiles too.

In a sentence. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as on the apostles at the beginning, and he remembered the Lord’s words that John baptised with water, but they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

For worship. The same Spirit, the same gift, for every believer. There is one baptism of the Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?

If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us. Key words. “The same gift”: no difference.

When we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. The gift came with faith, for Jews and Gentiles alike. Not with circumcision, not with law-keeping.

Who was I that I could stand in God’s way? “Stand in God’s way” (kōlysai): hinder, prevent. The same word as “withhold water” (10:47). To refuse those whom God has accepted is to fight God (5:39).

In a sentence. Peter asked that if God gave them the same gift he gave the apostles when they believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was he to stand in God’s way?

On a Tuesday. Don’t stand in God’s way. If he has accepted someone, accept them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

When they heard these things they fell silent. Their objection is answered.

And they glorified God. From criticism to praise. A good response to correction.

Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life. Key words. “Granted”: repentance is God’s gift (5:31; 2 Timothy 2:25). Not something we produce, but something he gives. “That leads to life”: eternal life. The great conclusion: Gentiles are saved the same way as Jews, by God’s grace, through repentance and faith.

Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen. Luke goes back to 8:4, picking up another thread.

Traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch. Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee, around Tyre and Sidon. Antioch in Syria was the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, with perhaps half a million people and a large Jewish community.

Speaking the word to no one except Jews. At first.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they had no more objections and praised God, saying that God had granted the Gentiles too repentance leading to life; meanwhile those scattered by the persecution after Stephen had travelled to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, telling the message only to Jews.

For worship. Repentance is God’s gift. If you have it, thank him. If someone you love lacks it, ask him to grant it.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death travelled to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, telling the message only to Jews. But some from Cyprus and Cyrene went to Antioch and began speaking to Greeks as well, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus. The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. When news reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Arriving and seeing what God’s grace had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord. Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, found him and brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught great numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. During this time some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, Agabus, predicted through the Spirit that a severe famine would spread over the entire Roman world, which happened during the reign of Claudius. The disciples, each according to their ability, decided to provide help for the believers living in Judea, and sent their gift to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the model the New Testament actually gives us for a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with unnamed laymen doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was established by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first corporate act was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Reformed missiology has drawn the pattern out: rooted in the word, generous beyond its own borders, and willing to give away its best men — for within two chapters Antioch will send Barnabas and Saul off on the first missionary journey, which is to say it exported its two finest teachers and kept none of them. A church is not measured by what it gathers. It is measured by what it is prepared to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The single most important barrier in Christian history was crossed by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Luke knows their home towns and not their names, which tells you they were never anybody's leadership. Now: The work that turns out to have mattered most in any generation is very often done by people who will not appear in an account of it — who simply spoke to whoever was in front of them, because it did not occur to them to check first whether they were allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene. Key words. Unnamed believers, Greek-speaking Jews from abroad. Not apostles. The first deliberate preaching to Gentiles in a Gentile city was done by ordinary, nameless Christians. God uses ordinary people.

Who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also. “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles, in contrast to “Jews” in v. 19. Some manuscripts read “Greeks.”

Preaching the Lord Jesus. To Gentiles, they didn’t start with “Jesus is the Messiah,” a Jewish title, but “Jesus is Lord,” which Gentiles would understand. Wise evangelism adapts its words, not its message.

And the hand of the Lord was with them. God’s power and blessing (Isaiah 59:1).

And a great number who believed turned to the Lord. Faith and turning: belief and repentance together.

In a sentence. But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and spoke to the Greeks too, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus, and the Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need a title to share Christ. Nameless believers started the church that evangelised the world.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,

They sent Barnabas to Antioch. A wise choice. Barnabas was from Cyprus, like some of the evangelists, and was the son of encouragement (4:36).

When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad. Key words. Barnabas looked for the grace of God and saw it. He didn’t look for problems, or for what they were doing wrong. He saw God at work and rejoiced. A lesson for all church leaders visiting new works.

And he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose. “Exhorted” (parekalei): encouraged, the root of his nickname. “With steadfast purpose”: literally with purpose of heart, a settled resolve. New believers need encouragement to keep going.

In a sentence. When news reached the Jerusalem church, they sent Barnabas to Antioch, and when he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts.

For worship. Look for the grace of God in other believers, and rejoice when you see it.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.

For he was a good man. Key words. Rarely said of anyone in Scripture. Luke explains Barnabas’s response by his character. A good man sees good.

Full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. As Stephen was (6:5).

And a great many people were added to the Lord. Goodness and the Spirit bear fruit.

In a sentence. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great many people were brought to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Pray to be a good person, full of the Spirit and faith. Character matters more than talent.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul. Key words. Barnabas knew he needed help, and he knew whom God had called to the Gentiles (9:15). He didn’t try to keep the work for himself. “Look for” (anazētēsai): search hard. It took effort to find him.

And when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. About ten years after his conversion. The hidden years were over.

For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. Teaching. Converts need grounding.

And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. Key words. “Christians” means “Christ’s people,” probably a nickname given by outsiders, like “Herodians” for Herod’s supporters. Perhaps mocking. Outsiders noticed they talked about Christ all the time. Believers later accepted the name (1 Peter 4:16). In Antioch, a church of Jews and Gentiles needed a new name: neither Jew nor Gentile, but Christ’s.

In a sentence. Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Saul, brought him to Antioch, and for a whole year they met with the church and taught many people, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.

For worship. You bear Christ’s name. Let people see why.
verseByVerse.note: “Christians” means “Christ’s people” — probably a nickname given by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).

Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. Prophets were a recognised ministry in the early church (13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11), part of the foundation era (Ephesians 2:20).

And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world. Agabus appears again in 21:10–11, foretelling Paul’s arrest. “All the world”: the Roman world.

This took place in the days of Claudius. The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record a series of severe famines in his reign, including one in Judea around AD 45–48. Josephus tells how Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for Jerusalem. Luke ties his story to verifiable history.

In a sentence. In those days prophets came from Jerusalem to Antioch, and one named Agabus stood up and predicted by the Spirit a severe famine over the whole world, which happened under Claudius.

On a Tuesday. God warned his church ahead of time so it could prepare to help. Use your foresight for others’ good.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record severe famines in his reign, including in Judea.

parallels.desc: Agabus again

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability. Key words. The response to prophecy was not speculation but generosity. “According to his ability”: proportionate giving, each as able (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:11–12). Not equal amounts, but equal sacrifice.

To send relief to the brothers living in Judea. “Relief” (diakonian): ministry, service. A largely Gentile church helping the Jewish mother church. The new unity in Christ expressed in money. Paul would later organise a much larger collection for Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27).

And they did so, sending it to the elders. The first mention of elders in the Christian church. The Jerusalem church now had elders alongside the apostles (15:2).

By the hand of Barnabas and Saul. Trustworthy men to carry the gift (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Probably the visit Paul mentions in Galatians 2:1–10.

In a sentence. The disciples decided to send relief to the believers in Judea, each according to his means, and they did, sending it to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.

For worship. Love crosses every boundary with open hands. Give according to your ability to believers in need.

parallels.desc: remember the poor

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. Acts 11:18 contains one of the clearest biblical statements of the Reformed doctrine of monergism in conversion: “God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards with salvation; it is itself a divine gift, granted by God to those he is drawing to himself. This does not eliminate human responsibility — the Gentiles in Cornelius’s house genuinely repented, genuinely believed, genuinely turned to Christ. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the grammar of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory. Antioch is not merely a sociological phenomenon — it is a theological one: God giving repentance to people who had no claim on him, because he is the God of all grace.
11.examples:
Then: Anonymous men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names are not recorded in Scripture, who crossed the ethnic boundary no one else had thought to cross, and started the church in Antioch. The hand of the Lord was with them. History turned on their obedience.

Now: The church at Antioch is the model of a healthy sending church: multi-ethnic, Spirit-filled, taught by gifted teachers, responsive to need (the famine collection), and willing to send its best people out on mission. Every local church must ask whether it looks more like the fearful circumcision party in Jerusalem or the glad, generous, outward-facing church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
A new persecution comes from the top. Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, had grown up in Rome as a friend of the imperial family; the emperors Caligula and Claudius gave him his grandfather’s whole kingdom, and from AD 41 to 44 he ruled Judea, courting Jewish favour by careful religious observance. To please the Jewish leaders he has James the brother of John executed with the sword, the first apostle to be martyred, and arrests Peter during the Passover festival, intending a public trial afterwards. Peter is chained between two soldiers, with sixteen guarding him in shifts, while the church prays earnestly. On the night before the trial an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards and through the iron city gate, which opens by itself.

Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many are praying. The servant girl Rhoda is so excited to hear his voice that she runs to tell the others without opening the door, and they tell her she is mad, or that it must be his angel. When they finally let him in, Peter tells them what happened, asks them to tell James, the Lord’s brother, and leaves for another place. Herod executes the guards. Then, at Caesarea, while the crowd hails his speech as the voice of a god, he is struck down by an angel and dies, eaten by worms, an event the Jewish historian Josephus also records. The tyrant dies, and the word of God keeps growing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About that time King Herod arrested some who belonged to the church, intending to persecute them. He had James, John’s brother, put to death with the sword. Seeing that this pleased the Jewish leaders, he arrested Peter too, during the Festival of Unleavened Bread. He put him in prison under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each, planning to bring him out for public trial after the Passover. So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was praying earnestly to God for him. The night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries at the entrance. Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, woke him and told him to get up quickly, and the chains fell off his wrists. The angel told him to put on his clothes, sandals and cloak and follow him. Peter followed, not knowing whether it was real or a vision. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself, and when they had walked the length of a street the angel left him. Then Peter came to himself and realised that the Lord had sent his angel to rescue him from Herod and from everything the Jewish people were hoping for. He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John called Mark, where many were praying. When he knocked at the outer gate, a servant named Rhoda came to answer; recognising Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she ran back without opening it and announced that Peter was at the door. They told her she was out of her mind, and when she insisted, they said it must be his angel. Peter kept knocking, and when they opened the door they were astonished. He motioned for silence, described how the Lord had brought him out of prison, asked them to tell James and the other believers, and then left for another place. In the morning there was great commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. Herod searched for him, cross-examined the guards and ordered their execution, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there. Herod had been quarrelling with the people of Tyre and Sidon; they sought an audience, secured the support of Blastus, the king’s trusted servant, and asked for peace, because they depended on the king’s country for their food. On the appointed day Herod, in his royal robes, sat on his throne and addressed the people. They shouted that this was the voice of a god, not a man. Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God continued to spread and flourish. Barnabas and Saul, having completed their mission, returned, taking with them John, also called Mark.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

This chapter is where a theology of prayer either becomes honest or becomes cruel. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; the church, we may be sure, had prayed for James too, and James was buried. Luke gives no reason, and the Reformed tradition has been right to refuse to supply one. Prayer is not a mechanism that produces outcomes in proportion to fervency — if it were, the only conclusion available about James would be an obscene one. What prayer is, is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God who answers according to his own purposes and does not explain them. And notice that Luke reports the failure of the church's expectation in the same breath as the success of its prayer: God answered a request offered by people who did not believe it would be answered, which settles for ever the question of whether the power lies in the praying or in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda's announcement was met with you are out of your mind from the very people who had been up all night asking for exactly this. Luke records it without a word of rebuke, and the deliverance stood. Now: A great many Christians pray for things while quietly not expecting them, and then feel like frauds. This chapter is unusually kind to that condition. The answer arrived and stood knocking at the gate while the intercessors argued about whether it could be him.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,

Meaning first. Acts 12 sets two kings side by side. Herod kills an apostle, imprisons another, and is worshipped as a god. The church has no weapon but prayer. By the end, Peter is free, Herod is dead, eaten by worms, and the word of God keeps growing. It is a picture of the whole of history: the kingdoms of this world rage against Christ’s church, and fall; the word of God endures.

About that time Herod the king. This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who killed the infants of Bethlehem, and nephew of Herod Antipas, who killed John the Baptist and mocked Jesus. Raised in Rome, a friend of the emperors Caligula and Claudius, he was made king of all Judea in AD 41, ruling the whole kingdom of his grandfather. He worked hard to please the Jews.

Laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. The first persecution by the state, rather than the religious leaders.

He killed James the brother of John with the sword. Key words. Beheaded, probably. James, one of the inner three with Peter and John, the first of the Twelve to die, around AD 44. Jesus had told James and John they would drink his cup (Mark 10:38–39). One sentence records it. Unlike Judas, no replacement was chosen (1:21–22): the Twelve were witnesses for a generation, not an office to be passed on.

In a sentence. About that time King Herod began violently attacking some of the church, and had James the brother of John killed with the sword.

On a Tuesday. Some of God’s servants are delivered; others die. Both are in his hands. Be faithful either way.
verseByVerse.note: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. James is the first of the Twelve to die for his faith.

parallels.desc: the cup that I drink you will drink

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.

And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. Key words. A politician acting to please the crowd. The Jewish people had turned against the church after Stephen, especially after Peter ate with Gentiles.

This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. Passover week, the same week Jesus was arrested, more than ten years earlier. Peter’s story echoes his Lord’s.

Delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him. Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the four watches of the night. Sixteen men for one fisherman. Peter had escaped prison before (5:19).

Intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. For a public trial and execution, after the feast.

In a sentence. Seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod arrested Peter too during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and put him in prison under four squads of four soldiers, planning to bring him out to the people after Passover.

For worship. Herod piled up guards. God needed one angel. Never measure your danger without measuring your God.
verseByVerse.note: Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the night watches.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.

So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Key words. The great “but.” Herod had soldiers; the church had prayer. “Earnest” (ektenōs): stretched out, intense, the word used of Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). Continuous, fervent, united prayer. The church’s weapon against the state was not politics or violence, but prayer.

On that very night. The last night before execution. God often waits till the last moment.

Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Key words. Sleeping, the night before his execution. Peace that passes understanding (Philippians 4:7). Perhaps he remembered Jesus’ words that he would grow old (John 21:18). He slept like a man whose life was in God’s hands (Psalm 4:8).

And sentries before the door were guarding the prison. Every human precaution.

In a sentence. Peter was kept in prison, but the church was praying earnestly to God for him, and the night before Herod was to bring him out, Peter was asleep between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with guards at the door.

On a Tuesday. When you can do nothing else, pray, and pray together. And sleep in peace.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands.

And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. Light in the darkness of the prison.

He struck Peter on the side and woke him. Peter was so deeply asleep that the angel had to hit him.

Get up quickly. No time to lose.

And the chains fell off his hands. Key words. Without a sound, without waking the guards. A picture of the gospel: Christ frees the prisoners (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1).

In a sentence. Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood beside him, light shone in the cell, and he struck Peter on the side to wake him, telling him to get up quickly, and the chains fell from his wrists.

For worship. Chains fall when God says so. Pray for those in chains, literal and spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.

Dress yourself and put on your sandals. Key words. The angel gives simple, practical instructions, almost humorous in their detail. God does the impossible (the chains), and leaves us to do the possible (the sandals).

Wrap your cloak around you and follow me. Follow me: Jesus’ words to Peter (John 21:19).

He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. It was too good to be true. Peter, who had seen visions (10:10), thought this was another.

In a sentence. The angel told him to dress and put on his sandals, and then to wrap his cloak around him and follow, and Peter followed him out, not realising it was really happening but thinking it was a vision.

On a Tuesday. God’s rescue sometimes seems too good to be real. Follow anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.

When they had passed the first and the second guard. Past two guard posts unseen.

They came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord. Key words. “Of its own accord” (automatē): by itself, automatically. No hand touched it. Every barrier gave way.

And they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. Once Peter was safe and able to think for himself, the angel left. God doesn’t do for us what we can do ourselves.

In a sentence. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate into the city, which opened by itself, and they went out and along one street, and the angel suddenly left him.

For worship. No gate is too strong for God. He opens doors no one can shut (Revelation 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.

When Peter came to himself. In the cool night air, he realised it was real.

Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod. Key words. Peter gives the credit to the Lord.

And from all that the Jewish people were expecting. They had expected an execution.

He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark. John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10). His mother’s house, large enough for a gathering with a gate and a servant, was a centre of the Jerusalem church, perhaps where the Last Supper was held. Church tradition says Mark wrote his Gospel from Peter’s preaching (1 Peter 5:13).

Where many were gathered together and were praying. In the middle of the night. Still praying.

In a sentence. When Peter came to his senses, he said he now knew for sure that the Lord had sent his angel to rescue him from Herod and from what the people expected, and he went to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where many were gathered praying.

On a Tuesday. Open your home for prayer. Great things happen in houses where people pray.
verseByVerse.note: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas. His mother’s house was large enough to hold a gathering.

parallels.desc: God sent his angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.

A servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Rhoda means “rose.” A slave girl, named by Luke, who remembered small people.

Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate. Key words. One of the most human, almost comic scenes in Scripture. In her excitement she forgets to let him in, leaving the escaped prisoner standing in the street. An angel opened the iron gate; a joyful girl kept the wooden one shut.

But ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. The first witness of his release, like the women at the tomb, was a woman, and not believed.

In a sentence. When he knocked at the outer gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came, and recognising Peter’s voice she was so overjoyed that she ran in without opening it and told them Peter was at the gate.

For worship. Joy at answered prayer can make us forget our heads. God smiles at it.
verseByVerse.note: Rhoda means “rose.”

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.

They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” Key words. They were praying for Peter, and when the answer came, they didn’t believe it. Like us. Their faith was real but weak. God answered their prayers beyond their faith (Ephesians 3:20).

It is his angel! Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel, who might look like them. Jesus spoke of children’s angels (Matthew 18:10); Hebrews says angels serve those who inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). But Scripture doesn’t teach much detail, and we shouldn’t build on popular beliefs reported here.

But Peter continued knocking. Persistent, and probably nervous, in the street of a city hunting for him.

And when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. Prayer answered.

In a sentence. They told her she was mad, but she insisted, so they said it must be his angel, while Peter kept knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.

On a Tuesday. Pray expecting answers. And when they come, open the door.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place.
