Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.

Motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. Again, the Lord did it.

Tell these things to James and to the brothers. Key words. This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9), and wrote the letter of James. From here on he leads in Jerusalem.

Then he departed and went to another place. Key words. Luke doesn’t say where, perhaps to protect him. Peter appears again at the council in Jerusalem (15:7), and later in Antioch (Galatians 2:11) and perhaps Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:12).

Where Christians differ: did Peter go to Rome? Some Roman Catholic tradition says Peter went to Rome at this point and was bishop there for twenty-five years. Verdict: there is no evidence that Peter went to Rome now; he is in Jerusalem a few years later (15:7). Paul’s letter to the Romans, written around AD 57, greets many people in Rome but never mentions Peter. Peter probably did go to Rome late in his life and died there under Nero, as early tradition says. But the New Testament never presents him as bishop of Rome or head of the church.

No little disturbance among the soldiers. Understatement.

In a sentence. Peter signalled them to be quiet, told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison, asked them to tell James and the brothers, and left for another place; at daybreak the soldiers were in great confusion about what had happened to Peter.

For worship. Tell others what the Lord has done for you. It strengthens the whole church.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.

After Herod searched for him and did not find him. Herod could not find Peter. God hides his own.

He examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty (16:27; 27:42). Herod’s cruelty claims innocent lives. This is the kind of king he was.

Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. To his coastal capital, where he would die.

In a sentence. When Herod searched and couldn’t find him, he cross-examined the guards and had them executed, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

On a Tuesday. Cruel power destroys even its own servants. Pray for those who live under such rulers.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.

Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain, since they had little farmland of their own (1 Kings 5:11; Ezekiel 27:17). We don’t know why he was angry.

Having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain. Probably by a bribe. The man in charge of the king’s private rooms.

On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes. Josephus says this was at games held in honour of the emperor, and that Herod wore a robe woven of silver, which shone dazzlingly in the morning sun.

Took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. Power on display.

In a sentence. Herod was angry with Tyre and Sidon, and they came together to him, won over Blastus his chamberlain, and asked for peace, since they depended on his land for food, and on the appointed day Herod, dressed in royal robes, sat on his throne and gave a speech.

For worship. The world’s power dazzles for a moment. Christ’s glory is for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.

The voice of a god, and not of a man! Flattery, and blasphemy. Ancient rulers were often hailed as gods.

Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory. Key words. The same angel of the Lord who freed Peter strikes Herod. Herod’s sin was accepting worship. Compare Peter, who refused it (10:26), and Paul and Barnabas (14:14–15). God shares his glory with no one (Isaiah 42:8).

And he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death after accepting divine honours, with severe abdominal pains, five days later, in AD 44. Two independent accounts. The man who was hailed as a god was eaten by worms. Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18; Daniel 4:30–37).

In a sentence. The people shouted that this was the voice of a god, not a man, and at once an angel of the Lord struck him down because he did not give glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.

On a Tuesday. When praised, give God the glory. Quickly.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.

But the word of God increased and multiplied. Key words. The contrast is the point of the whole chapter. Herod killed, imprisoned, persecuted, and was worshipped; now he is dead. The word of God grows. Kings die; the word lives (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service. The famine relief (11:29–30). Some manuscripts read “to Jerusalem,” but “from Jerusalem” to Antioch fits the story.

Bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark. Barnabas’s cousin, from the praying house of v. 12. He will join their first missionary journey (13:5), leave them (13:13), and cause a split between Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39). But later he is restored, and Paul calls him useful (2 Timothy 4:11). He wrote the second Gospel.

In a sentence. But the word of God kept spreading and growing, and Barnabas and Saul, having finished their service, returned from Jerusalem, taking John Mark with them.

For worship. Tyrants die, but the word of God grows. Take heart.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door a few streets from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The third stage of Acts 1:8, “to the end of the earth”, begins in earnest. The church at Antioch, led by a strikingly mixed group of prophets and teachers, is worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special work. With prayer and the laying on of hands they send them off, with John Mark as their assistant. They sail to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island, preach in synagogues from Salamis in the east to Paphos in the west, and there meet the Roman governor, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet, Elymas, who tries to turn him from the faith. Saul, from now on called by his Roman name Paul, rebukes Elymas, who is struck blind, and the proconsul believes.

They sail to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where Mark leaves them, and travel inland over the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony on the high plateau. In the synagogue Paul is invited to speak and gives the first of his sermons recorded in Acts: God chose Israel, brought them out of Egypt, gave them the land, judges and kings, and from David’s line has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. The people of Jerusalem condemned him, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is proclaimed and everyone who believes is freed from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathers. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas announce that they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. Opposition drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet, while the new disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he had called them. After more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on them and sent them off. Sent out by the Spirit, the two went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper. They travelled through the whole island to Paphos, where they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, an intelligent man, sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name was translated, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. Then Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, looked straight at Elymas and called him a child of the devil, an enemy of everything right, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the Lord’s right ways. The Lord’s hand was against him, and he would be blind for a time. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had been sent to build up that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting. A church's seriousness about mission is not measured by what it collects for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in verse 1 is the most cosmopolitan leadership team in the New Testament, and it was assembled by a persecution. Every man on it was in Antioch because something had gone wrong somewhere else. Now: Congregations tend to produce leaders who resemble each other, and to regard that as normal rather than as a symptom. Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what the room looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”

Meaning first. Acts 13 begins the third part of the book: the gospel to the ends of the earth (1:8). The church in Antioch, prompted by the Spirit, sends out Barnabas and Saul on the first deliberate missionary journey. In Cyprus a Roman governor believes; in Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches his first recorded sermon, the gospel of forgiveness and justification through Jesus; many Gentiles believe, “as many as were appointed to eternal life”; and the pattern of Paul’s mission is set: to the Jew first, then to the Gentile.

Prophets and teachers. Leaders of the church.

Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen... and Saul. Key words. A diverse leadership. Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa; some suggest he was Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross (Mark 15:21). Lucius from Cyrene in North Africa. Manaen, “a lifelong friend” (syntrophos, foster brother, brought up with) of Herod Antipas, the ruler who beheaded John the Baptist. A Levite from Cyprus, an African, a courtier, and a former Pharisee. The church of Christ is for all.

While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting. “Worshiping” (leitourgountōn): serving, ministering, the word for priestly service. The church’s great missionary step came out of worship and prayer.

Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. Key words. The Spirit speaks, probably through one of the prophets. “For me”: they belong to him. “I have called”: the Spirit had already called them; the church recognises it. Mission is the Spirit’s initiative. Note too that the church sends its best two leaders, not those it can spare.

In a sentence. In the church at Antioch were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen who grew up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul, and while they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work he had called them to.

On a Tuesday. Be willing to send your best for the gospel. And listen for the Spirit in worship and prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.

Then after fasting and praying. More prayer before sending.

They laid their hands on them. Laying on hands commissioned them for the task (6:6). Not ordination to a higher rank, since they were already leaders, but identification and blessing: the church was with them.

And sent them off. Literally “released them,” let them go. The Spirit sent them (v. 4); the church released them. Both are needed.

In a sentence. After fasting and praying, they laid hands on them and sent them off.

For worship. Pray for the missionaries your church has sent. You share in their work.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.

So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit. Key words. The Spirit is the sender. Mission belongs to God.

They went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. Seleucia was Antioch’s port, sixteen miles away. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island (4:36), with a large Jewish community. A wise starting point: where there were connections.

When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. Salamis, the main city on the east coast. Paul’s pattern: start with the synagogue. Jews and God-fearers there knew the Scriptures and were waiting for the Messiah. To the Jew first (Romans 1:16).

And they had John to assist them. John Mark, as helper (hypēretēn), perhaps handling practical arrangements or teaching new converts.

In a sentence. Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, and at Salamis they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper.

On a Tuesday. Start your witness where you have connections. God uses relationships.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.

When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos. About ninety miles, east to west. Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end.

A certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. “Bar-Jesus”: son of Joshua, or son of Jesus. A Jew practising sorcery, against the law (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Like Simon in Samaria (8:9), an occult figure attached to the powerful.

He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. A proconsul governed a senatorial province on behalf of the Roman Senate. Luke uses the exact correct title: Cyprus became a senatorial province in 22 BC. An inscription mentioning a Paulus as proconsul has been found. Luke is precise.

A man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. A thoughtful, open man. Not all the powerful are closed to the gospel.

In a sentence. When they had travelled across the island to Paphos, they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, an attendant of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man who sent for Barnabas and Saul wanting to hear the word of God.

For worship. God opens the hearts of the powerful too. Pray for leaders to hear the word.
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.

But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name). “Elymas” may be from an Arabic or Aramaic word for wise man or sorcerer. A title.

Opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Key words. Spiritual opposition. If the proconsul believed, the magician would lose his influence and his living. The occult resists the gospel (Ephesians 6:12).

In a sentence. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name means, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith.

On a Tuesday. When someone is close to faith, expect opposition. Pray.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?

But Saul, who was also called Paul. Key words. Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on Luke calls him Paul. Most Jews of the Dispersion had two names (12:12). As he turns to the Gentile world, he uses his Gentile name. Some note it means “small.” And from now on Paul usually leads: “Paul and Barnabas,” not “Barnabas and Saul” (v. 13).

Filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him. Spirit-filled discernment.

You son of the devil. A play on his name: Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus (or Joshua, meaning “the Lord saves”), is really a son of the devil (John 8:44).

You enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy. Strong words, exposing evil.

Will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? John the Baptist prepared straight paths (Luke 3:4; Isaiah 40:3). The false prophet twists them.

In a sentence. But Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, stared at him and called him a son of the devil, an enemy of all righteousness, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord.

For worship. The Spirit gives boldness to expose evil when the gospel is at stake. Ask him for discernment.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

The hand of the Lord is upon you. In judgment.

And you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time. Key words. “For a time”: a judgment with mercy in it, room to repent. Paul knew what it was to be struck blind and led by the hand (9:8). Perhaps he hoped Elymas would find the same grace.

Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Luke the doctor describes a progressive blindness: mist, then darkness.

Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. Key words. Not the miracle alone, but “the teaching of the Lord” astonished him. The sign drew him to the word. The first named Gentile ruler to believe.

In a sentence. Paul said the Lord’s hand was against him and he would be blind for a while, and at once mist and darkness came over him and he groped for someone to lead him, and when the proconsul saw this, he believed, astonished at the Lord’s teaching.

On a Tuesday. Signs point to the word. It is the teaching of the Lord that saves.

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The missionaries sail to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and go inland to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, Paul retells Israel’s story from the exodus to King David, and announces that from David’s line God has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. Jerusalem’s leaders condemned him, unknowingly fulfilling the prophets, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is offered: everyone who believes is set free from everything the law could not free them from. Many want to hear more, and the next Sabbath almost the whole city comes. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas declare that, since the word has been rejected, they now turn to the Gentiles, as Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations require. The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed for eternal life believe, and the word spreads, until opponents stir up the city’s leading people and expel the missionaries. They shake the dust from their feet and go on, leaving disciples full of joy and the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified — a courtroom word, the word for a judge declaring a man to be in the right. The law cannot issue that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends on Habakkuk's word to scoffers, be astounded and perish (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.

Paul and his companions. Paul now leads.

Came to Perga in Pamphylia. Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor, modern Turkey.

And John left them and returned to Jerusalem. Key words. We aren’t told why: homesickness, fear of the dangerous mountain journey ahead, illness, or discomfort with Paul taking over from his cousin Barnabas, or with the Gentile mission. Paul saw it as desertion (15:38). But Mark was later restored (Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11). Failure need not be final.

But they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. Pisidian Antioch lay about a hundred miles inland, over the Taurus mountains, a hard and dangerous road with bandits (2 Corinthians 11:26). A Roman colony, different from Syrian Antioch. Some think Paul was ill at the time; Galatians 4:13 says he first preached there because of a bodily ailment.

And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. Paul’s usual practice (17:2).

In a sentence. From Paphos Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them and went back to Jerusalem, while they went on to Pisidian Antioch, and on the Sabbath they went into the synagogue and sat down.

For worship. If you have turned back from God’s work, he can restore you, as he did Mark.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.”

After the reading from the Law and the Prophets. Setting and background. A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets, followed by an exposition. Prayers, the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), readings, a sermon, and a blessing. The pattern of Christian worship grew from it.

The rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them. Lay leaders who organised the service. Visiting teachers were often invited to speak (Luke 4:16–17).

If you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it. An open door. “Word of encouragement” (logos paraklēseōs): a sermon (Hebrews 13:22).

In a sentence. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders invited them to speak a word of encouragement to the people.

On a Tuesday. When an opportunity opens to speak of Christ, take it.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it.

So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand. His first recorded sermon. Like Stephen’s, it retells Israel’s history, but its aim is to show that God’s promises are fulfilled in Jesus.

Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God, like Cornelius. Two groups in the congregation.

The God of this people Israel chose our fathers. Key words. The story begins with God’s choice, election. Israel was chosen not for its greatness but by God’s love (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).

And made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. The exodus, God’s great act of salvation in the Old Testament (Exodus 6:6).

In a sentence. Paul stood, gestured, and addressed the men of Israel and the God-fearers, saying that the God of Israel chose their fathers, made the people great in Egypt, and led them out with his mighty arm.

For worship. Salvation always begins with God’s choice. He chose his people, and he chose you.
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance.

And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. Key words. “Put up with” (etropophorēsen): bore with their ways. Some manuscripts read etrophophorēsen, carried them like a nurse (Deuteronomy 1:31). Either way, God’s patience with a grumbling people.

After destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan. Deuteronomy 7:1.

He gave them their land as an inheritance. A gift, not an achievement.

In a sentence. God put up with them for about forty years in the wilderness, and after overthrowing seven nations in Canaan, gave them their land as an inheritance.

On a Tuesday. God bears with his people patiently. He has borne with you. Bear with others.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.

All this took about 450 years. The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest: 400 in Egypt, 40 in the wilderness, and about 7 to conquer the land. Some manuscripts place the figure differently, linking it to the judges. A round number.

And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. “Gave”: the judges were God’s gift of deliverers.

In a sentence. All this took about 450 years, and afterwards God gave them judges until the prophet Samuel.

For worship. God works across centuries. His plans are never late.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’

Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 is damaged, and Josephus also gives forty years. Paul, himself named Saul and of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), mentions his namesake.

And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king. “Raised up”: the same word used of the resurrection (v. 30, 37). God raises up his king.

I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will. A combination of Psalm 89:20, 1 Samuel 13:14 and Isaiah 44:28.

In a sentence. When they asked for a king, God gave them Saul son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years, and after removing him he made David their king, of whom he said he had found in David son of Jesse a man after his heart who would do all his will.

On a Tuesday. Pray to be a person after God’s own heart, who does all his will.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.

Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. Key words. The climax of the history: from David to Jesus. God promised David an eternal descendant on his throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus is that son. “Savior” (sōtēra): rescuer. The whole of Israel’s history was leading to him.

In a sentence. From David’s descendants God has brought Israel a Saviour, Jesus, as he promised.

For worship. All of history leads to Jesus. He is the Saviour God promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’

Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. John the Baptist was widely known, even in the Dispersion (19:3).

As John was finishing his course. “Course” (dromon): race. Paul uses the same image of his own life (20:24; 2 Timothy 4:7).

I am not he. John refused to be thought the Messiah (John 1:20).

After me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie. Untying sandals was a slave’s job (Luke 3:16). The greatest prophet was not worthy to be Jesus’ slave.

In a sentence. Before Jesus came, John preached a baptism of repentance to all Israel, and as he finished his work, said he was not the one they thought, but one was coming after him whose sandals he was not worthy to untie.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation.

Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God. Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. Paul addresses them both, warmly.

To us has been sent the message of this salvation. Key words. “To us”: this message is for you, here, now. Not for someone else.

In a sentence. Paul told the descendants of Abraham and the God-fearers that the message of this salvation had been sent to them.

For worship. The message of salvation has been sent to you. Receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed.

Because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath. Key words. The tragic irony: they heard the prophets every week, and did not recognise the one they spoke of (2 Corinthians 3:14–15).

Fulfilled them by condemning him. By rejecting Jesus, they fulfilled the very prophecies they failed to understand (Isaiah 53).

And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. The innocent condemned.

In a sentence. The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise Jesus or understand the prophets read every Sabbath, and fulfilled them by condemning him, asking Pilate to execute him though they found no grounds for death.

On a Tuesday. You can hear the Bible every week and miss Christ. Ask God to open your eyes as you read.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.

And when they had carried out all that was written of him. Key words. Everything Scripture foretold happened. Nothing was left undone (John 19:28, 30).

They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. The tree, the place of the curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). And the tomb: he truly died and was buried (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

In a sentence. When they had done all that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.

For worship. Every prophecy fulfilled, to the last detail. Your Saviour’s death was no accident.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.

But God raised him from the dead. Key words. The great reversal, again (2:24; 3:15; 4:10).

And for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. Forty days (1:3).

Who are now his witnesses to the people. Paul, himself a witness of the risen Lord, points to the original witnesses too.

In a sentence. But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses.

For worship. But God raised him. Two words that change everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’

And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus. Key words. The gospel is the fulfilment of the Old Testament promises. Not a new religion, but the completion of the old.

As also it is written in the second Psalm, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you.” From Psalm 2:7, a coronation psalm for the king of David’s line, on the day he was enthroned. Paul applies it to the resurrection: the day God installed Jesus as king, declaring him Son with power (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God’s Son at the resurrection, as if he were not his Son before. He is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; 17:5). The resurrection publicly declared and installed him as the messianic Son and King. “Begotten” here is the language of royal enthronement.

In a sentence. Paul announced the good news that what God promised the fathers he has fulfilled for their children by raising Jesus, as the second Psalm says: you are my Son, today I have begotten you.

For worship. The risen Jesus is the King on David’s throne. Bow before the Son (Psalm 2:12).

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’

No more to return to corruption. Key words. Jesus will never die again (Romans 6:9). Unlike Lazarus.

I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David. From Isaiah 55:3, God’s everlasting covenant of steadfast love to David. The blessings promised to David are given to us through his risen Son. They are sure because he lives for ever.

You will not let your Holy One see corruption. Psalm 16:10, as Peter used it (2:27).

In a sentence. As for raising him from the dead never to decay, God said he would give them the holy and sure blessings of David, and in another psalm, that he would not let his Holy One see decay.

On a Tuesday. God’s blessings are sure because Christ lives for ever. Rest on them.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption.

For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation. Key words. A beautiful epitaph. David served God’s purpose in his own time. Every believer has a generation to serve. We can’t serve every age, but we can serve ours.

Fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption. David died and decayed. The psalm can’t be fully about him.

But he whom God raised up did not see corruption. Jesus did not. So the psalm is about Jesus.

In a sentence. David served God’s purpose in his generation, then died, was buried with his ancestors and decayed, but the one God raised did not see decay.

For worship. Serve God’s purpose in your own generation. That is your calling.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.

Through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you. Key words. The heart of the sermon. Forgiveness through Jesus, offered to you.

And by him everyone who believes is freed from everything. Key words. “Freed” (dikaioutai): justified, declared righteous. The first time Acts uses Paul’s great word. “Everyone who believes”: by faith alone. “From everything”: every sin, completely.

From which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. Key words. The law could not justify. It showed sin but could not remove it (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). The sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). What the law could not do, Christ does.

Where Christians differ: justification. Some teach that justification is a process in which faith and works, or faith and sacraments, together make us righteous. Verdict: Paul says everyone who believes is justified, declared righteous, from everything, through Christ, not by the law. Justification is God’s legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to us (Romans 4:5; 5:1; Philippians 3:9). Good works follow as fruit, not as ground.

In a sentence. Paul declared that through this man forgiveness of sins was proclaimed to them, and through him everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify them from.

For worship. Everyone who believes is justified from everything. Everything. Rejoice in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: ‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’

Beware, therefore. Paul ends with a warning, as Peter did (3:23).

Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish. Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians (Habakkuk 1:5), which Israel would not believe. Now God is doing an even more astonishing work: salvation through a crucified Messiah, and judgment on those who scoff at it.

For I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you. A warning against unbelief. The gospel is too wonderful for some to believe.

In a sentence. Paul warned them to beware that the prophets’ words not come true of them: look, you scoffers, marvel and perish, for God is doing a work in your days you would not believe even if told.

On a Tuesday. Don’t scoff at the gospel because it seems too simple or too good. Believe it.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.

The people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. Hungry for more.

Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas. Converts to Judaism are proselytes, Gentiles who had become Jews.

Who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. Key words. “Continue in the grace of God”: not in the law, not in their own efforts, but in grace. The Christian life begins and continues by grace (Galatians 5:4; Colossians 2:6).

In a sentence. As they left, the people asked them to speak again the next Sabbath, and after the meeting many Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, who urged them to continue in the grace of God.

For worship. Continue in the grace of God. You began by grace; go on by grace.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.

The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. Key words. The news spread through the week. Gentiles flooded the synagogue.

But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy. Jealousy again (5:17). Perhaps that Gentiles were being welcomed without becoming Jews; perhaps at Paul’s popularity.

And began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. “Reviling” (blasphēmountes): blaspheming, slandering. Opposing the word of the Lord.

In a sentence. The next Sabbath almost the whole city came to hear the Lord’s word, but when the Jews saw the crowds, they became jealous and contradicted what Paul said, abusing him.

On a Tuesday. Beware of jealousy when God blesses others, even outsiders. It is the opposite of love.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’”

It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Key words. To the Jew first: God’s order (Romans 1:16). Israel had the first right to the gospel.

Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life. Key words. “Thrust aside”: the word Stephen used of Israel rejecting Moses (7:27, 39). They judged themselves. God didn’t shut them out; they shut themselves out.

Behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. Not abandoning Jews everywhere; in the next city, they go to the synagogue again (14:1). But here, they turn.

I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth. From Isaiah 49:6. The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out by Christ through his messengers. Simeon applied it to the baby Jesus (Luke 2:32). The apostles share the Servant’s mission.

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas answered boldly that they had to speak God’s word to them first, but since they rejected it and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, they were turning to the Gentiles, as the Lord commanded: I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.

For worship. The light of Christ is for every nation. Shine it where you are.
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.

When the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord. Joy at being included.

And as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Key words. One of the clearest statements of election in Scripture. “Appointed” (tetagmenoi): ordained, assigned, a perfect passive participle, meaning they had been appointed already, by God. Luke doesn’t say “as many as believed were appointed,” but “as many as were appointed believed.” God’s appointment came first; their faith followed as its result. Those who rejected the word judged themselves unworthy (v. 46); those who believed did so because God had appointed them to life. Both are true.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians read this as “disposed to” eternal life, by their own inclination, or say God appointed those he foresaw would believe. Verdict: the passive voice points to an outside agent, God; and the word is used elsewhere of being appointed by authority (Romans 13:1, “instituted”). God’s sovereign choice is the cause of faith (Ephesians 1:4–5; John 6:37). It is a reason for joy and humility, not pride: they believed because grace chose them. And it fuels mission: God has his people in every city, waiting to hear (18:10).

And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. Election never stops evangelism; it powers it.

In a sentence. When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and honoured the Lord’s word, and all who were appointed to eternal life believed, and the word of the Lord spread through the whole region.

For worship. If you believe, it is because God appointed you to eternal life. Bow in gratitude, and go tell others.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.

But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city. Influential God-fearing women, wives of city officials, persuaded to act through their husbands.

Stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. Persecution follows fruitfulness. Perhaps this is when Paul was beaten with rods (2 Timothy 3:11; 2 Corinthians 11:25).

But they shook off the dust from their feet against them. Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to its own responsibility, as Jesus commanded (Luke 9:5; 10:11). Jews did this when returning from Gentile lands. A solemn warning.

And went to Iconium. About ninety miles east. Persecution moves the gospel on (8:4).

In a sentence. But the Jews stirred up devout, prominent women and the city’s leading men, started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of the region, so they shook the dust off their feet as a warning and went to Iconium.

On a Tuesday. When doors close, move on. God has other doors open.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment. Iconium lay about 80 miles to the east.

parallels.desc: persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. Key words. The new believers, left behind without their teachers, in a hostile city, are filled with joy. Persecution couldn’t take it away (John 16:22). The Spirit gives joy in suffering (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The apostles left, but the Spirit stayed.

In a sentence. The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

For worship. The Spirit gives joy no one can take away. Ask him to fill you.

parallels.desc: joy of the Holy Spirit in much affliction

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The first missionary journey continues through the cities of southern Galatia, in the heart of modern Turkey, and the pattern of chapter 13 repeats: preaching in the synagogue, many believing, opposition, and moving on. At Iconium a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, and the Lord confirms the message with signs, but the city divides and a plot to stone the apostles drives them to Lystra and Derbe, small towns in the district of Lycaonia. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd, shouting in their local language, decide that the gods Zeus and Hermes have come down in human form. A Roman poet, Ovid, tells a local legend that the two gods once visited this region in disguise and were turned away by everyone except an old couple; the people of Lystra were not going to make that mistake again. The priest of Zeus brings bulls and garlands to sacrifice, and Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes in horror and rush into the crowd. In a short sermon Paul tells these pagans about the living God, Creator of heaven and earth, who in past ages let the nations go their own way but left evidence of his goodness in rain, harvests and gladness.

Opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, turn the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead, but he gets up and goes back in, and the next day leaves for Derbe. After making many disciples there, Paul and Barnabas courageously retrace their steps through the cities that had persecuted them, strengthening the believers, warning that we must enter God’s kingdom through many hardships, and appointing elders in every church with prayer and fasting. Finally they sail back to Syrian Antioch and report to the church all that God had done, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Iconium Paul and Barnabas spoke so effectively in the synagogue that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. But Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the believers. The apostles stayed a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirmed his message of grace by enabling them to do signs and wonders. The city was divided, and when Gentiles and Jews with their leaders plotted to mistreat and stone them, they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding country, and kept preaching the gospel. At Lystra sat a man lame from birth who had never walked. He listened to Paul, who looked at him, saw he had faith to be healed, and called out to him to stand up on his feet. He jumped up and began to walk. When the crowd saw this, they shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form. They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he did the speaking. The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the gates, wanting to offer sacrifices with the crowd. When Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting that they were only human, like them, bringing good news that they should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them. In the past he let all nations go their own way, yet he did not leave himself without testimony: he showed kindness by giving rain and crops in their seasons, and filled them with food and joy. Even with these words they had difficulty stopping the crowd from sacrificing to them. Then Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead. But after the disciples gathered round him, he got up and went back into the city, and the next day left with Barnabas for Derbe. They preached there and made many disciples, then returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, urging them to remain true to the faith, and telling them that we must go through many hardships to enter God’s kingdom. They appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord in whom they had put their trust. After passing through Pisidia they came into Pamphylia, preached in Perga, went down to Attalia and sailed back to Antioch, where they had been commended to God’s grace for the work they had now completed. On arriving they gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they stayed there a long time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city, and left for Derbe the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.
