Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling made money for her owners, who drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them, as Jews, of disturbing the city with un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and put in the stocks in the inner prison. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors and loosens everyone’s chains. The jailer, about to kill himself, cries out, “What must I do to be saved?” and is told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and he rejoices that he has come to believe in God. In the morning, when the magistrates order their release, Paul reveals that they are Roman citizens, beaten without trial, and insists that the officials come and escort them out, protecting the young church before he leaves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Lystra Paul found a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers there and in Iconium. Paul wanted to take him on the journey, so he circumcised him because of the Jews in the area, who all knew his father was Greek. As they travelled from town to town, they delivered the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in numbers. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they reached the border of Mysia and tried to enter Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them, so they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them. After the vision, Luke writes, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. From Troas we sailed straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a Roman colony and leading city of that district of Macedonia, and stayed there several days. On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down to speak to the women who had gathered. One of them was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, a worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and her household had been baptised, she invited us to stay at her house if we considered her a believer in the Lord, and she persuaded us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit's Direction of Mission

The second missionary journey is notable for the Spirit's specific prevention and redirection: 'they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them' to go to Bithynia. The door to Europe opens only because two Asian doors close. Reformed missiology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over missional geography: the Spirit is not merely the empowerer of human initiative but the director of the mission's course. The church's task is to be obedient to both open doors and closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia's household was the first European church — gathered in a businesswoman's home around the word of God and the Lord's Supper. Now: The church continues to be built wherever the Lord opens hearts — in homes as often as in purpose-built buildings, through business relationships as often as through formal religious programs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium.

Meaning first. Acts 16 tells how the gospel crossed into Europe. Paul gains a young helper, Timothy. The Spirit closes doors in Asia and Bithynia, and opens one in a vision: Come over to Macedonia. In Philippi three very different people are saved: Lydia, a wealthy businesswoman whose heart the Lord opened; a slave girl freed from a spirit; and a Roman jailer who asks, What must I do to be saved? Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing at midnight, and see God shake the prison. Every kind of person, every kind of bondage, and one answer: Believe in the Lord Jesus.

A disciple was there, named Timothy. Key words. Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois, both believers, who taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). He became Paul’s closest co-worker, his “true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2), and received two letters. Probably converted during Paul’s first visit, when Paul was stoned (2 Timothy 3:10–11).

The son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. A mixed marriage. His father, a Gentile, apparently did not believe and had not let his son be circumcised.

He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. A good reputation, a qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:7).

In a sentence. Paul came to Derbe and Lystra, where there was a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers in Lystra and Iconium.

On a Tuesday. Mothers and grandmothers, teach your children the Scriptures. God may make a Timothy of them.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him. To replace John Mark as helper.

And he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. Key words. Surprising, right after the council. But the reason is not salvation; it is mission. Jews regarded the son of a Jewish mother as Jewish. An uncircumcised Jew would be seen as an apostate, and would close synagogue doors to Paul. Paul became a Jew to the Jews to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The difference with Titus. Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Titus was a Gentile, and the gospel was at stake. Timothy was ethnically Jewish, and circumcision was a matter of removing an obstacle. The same act can be right or wrong depending on why it is done. When circumcision is demanded as a condition of grace, refuse; when it is chosen to open a door, it can be freedom (1 Corinthians 7:19).

In a sentence. Paul wanted Timothy to go with him, and circumcised him because of the Jews in that area, who all knew his father was a Greek.

For worship. Never compromise the gospel. But be willing to give up your rights to win others.
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.

They delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders. “Decisions” (dogmata): the council’s decrees. The same Paul who circumcised Timothy delivered the letter that freed Gentiles from circumcision. No contradiction: grace for salvation, love for fellowship.

So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. Key words. Another progress report (6:7; 9:31). Strength and growth together. Clear teaching about grace strengthens churches.

In a sentence. As they went through the towns, they passed on the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in number.

On a Tuesday. Churches grow strong when they understand grace. Teach it clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. Key words. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its capital. Not the continent. Why forbidden? Not that God didn’t care for Asia; Paul would later spend three years in Ephesus (19:10). It was not yet the time. We aren’t told how the Spirit forbade them: a prophecy, an inner conviction, circumstances.

They attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Bithynia, in the north. “The Spirit of Jesus”: a unique phrase, showing that the Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus (Romans 8:9; Philippians 1:19). Jesus directs his mission by his Spirit.

Closed doors. Paul and his team didn’t sit and wait. They kept moving, and the Spirit closed doors. God guides moving feet. A closed door is guidance too.

In a sentence. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, since the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia, and when they reached Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.

On a Tuesday. When God closes a door, trust him. He is leading you somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.

So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy. They had come as far as they could go. The sea was before them. Perhaps they were puzzled. God had a plan.

In a sentence. So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.

For worship. When you reach the end of your road, God has a way you haven’t seen.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

A man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” Key words. Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, the gospel’s first entry into Europe. The cry for help: the world’s deepest need, though it doesn’t know it, is the gospel.

Immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia. Key words. “We”: the first of the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), where Luke joins the story as an eyewitness. Luke may have joined Paul at Troas, perhaps as his doctor.

Concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. “Concluding” (symbibazontes): putting it together. The closed doors, the vision, and the team’s discernment together showed God’s will. Guidance is often confirmed by putting the pieces together, with others.

In a sentence. In the night Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them, and after this vision they immediately set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had called them to preach the gospel there.

For worship. The world is crying, “Come and help us.” Answer with the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days.

We made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis. A quick crossing with a following wind, two days. (The return trip took five, 20:6.) Neapolis was Philippi’s port.

And from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. Key words. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled by veterans, a little Rome abroad, proud of Roman law and citizenship. Named after Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. Paul later wrote to the church here: our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), a phrase they would understand.

In a sentence. Sailing from Troas, they went straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a leading city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony, where they stayed some days.

On a Tuesday. You are a citizen of heaven living in a colony on earth. Live by its laws.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.

And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer. There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open by the river. A synagogue needed ten Jewish men; Philippi didn’t have them. The River Gangites, west of the city.

And we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. Key words. The first gospel preaching in Europe was to a women’s prayer meeting by a river. Paul, the former Pharisee, sat down and taught women. The gospel honours women.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate to the river, where they expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down and spoke to the women gathered there.

For worship. Great things can begin in small prayer meetings. Don’t despise them.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us.

A woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods. Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury for the wealthy. Lydia was a businesswoman, probably well off, with a house large enough to host the team and the church (v. 40). Thyatira was in the province of Asia, where the Spirit had forbidden them to preach; now an Asian is converted in Europe.

Who was a worshiper of God. A God-fearing Gentile.

The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. Key words. One of the clearest statements of God’s work in conversion. Paul spoke; the Lord opened. Paul could reach her ears; only the Lord could open her heart. This is effectual grace: God opens hearts to receive the gospel (2 Corinthians 4:6; Ephesians 1:18). Lydia did pay attention, really, freely; but she did so because the Lord opened her heart. Both human preaching and divine opening are needed.

And after she was baptized, and her household as well. Her household: servants, and perhaps children.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as including infants, and so supporting infant baptism. Verdict: no infants are mentioned in any household baptism in Acts. In the jailer’s case, the word was spoken to all in the house and the whole household believed and rejoiced (vv. 32, 34). In Cornelius’s, all heard and received the Spirit (10:44). The households baptised were households who heard and believed. Credobaptists hold this charitably, respecting brothers and sisters who read it differently.

If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay. Faith shows itself at once in hospitality. The first church in Europe met in her home.

In a sentence. One of the listeners was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira who worshipped God, and the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message, and after she and her household were baptised, she urged them to stay at her home if they judged her faithful to the Lord, and persuaded them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Lord to open hearts as you speak. You can reach ears; only he can reach hearts.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A slave girl whose fortune-telling earned money for her owners follows the missionaries for days, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God, until Paul casts the spirit out of her in Jesus’ name. Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them as Jews of promoting un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens every door and loosens every chain. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul, falls before them and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and speak the word to his whole household. He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and they rejoice together over a meal. In the morning Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the alarmed magistrates come in person to escort them out. After encouraging the believers at Lydia’s house, they leave.
verseByVerse.theology:
Midnight Praise and the Ministry of Suffering

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight — after being stripped and beaten with rods — and the other prisoners listen. The praise is not despite the suffering but in it: the same Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship. Reformed theology sees in this midnight scene the confirmation of what Paul will later write: 'we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance' (Romans 5:3). The songs at midnight are the most powerful proclamation the prisoners that night will ever hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked 'What must I do to be saved?' — the question of Pentecost (2:37) repeated in a Philippian prison. The answer is the same: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' Now: The gospel's answer to the question of salvation is always the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.”

A slave girl who had a spirit of divination. Key words. The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python,” linked with the Python, the serpent of Apollo’s oracle at Delphi. People believed such girls spoke Apollo’s messages. She was possessed by a demon.

And brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. Exploited twice over: by a demon, and by her owners.

These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation. True words, as demons spoke true words about Jesus (Mark 1:24; 5:7). But “the Most High God” could mean Zeus to pagans, and “a way of salvation,” one among many. Endorsement from a demon is no help to the gospel; it confuses the message, linking it with the occult.

In a sentence. On the way to the place of prayer they met a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who made her owners a lot of money by fortune-telling, and she followed Paul and the others, shouting that these men were servants of the Most High God telling them the way of salvation.

For worship. Christ needs no help from the occult. Keep the gospel clear and pure.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python” — linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.

And this she kept doing for many days. Paul waited before acting.

Paul, having become greatly annoyed. “Greatly annoyed” (diaponētheis): troubled, distressed, worn out. Perhaps at the confusion, and for the girl.

I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. Key words. Paul speaks to the spirit, not the girl. In the name of Jesus Christ: by his authority. Jesus’ name is stronger than Apollo’s python.

And it came out that very hour. At once. The girl was set free. We don’t hear what became of her, but perhaps she joined the church that met at Lydia’s.

In a sentence. She kept this up for many days, until Paul, greatly troubled, turned and commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her, and it came out at once.

On a Tuesday. The name of Jesus is above every power of darkness. Fear no spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.

But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone. Key words. A play on words: “gone” (exēlthen) is the same verb as the spirit “came out” in v. 18. When the spirit went out, their profit went out with it. They cared more for money than for the girl’s freedom. The gospel threatens those who profit from evil (19:25–27).

They seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. Paul and Silas, the leaders, and both Jews. Timothy and Luke, perhaps looking Greek, were left alone.

These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city. An appeal to prejudice. Anti-Jewish feeling was common; the emperor Claudius had recently expelled Jews from Rome (18:2).

In a sentence. When her owners saw their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace, telling the magistrates these Jews were throwing their city into confusion.

For worship. When the gospel threatens profit, expect resistance. Stand firm.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.

They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice. Key words. A legal charge. Romans were not supposed to adopt foreign religions without permission, especially by converting from the state gods. The real reason (money) is hidden behind a respectable one (religion and patriotism).

In a sentence. They said these men promoted customs that Romans were not allowed to accept or practise.

On a Tuesday. When people oppose the gospel, the stated reason is often not the real one.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely.

The crowd joined in attacking them. Mob justice.

And the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors, who carried bundles of rods as a sign of authority. Paul was beaten with rods three times (2 Corinthians 11:25). No trial, no hearing.

And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison. Bloodied, bruised, and locked up.

Ordering the jailer to keep them safely. Securely, on pain of his own life.

In a sentence. The crowd joined the attack, and the magistrates had their clothes torn off and ordered them beaten with rods, and after a severe beating threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to guard them carefully.

For worship. The servants of Christ were beaten for setting a slave free. Remember the persecuted church.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

He put them into the inner prison. The most secure cell, probably windowless, damp and dark.

And fastened their feet in the stocks. Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet, sometimes stretched wide apart to cause pain. With their backs torn open, they could not lie down comfortably.

In a sentence. With these orders, he put them in the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

On a Tuesday. Some of God’s greatest works begin in the darkest places.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened.

About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God. Key words. Not groaning or complaining, but praying and singing. In pain, in chains, in the dark, at midnight. Joy in suffering (5:41; Philippians 4:4, written later to this church). Perhaps they sang Psalms.

And the prisoners were listening to them. “Listening” (epēkroōnto): listening intently. Their singing was a witness. Prisoners had never heard anything like it.

And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. God’s answer (4:31).

And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. Not just theirs, everyone’s. A picture of the gospel: Christ frees the prisoners (Luke 4:18).

In a sentence. About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God while the prisoners listened, and suddenly a great earthquake shook the prison’s foundations, and at once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose.

On a Tuesday. Sing in your midnight. Others are listening.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.”

He drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty (12:19). Suicide was considered more honourable than execution in Roman culture.

But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” Key words. Paul cares for the man who chained him. And the prisoners didn’t run. Perhaps Paul’s and Silas’s example held them. Love for an enemy.

In a sentence. When the jailer woke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped, but Paul shouted for him not to harm himself, for they were all there.

For worship. Love your enemies. Paul did, in a prison cell, with a bleeding back.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

Trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Shaken by the earthquake, by his near death, and by the presence of God.

Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” Key words. The greatest question anyone can ask. He may have heard the slave girl’s words, “the way of salvation” (v. 17), or the hymns. The earthquake had shaken more than the prison; it shook his soul. He knew he needed saving, from more than Roman punishment.

In a sentence. The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas, then brought them out and asked what he must do to be saved.

On a Tuesday. Has this question gripped you? It is the most important question you will ever ask.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. Key words. The simplest, clearest statement of the gospel in Acts. Not “do,” but “believe.” Not circumcision, not law-keeping, not penance, not good works. Trust in the Lord Jesus. “The Lord Jesus”: Jesus as Lord, not merely as teacher. Salvation is by faith alone, in Christ alone.

You and your household. Not that his faith would save his family automatically, but that the same offer was open to them on the same terms. They too must believe, and did (v. 34). The word was spoken to all of them (v. 32).

In a sentence. They answered that he should believe in the Lord Jesus and he would be saved, he and his household.

For worship. Believe in the Lord Jesus. That is the whole answer, then and now.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family.

And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. They explained the gospel more fully, to everyone.

And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds. Key words. The change is immediate. The man who fastened them in the stocks now washes their wounds. He washed their stripes; they washed him in baptism. Repentance shows itself in deeds.

And he was baptized at once, he and all his family. In the middle of the night. No delay.

In a sentence. They spoke the word of the Lord to him and all in his household, and at that hour of the night he washed their wounds, and he and all his family were baptised at once.

On a Tuesday. True faith changes behaviour at once. What has Christ changed in you?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God.

Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. Hospitality, like Lydia’s. Fellowship at table between a Roman jailer and two Jewish prisoners.

And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. Key words. Joy, again. The whole household rejoiced, because all had believed. His despair at midnight became joy before dawn.

Three conversions. In Philippi, God saved a wealthy Asian businesswoman, a poor Greek slave girl, and a Roman jailer. Different nations, classes, sexes, and needs. One gospel, one church. Paul later wrote: there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28).

In a sentence. He brought them into his house and gave them food, and he and his whole household rejoiced that he had come to believe in God.

For worship. The gospel turns midnight despair into morning joy. Rejoice in your salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.”

But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” “Police” (rhabdouchous): rod-bearers, the lictors who had beaten them. Perhaps the earthquake had frightened the magistrates, or they thought a night in prison was enough.

Come out now and go in peace. The jailer’s farewell: go in peace, now spoken as a brother.

In a sentence. At daybreak the magistrates sent their officers to release them, and the jailer told Paul they could leave and go in peace.

For worship. God turned the hearts of the rulers overnight. He rules over rulers.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.”

They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens. Key words. Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial. The Porcian and Valerian laws protected citizens from such punishment. The magistrates had committed a serious crime. Why didn’t Paul say so earlier? Perhaps he did, and wasn’t heard in the uproar; or perhaps he chose to suffer for Christ first.

And do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out. Not pride or revenge, but protection for the new church. A public acknowledgment that they had been wronged would protect the believers in Philippi from similar treatment. Christians may use their legal rights for the sake of the gospel and the church (22:25; 25:11).

In a sentence. But Paul said they had been beaten publicly without trial, though they were Roman citizens, and thrown into prison, and now the magistrates wanted to get rid of them secretly; no, let the magistrates come and escort them out themselves.

On a Tuesday. Christians may use their legal rights, not for revenge, but to protect others and the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city.

They were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. They could lose their positions, or worse.

So they came and apologized to them. Key words. A public apology. The church in Philippi was protected.

And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. Asked, not ordered.

In a sentence. When the officers reported this, the magistrates were alarmed to hear they were Roman citizens, came and apologised, escorted them out and asked them to leave the city.

For worship. God can vindicate his servants publicly. Leave your vindication to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.

So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. To the church in her house.

And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed. Key words. The beaten men encourage the others, not the other way round. The church at Philippi became one of Paul’s most loving and generous churches (Philippians 1:3–5; 4:15–16). Luke seems to have stayed behind: the “we” stops here and resumes at Philippi in 20:5.

In a sentence. They left the prison and went to Lydia’s house, and after seeing and encouraging the believers, they departed.

On a Tuesday. Those who suffer for Christ can encourage others. Let your trials become someone else’s strength.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual Calling and the Opened Heart. Acts 16:14 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of what the Reformed tradition calls effectual calling: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” The Word is preached by Paul; the heart is opened by the Lord. Both acts are real and necessary. Without Paul’s preaching, Lydia has no content to respond to. Without the Lord’s opening of her heart, Paul’s words remain external noise. The Spirit works through the Word, but the Spirit’s work is the decisive one — the inward illumination that turns external proclamation into saving faith. This is why prayer for the lost must accompany every act of evangelism: we can preach; only God can open hearts.
16.examples:
Then: A purple-goods merchant, a slave girl, a Roman jailer — three people who could not have been more different in status, ethnicity, or circumstance — all met by one gospel in one city. The Philippian church is born from this unlikely trio, and Paul will write his most joyful letter to it from a prison cell a dozen years later.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts today. The Spirit who directed Paul away from Asia and toward Macedonia still directs his church. The closed doors are guidance; the midnight songs are witness; the simplest answer is still the truest: believe in the Lord Jesus. The gospel has not grown more complicated. We have.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Leaving Philippi, Paul and Silas travel west along the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway, to Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia and a busy port. For three Sabbaths Paul reasons in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and a number of leading women believe. Jealous opponents gather a mob, and when they cannot find Paul they drag his host Jason before the city officials, accusing the believers of turning the world upside down and defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Paul and Silas slip away by night to Berea, where the Jews receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to check what Paul says. Opponents from Thessalonica follow, and Paul is sent on to Athens.

Athens was no longer politically powerful, but it was still the intellectual capital of the Greek world, the city of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, crowded with temples and statues. Paul is distressed at so many idols. He reasons in the synagogue and in the marketplace, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dismiss him as a babbler, and is brought before the Areopagus, the ancient council that met on the Hill of Ares. His speech is a model of preaching to people without the Bible. He begins from an altar inscribed “to an unknown god”: the God they do not know is the Creator of everything, who does not live in temples or need anything from us, who made all nations from one man and set their times and places so that they would seek him, and who is not far from any of us; even their own poets said we are his offspring. So God cannot be like an image of gold or stone. He overlooked their ignorance in the past, but now commands everyone everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed, and has proved it by raising him from the dead. At the mention of resurrection some laugh, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including a member of the council, Dionysius, and a woman named Damaris.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Thessalonica Paul spends three Sabbaths in the synagogue showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believe, but jealous opponents start a riot, drag Paul’s host Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Released on bond, the believers send Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where the Jews are more open-minded, receiving the message eagerly and checking it daily against the Scriptures, and many believe. When opponents arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stay behind for a time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean Standard for Scripture Engagement

The Bereans 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.' Reformed theology has always prized this as the model of how the gospel should be received: not credulity (accepting whatever the preacher says without examination) and not skepticism (dismissing the gospel without engagement), but eager reception combined with rigorous scriptural testing. The Berean standard is the Protestant hermeneutical ideal: sola Scriptura applied in the actual practice of hearing and evaluating proclamation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'These men who have turned the world upside down' — the Thessalonian accusation is the most accurate description of the gospel's social effect in Acts. Now: The gospel still turns every human order that opposes the kingdom upside down. The question for the church is not whether the gospel is socially disruptive but whether it is disrupting the right things — the powers of sin, death, and injustice — rather than merely producing comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,

Meaning first. Acts 17 shows Paul preaching in three very different cities. In Thessalonica he reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise; a church is born and a riot follows. In Berea the Jews examine the Scriptures daily to test his message. In Athens, the intellectual capital of the world, he speaks to philosophers about the Creator God who does not live in temples, who calls all people to repent, and who will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead. One gospel, adapted wisely to Jews, God-fearers and pagan philosophers.

They came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road east to west. A strategic city. Paul later wrote two letters to the church there.

And Paul went in, as was his custom. His regular practice: to the synagogue first.

And on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures. Key words. “Reasoned” (dielexato): discussed, argued, dialogued. Not just a monologue, but engagement with questions. “From the Scriptures”: the Old Testament was the common ground. Christian preaching is reasonable; it appeals to the mind as well as the heart.

In a sentence. After passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue, and Paul went in as usual and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures.

On a Tuesday. Faith is reasonable. Be ready to reason with people from Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”

Explaining and proving. Key words. “Explaining” (dianoigōn): opening up, as Jesus opened the Scriptures to the disciples on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:32). “Proving” (paratithemenos): setting beside, laying out the evidence.

That it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead. Two steps. First: from Scripture, the Messiah must suffer and rise (Isaiah 53; Psalm 16; Psalm 22). Most Jews expected a conquering Messiah, not a suffering one.

This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ. Second: Jesus fits. He suffered and rose. Therefore he is the Messiah. A model of preaching: from Scripture to Christ.

In a sentence. He explained and showed that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and said that this Jesus he was proclaiming is the Messiah.

For worship. The Scriptures point to a suffering and risen Christ. Read them with Jesus in view.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.

And some of them were persuaded. Persuasion: God uses argument.

As did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. God-fearers, and prominent women. Paul’s letters show many Gentiles converted from idols (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

But the Jews were jealous. Jealousy again (13:45).

Taking some wicked men of the rabble. Literally “marketplace men”: loafers, thugs for hire.

They formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason. Jason was probably Paul’s host. Perhaps the Jason of Romans 16:21.

In a sentence. Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did many God-fearing Greeks and a number of prominent women, but the jealous Jews gathered some bad characters from the marketplace, formed a mob, started a riot and attacked Jason’s house, looking for Paul and Silas.

On a Tuesday. When the gospel bears fruit, expect opposition. And thank God for the Jasons who open their homes.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”

They dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities. The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica but nowhere in ancient literature. Critics once said Luke made it up. Inscriptions proved him exactly right.

These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also. Key words. A charge, and a compliment. The gospel turns the world the right way up. In a few years, the message had spread so widely that its enemies spoke of the whole world.

And they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus. Key words. A dangerous charge: treason. And true, in a sense. Jesus is King, the King of kings. Not a political rival to Caesar in the world’s way (John 18:36), but Lord over Caesar too. The early Christians refused to say “Caesar is Lord”; they said “Jesus is Lord.”

In a sentence. Not finding them, they dragged Jason and some believers before the city officials, shouting that these men who had turned the world upside down had come here, that Jason had welcomed them, and that they were defying Caesar’s decrees by saying there is another king, Jesus.

For worship. Jesus is King. Caesar isn’t. Live as a subject of the true King.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things.

And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. Treason was serious. The emperor Claudius was suspicious of disturbances among Jews (18:2). The city could lose its privileges as a free city.

In a sentence. The crowd and the city officials were thrown into turmoil by these accusations.

On a Tuesday. The claim that Jesus is King still disturbs. It should.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue.

When they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. A bond, guaranteeing good behaviour, probably that Paul would leave and not return. Perhaps this is the hindrance Satan put in Paul’s way to return (1 Thessalonians 2:18).

The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica, off the main road, a quieter town.

And when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. Undaunted, again to the synagogue.

In a sentence. After taking a bond from Jason and the others, the officials released them, and the believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where they went into the synagogue.

For worship. Persecution didn’t stop Paul; it only moved him. Keep going.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men.

Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica. Key words. “Noble” (eugenesteroi): open-minded, of noble character. Not by birth, but by attitude.

They received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Key words. Two things together: eagerness and examination. Not credulous, not cynical. Open to the message, but testing it by Scripture. “Examining” (anakrinontes): investigating, as in a court. Daily: not once, but persistently. Even Paul, an apostle, was tested by Scripture, and they were praised for it.

Where Christians differ: the final authority. Some say the church or tradition must interpret Scripture for the believer, and that individuals should not test teachers. Verdict: the Bereans tested an apostle by Scripture, and Luke calls it noble. Scripture is the final authority by which every teaching is tested (Isaiah 8:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1). This is sola Scriptura: not that teachers and tradition are useless, but that Scripture judges them all.

Many of them therefore believed. “Therefore”: examination led to faith. Honest study of Scripture leads to Christ (John 5:39).

In a sentence. These Jews were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica, receiving the message eagerly and examining the Scriptures every day to see whether what Paul said was true, and so many of them believed, along with a number of prominent Greek women and men.

On a Tuesday. Be a Berean. Receive the word eagerly, and test everything you hear, including this, by Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there.

The Jews from Thessalonica... came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Determined opposition, fifty miles away.

Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea. Paul was the main target.

But Silas and Timothy remained there. To strengthen the new believers.

In a sentence. When the Jews of Thessalonica learned Paul was preaching God’s word in Berea, they came and stirred up the crowds, so the believers sent Paul away to the coast at once, while Silas and Timothy stayed.

For worship. The gospel’s enemies are persistent. Be more persistent in the good.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed.

Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, home of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. By Paul’s day past its political glory, but still a famous university city, full of philosophers and temples.

After receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible. Paul didn’t like to be alone.

In a sentence. Those escorting Paul brought him to Athens, and left with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.

On a Tuesday. Even Paul needed companions. Don’t try to serve alone.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city’s idols and reasons daily in the synagogue and the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers mock him as a babbler of foreign gods, because he speaks of Jesus and the resurrection, and they bring him before the Areopagus to explain himself. Paul starts from an altar dedicated “to an unknown god”. The God they do not know made everything, lives in no temple, needs nothing, and gives life and breath to all. He made every nation from one man and arranged their times and places so that people would seek him, though he is near to each of us, as their own poets said. So he cannot be represented by images of gold or stone. He has overlooked past ignorance, but now commands everyone to repent, because he has fixed a day of judgement by the man he appointed and raised from the dead. Some mock at the mention of resurrection, others want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius of the council and a woman named Damaris.
verseByVerse.theology:
Natural Theology and Its Limits

Paul's Areopagus address is the New Testament's most extended engagement with natural theology — the knowledge of God available through creation. He acknowledges that God has not left himself without witness (14:17), that all nations are made from one blood and live in God-given boundaries (17:26), that the divine nature is reflected in creation sufficiently to leave humanity without excuse (Romans 1:20). But natural theology has limits: it can establish God's existence and general character; it cannot reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The movement from 'the God who made everything' to 'the man he has appointed' requires the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection; some said 'we will hear you again'; some believed. The three responses to the Areopagus address are the three responses to every gospel proclamation: dismissal, deferral, and faith. Now: The gospel continues to divide its hearers along these same three lines. The church's task is not to ensure the first response never comes but to preach in such a way that the third response is genuinely available to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.

His spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. Key words. “Provoked” (parōxyneto): stirred, distressed, angered. The same word as the sharp disagreement (15:39). Not admiring the art, but grieved at the idolatry. A Roman writer joked that in Athens it was easier to find a god than a man. Paul felt for God’s honour, and for the people.

So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons. As usual.

And in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with stalls, temples, and people debating. Socrates had taught there. Paul went where the people were.

In a sentence. While waiting for them in Athens, Paul was deeply distressed to see the city full of idols, so he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearers, and every day in the marketplace with whoever was there.

For worship. Let idolatry grieve you, and move you to speak. Go where people are.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities” — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. Setting and background. Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was pleasure, meaning tranquillity and freedom from pain and fear; there was no afterlife or judgment. Stoics taught that God was the reason in all things, and the aim of life was to live in harmony with nature and accept fate calmly, rising above emotions. Two great schools of the day.

What does this babbler wish to say? “Babbler” (spermologos): seed-picker, like a bird picking up scraps. One who picks up bits of ideas and passes them off as learning.

He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. Key words. They thought “Jesus” and “Resurrection” (Anastasis, a feminine word) were a god and goddess, a new divine couple. The same charge brought against Socrates: introducing new gods.

And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus. The Areopagus, “Hill of Ares” (Mars Hill), was both a hill and the ancient council that met there, which oversaw religion and education in Athens. Not a formal trial, but an examination.

In a sentence. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him, some calling him a babbler, others saying he seemed to preach foreign gods, because he preached Jesus and the resurrection, and they brought him to the Areopagus asking to know this new teaching.

On a Tuesday. You may be mocked for preaching Jesus and the resurrection. Keep preaching them; they are the heart of the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.

For you bring some strange things to our ears. “Strange” (xenizonta): foreign, surprising.

We wish to know therefore what these things mean. Curiosity, at least. An open door.

In a sentence. They said he was bringing strange ideas to their ears and they wanted to know what they meant.

For worship. Curiosity can be a doorway. Be ready to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new.

Would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. Key words. Luke’s wry comment. Athens loved novelty: ideas as entertainment. A danger for every generation: always learning and never coming to knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3:7; 4:3). The gospel is not a novelty; it is the truth.

In a sentence. All the Athenians and foreigners living there spent their time doing nothing but talking about or listening to the latest ideas.

On a Tuesday. Don’t treat the gospel as just another interesting idea. It calls for a response.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.

Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. Key words. “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious” (deisidaimonesterous). Paul starts respectfully, without mocking them, but without approving either.

I found also an altar with this inscription: “To the unknown god.” Ancient writers mention altars to unknown gods in Athens, set up to be sure no god was offended or left out. An admission that, for all their gods, they didn’t know the true one.

What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. Key words. Paul’s point of contact. Not that they worshipped the true God without knowing it, but that they admitted their ignorance. Paul will make the unknown God known. Their altar confessed that their religion was incomplete.

In a sentence. Paul stood in the Areopagus and said he could see the Athenians were very religious, for he had found an altar inscribed “To an unknown god,” and what they worshipped in ignorance he would now proclaim to them.

For worship. God is not unknown. He has made himself known in Christ. Tell others.
verseByVerse.note: “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious.” Ancient writers mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything.

The God who made the world and everything in it. Key words. Paul starts with creation, not with Scripture, which they didn’t know. Against the Epicureans’ distant gods and the Stoics’ impersonal reason, God is the personal Creator, distinct from the world. Against pantheism and materialism.

Being Lord of heaven and earth. Sovereign over all.

Does not live in temples made by man. Within sight of the Parthenon. As Stephen said (7:48).

Nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything. Key words. God is self-sufficient. He doesn’t need our sacrifices, our worship, or anything (Psalm 50:9–12). The Epicureans would agree, but Paul goes on.

Since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. We need him; he doesn’t need us. Everything is his gift.

In a sentence. Paul said the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in man-made temples or need human service, since he gives everyone life, breath and everything else.

On a Tuesday. God doesn’t need you. He gives you everything, including your next breath. Worship him for it.

parallels.desc: who gives breath to the people

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,

And he made from one man every nation of mankind. Key words. All humanity comes from one man, Adam (Genesis 1–2; Romans 5:12). A blow to Athenian pride: Athenians believed they sprang from the soil of Attica and were superior to all others. Every race is of one blood. This is the foundation of human equality and the end of racism.

Where Christians differ: one man. Some today regard Adam as a symbol rather than a historical person. Verdict: Paul here, and in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, treats Adam as a real man from whom all nations descend, and whose sin and death spread to all. The unity of the human race, and the gospel of the second Adam, rest on it.

Having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place. God’s providence rules history and geography: the times of nations and their borders (Deuteronomy 32:8).

That they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. “Feel their way” (psēlaphēseian): grope, as a blind man in the dark. Fallen humanity gropes for God but cannot find him by its own search (Romans 3:11). The purpose of providence is to lead people to seek God.

Yet he is actually not far from each one of us. God is near. The problem is not his distance, but our blindness.

In a sentence. From one man God made every nation to live on the whole earth, setting their times and boundaries, so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out and find him, though he is not far from any of us.

For worship. Every person on earth is your relative. Treat them as such.

parallels.desc: he fixed the borders of the peoples

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’
