In him we live and move and have our being. Probably from the Cretan poet Epimenides, about 600 BC, in a poem addressed to Zeus. Paul uses their own literature.

As even some of your own poets have said, “For we are indeed his offspring.” Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus, a Stoic poet from Cilicia, Paul’s home region, about 270 BC. Paul knew Greek literature, and used it as common ground.

What it does not mean. Paul is not endorsing Zeus or the poets’ theology. He takes true insights they had glimpsed, that we depend on God and are made in his image, and gives them their true meaning in the Creator God. All truth is God’s truth, wherever it is found. We are God’s offspring by creation, not by redemption; the latter comes only through Christ (John 1:12).

In a sentence. In God we live, move and exist, as some of their own poets had said, for we are his offspring.

On a Tuesday. Use common ground with unbelievers. But always lead from it to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides.

parallels.desc: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,

Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone. Key words. The logic: if we are made by God, God can’t be made by us. Idolatry is absurd. The child can’t make the parent. In the city of statues, Paul says: your gods are made by your hands.

An image formed by the art and imagination of man. Idols are human inventions.

The times of ignorance God overlooked. Not that he didn’t care, but that he held back judgment, in patience (14:16; Romans 3:25).

But now he commands all people everywhere to repent. Key words. “Now”: since Christ has come, the time of ignorance is over. “Commands”: not an invitation only, but an order. “All people everywhere”: universal. Philosophers too. Repentance is a change of mind about God and turning from idols to him (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

In a sentence. Since we are God’s offspring, we shouldn’t think God is like an image of gold, silver or stone made by human skill and imagination, and though God overlooked the times of ignorance, he now commands all people everywhere to repent.

For worship. God commands you to repent. Obey him today.

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.

Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness. Key words. Against the Epicureans, there is a judgment. Against the Stoics, history is not an endless cycle; it has an end, a fixed day. God will judge the whole world, justly.

By a man whom he has appointed. Jesus, though Paul doesn’t name him yet. The judge is a man, who knows what it is to be human (John 5:27).

And of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead. Key words. The resurrection is God’s proof. It shows Jesus is the appointed judge, and that judgment is coming. The resurrection is not just good news; it is a warning. The risen man will judge you.

In a sentence. For God has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed, and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.

On a Tuesday. The day of judgment is fixed on God’s calendar. Are you ready?

parallels.desc: he will judge the world in righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” So Paul went out from their midst.

Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. Key words. Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd. They believed the body was a prison for the soul, and the goal was to escape it. Aeschylus wrote, in a play set at the founding of this very council, that once a man dies there is no resurrection. The resurrection was the stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23; 15:12).

But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” Interested, or postponing.

So Paul went out from their midst. The speech was interrupted, as speeches often are in Acts. He had said enough.

In a sentence. When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some sneered, while others said they wanted to hear him again on this, and Paul left the council.

For worship. Don’t remove the resurrection to avoid mockery. It is the heart of the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.

But some men joined him and believed. Key words. Not many, but some. Some think Athens was a failure, and that Paul then decided to know nothing but Christ crucified in Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:2). But Luke presents it as a model speech with real fruit. Wise engagement with culture, and some believed.

Among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite. Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council, a man of high standing. Tradition says he became the first bishop of Athens.

And a woman named Damaris and others with them. We know nothing more of her. Named by Luke for ever.

In a sentence. But some men joined him and believed, including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others.

On a Tuesday. Measure faithfulness, not results. Some believed; that is enough.
verseByVerse.note: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council.

17.theology: General Revelation and the Necessity of the Gospel. Acts 17 contains the New Testament’s most developed account of what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God available to all humanity through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). Paul acknowledges the Athenians’ religious instinct as genuine — they are groping toward God. But groping is not finding. General revelation creates the question; the gospel alone provides the answer. The God who made all nations from one man, who determined their times and boundaries, who is not far from any of us — this God has now spoken definitively in a man he raised from the dead. The times of ignorance are over. The command is universal: all people everywhere must repent. General revelation without the gospel leaves no one saved; it only leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, spirit provoked, standing before the intellectual elite of the ancient world with nothing but the story of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mock. Some believe. He moves on. The church in Athens is small, but Dionysius and Damaris are there — and the gospel is in Europe to stay.

Now: The contemporary West is increasingly like Athens: intellectually sophisticated, spiritually restless, full of altars to unnamed gods, suspicious of exclusive truth claims. The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
From Athens Paul goes to Corinth, the wealthy, proud commercial city on the isthmus, capital of the province of Achaia (see the introduction to 1 Corinthians). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple recently expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, and works with them making tents. The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews because of riots “at the instigation of Chrestus”, probably disputes about Christ in the Jewish community, around AD 49. When Silas and Timothy arrive with support from Macedonia, Paul devotes himself fully to preaching. Opposed in the synagogue, he moves next door to the house of a God-fearer, Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus believes with his household, and many Corinthians are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul not to be afraid, because he has many people in this city, and Paul stays eighteen months.

When Jewish opponents bring Paul before the new proconsul, Gallio, he dismisses the case as a quarrel about Jewish words and names, not a Roman crime, a ruling that gave the church breathing space. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s year in office to about AD 51–52, one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. Paul then sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, leaves them there, and returns via Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch, completing his second journey. The third journey begins with a tour of the Galatian churches. Meanwhile an eloquent, learned Jew from Alexandria, Apollos, arrives in Ephesus, preaching accurately about Jesus but knowing only John’s baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and he goes on to Corinth, where he powerfully refutes the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, where he lodges and works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently expelled from Rome. He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath, and when Silas and Timothy arrive he gives himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Messiah. When the Jews oppose and abuse him, he shakes out his clothes and declares their blood is on their own heads; from now on he will go to the Gentiles. He moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearer. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his household believe, and many Corinthians believe and are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul to keep speaking without fear, for no one will harm him, and he has many people in this city. Paul stays a year and a half, teaching God’s word. Under the proconsul Gallio, the Jews bring Paul to court, accusing him of persuading people to worship God against the law, but Gallio refuses to judge questions of words, names and Jewish law and throws them out. The crowd beats Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, in front of the court, and Gallio does not care. After many days Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having had his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow. At Ephesus he reasons in the synagogue, but declines to stay longer, promising to return if God wills. He lands at Caesarea, greets the church in Jerusalem and goes down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — protected Paul's preaching at Corinth by treating it as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,

Meaning first. Acts 18 tells of Paul’s eighteen months in Corinth, a wealthy, immoral city, where he works with his hands, preaches in the synagogue and then next door to it, and is told by the Lord in a vision: I have many in this city who are my people. A Roman proconsul refuses to try him, setting a precedent of tolerance. Then the second journey ends, the third begins, and a gifted preacher named Apollos is taught the way of God more accurately by a married couple, Priscilla and Aquila. God’s work goes on through ordinary believers.

After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy port city on the narrow isthmus between two seas, known for trade and immorality. “To Corinthianise” meant to live immorally. The temple of Aphrodite stood above it. Paul later wrote two letters to the church there.

He found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla. Key words. A married couple who became Paul’s close friends and co-workers (Romans 16:3–5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). Priscilla (Prisca) is often named first, perhaps because she was more prominent or of higher social standing. They may already have been believers, from the church in Rome.

Because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting at the instigation of “Chrestus,” probably a garbled form of Christ, around AD 49. Disputes about Christ in the synagogues of Rome.

In a sentence. After this Paul left Athens for Corinth, where he met a Jew named Aquila from Pontus, recently arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome, and he went to see them.

On a Tuesday. God brings his people together through even the decrees of emperors. Your moves are in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy trading city with a reputation for immorality. The Roman historian Suetonius mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome over disturbances, around AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.

Because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. Key words. Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth, making tents, awnings and perhaps sails. Jewish teachers commonly learned a trade, so as not to make money from teaching the law. Paul supported himself, so as not to be a burden and to remove any suspicion that he preached for money (20:34; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8).

Where Christians differ: should ministers be paid? Some say ministers should always work a trade like Paul; others that the church must always support them. Verdict: Paul teaches that those who preach the gospel have a right to live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18), and he accepted gifts (Philippians 4:15–16; 2 Corinthians 11:8–9). But he sometimes gave up that right for the gospel’s sake. Both patterns are biblical. Churches should support their ministers generously; ministers may work when the work requires it.

In a sentence. Because he had the same trade, he stayed and worked with them, for they were tentmakers.

For worship. Ordinary work can serve the gospel. Do yours as for the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth. Jewish teachers commonly had a trade; Paul supported himself so as not to burden the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.

And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. Work during the week, preaching on the Sabbath.

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word. Key words. “Occupied” (syneicheto): wholly absorbed, pressed. Silas and Timothy brought gifts from the Macedonian churches (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15), so Paul could stop tentmaking and preach full-time. And good news from Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:6).

Testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. His constant theme.

In a sentence. Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks, and when Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.

On a Tuesday. Support those who preach, so they can give themselves to the word.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue.

And when they opposed and reviled him. “Reviled” (blasphēmountōn): blasphemed, insulting Christ.

He shook out his garments. Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility, like shaking off dust (13:51; Nehemiah 5:13).

Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. Key words. Ezekiel’s watchman language (Ezekiel 33:1–9). Paul had warned them; their blood was on them, not on him. A sobering view of the preacher’s responsibility: to warn. Paul used it again in Ephesus (20:26).

From now on I will go to the Gentiles. In Corinth, at least.

He left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. Right next door! A bold, perhaps provocative, choice. Some identify him with Gaius, Paul’s host in Corinth (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14).

In a sentence. When they opposed and insulted him, Paul shook out his clothes and told them their blood was on their own heads, he was innocent, and from then on he would go to the Gentiles, and he moved to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearer, next door to the synagogue.

For worship. Warn people faithfully. Then leave the result with God.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility.

parallels.desc: his blood shall be on his own head

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized.

Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. Key words. The leader of the synagogue that rejected Paul came over. One of the few Paul baptised himself (1 Corinthians 1:14). A great blow to the opposition, and a great joy.

And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. Hearing, believing, baptism: the order again. Paul later described the kind of people they had been: idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards; but you were washed (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

In a sentence. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord, and many Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptised.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond the gospel: synagogue rulers, or the worst sinners of Corinth.

parallels.desc: I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.”

Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent. Key words. Paul was afraid. He came to Corinth in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3). Beaten in Philippi, chased out of Thessalonica and Berea, mocked in Athens. Even the great apostle needed encouragement.

For I am with you. The promise of God to his servants throughout Scripture (Joshua 1:9; Jeremiah 1:8; Matthew 28:20).

And no one will attack you to harm you. Protection for this time.

For I have many in this city who are my people. Key words. Before they believed, they were already the Lord’s people. Corinth, wicked as it was, held many whom God had chosen. Not yet converted, but already his. This is election, and it is the greatest encouragement to evangelism. Paul preached not knowing who they were; God knew. The gospel would find them.

Where Christians differ: does election discourage evangelism? Some think that if God has chosen his people, there is no need to preach. Verdict: here election is the reason to keep preaching. God has his people; the gospel is the means by which they are called (Romans 10:14–17; 2 Timothy 2:10). Election guarantees that preaching will not be in vain.

In a sentence. One night the Lord told Paul in a vision not to be afraid but to keep speaking and not be silent, for the Lord was with him, no one would harm him, and he had many people in this city.

For worship. God has many people in your city who are his. Keep speaking; he will gather them.

parallels.desc: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. Key words. Eighteen months, his longest stay so far. Teaching: grounding the church. Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this time (1 Thessalonians 3:6).

In a sentence. He stayed a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.

For worship. Churches need patient teaching of God’s word. Sit under it gladly.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.”

But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia. Key words. An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52. This gives one of the firmest dates in Paul’s life, anchoring the chronology of his journeys and letters. Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca, tutor to Nero, and known for his charm.

The Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal. The tribunal (bēma), the judgment platform. Its remains still stand in the Corinth forum. Perhaps they hoped a new governor would favour them.

This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law. Which law? Roman law, permitting Judaism as a legal religion; or Jewish law. They wanted Rome to rule that Christianity was not Judaism and so illegal.

In a sentence. When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews united against Paul and brought him to the judgment seat, accusing him of persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.

On a Tuesday. The Bible is rooted in real history, with real names and dates. Your faith rests on facts.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52 — one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. The tribunal (bema) still stands in the Corinthian marketplace.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.”

But when Paul was about to open his mouth. Paul didn’t even need to defend himself.

If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. Gallio separates crime from religious opinion.

But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. Key words. Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a crime under Roman law. A crucial ruling: it meant Christianity was treated, for now, as a form of Judaism, a permitted religion. A senior Roman judge’s decision protected the gospel for years, until Nero. Luke records it partly to show Theophilus that Christianity was not a threat to Rome.

I refuse to be a judge of these things. Indifference, but useful indifference. God used it.

In a sentence. Before Paul could speak, Gallio told the Jews that if it were a crime he would hear them, but since it was a dispute about words, names and their own law, they must settle it themselves, for he would not judge such matters.

For worship. God can use even a pagan judge’s indifference to protect his church. He rules over courts.
verseByVerse.note: Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a Roman crime.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he drove them from the tribunal.

And he drove them from the tribunal. Dismissed them. Perhaps with his lictors. The case was thrown out.

In a sentence. He had them ejected from the court.

On a Tuesday. The Lord promised no one would harm Paul. He kept his word.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.

They all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. Probably Crispus’s successor, leader of the failed case. Who beat him? Perhaps Greeks, venting anti-Jewish feeling; or Jews, angry at his failure. A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer (1 Corinthians 1:1). If the same man, the beating led him to Christ.

But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. Indifference.

And then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. Heading home to Antioch.

At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port, where a church grew (Romans 16:1). The vow was probably a Nazirite-type vow of thanksgiving (Numbers 6:1–21), during which the hair was not cut. Paul, free from the law, still kept some Jewish customs voluntarily (21:23–26; 1 Corinthians 9:20). Freedom in Christ is freedom to keep customs too, when not for salvation.

In a sentence. Then they all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the court, but Gallio took no notice, and Paul stayed on some time, then said goodbye to the believers and sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having cut his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow.

For worship. Freedom in Christ means you may keep good customs, as long as you don’t trust them for salvation.
verseByVerse.note: A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port. Cutting the hair marked the end of a vow of special devotion.

parallels.desc: the Nazirite vow
Phoebe of Cenchreae

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.

And they came to Ephesus. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, the province where the Spirit had earlier forbidden Paul to preach (16:6). Now the door opens.

And he left them there. Priscilla and Aquila stayed, preparing the ground for Paul’s return.

But he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. As always.

When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. An open door, but not yet. Paul wanted to reach Jerusalem, perhaps for a feast.

In a sentence. When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there and went into the synagogue to reason with the Jews, and when they asked him to stay longer, he declined.

On a Tuesday. Not every open door is for now. Wait for God’s timing.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.

I will return to you if God wills. Key words. “If God wills”: Paul’s plans were always submitted to God (James 4:13–15; 1 Corinthians 4:19). Not a superstitious formula, but a humble acknowledgment. And God did will it (19:1).

When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church. “Went up”: to Jerusalem, the mother church.

And then went down to Antioch. Home to the sending church. The end of the second missionary journey, about three years and some 2,800 miles.

In a sentence. As he left them, he promised to return if God willed, and sailed from Ephesus to Caesarea, went up to greet the church in Jerusalem, and then went down to Antioch.

For worship. Make your plans, and add, “if God wills.” Mean it.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After some time in Antioch, Paul set out on his third journey and travelled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a learned man with a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and spoke with great fervour, teaching accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him to their home and explained to him the way of God more adequately. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On arriving, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed, for he vigorously refuted his Jewish opponents in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping short of the full apostolic message — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

After spending some time there, he departed. Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey, around AD 53. It will centre on Ephesus.

And went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. Key words. Visiting the churches founded on the first journey. “Strengthening”: the pastoral heart of an apostle (14:22; 15:41).

In a sentence. After some time in Antioch, Paul set out and travelled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen those who follow Christ. Visit, encourage, teach.
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.

Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria. Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community, home of the philosopher Philo and of the Greek translation of the Old Testament.

He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. Key words. “Eloquent” (logios): learned, articulate. “Competent” (dynatos): powerful, mighty in the Scriptures. A gifted preacher. Some in Corinth later preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6). Some have suggested he wrote Hebrews.

He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. He knew the basics.

And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus. “Fervent” (zeōn): boiling, burning with zeal, perhaps by the Spirit (Romans 12:11). His teaching about Jesus was accurate, as far as it went.

Though he knew only the baptism of John. Key words. He knew of John’s baptism of repentance and Jesus as the coming one, perhaps even of his life and death, but not the full message of Pentecost: the Spirit given, baptism in Jesus’ name. His knowledge was real but incomplete.

In a sentence. A Jew named Apollos from Alexandria came to Ephesus, an eloquent man with a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, who spoke with burning zeal and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only John’s baptism.

For worship. Zeal and gifts are wonderful, but must be joined to full truth. Keep learning.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Bold, gifted, and incomplete.

But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside. Key words. Not publicly correcting or embarrassing him, but privately, perhaps in their home. Wise, gentle, humble correction. Tentmakers taught a scholar.

And explained to him the way of God more accurately. “More accurately”: building on what he had, filling the gaps. And Apollos, though learned and eloquent, was humble enough to learn from them.

Where Christians differ: Priscilla and women teaching. Some use this verse to argue that women may serve as pastors or preachers in the church. Verdict: Priscilla, with her husband, instructed Apollos privately in their home; this was not preaching in the gathered church or exercising authority as an elder. Scripture reserves the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the church’s gathering to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women like Priscilla rightly teach, explain, and serve in many ways. This is the complementarian view, held with deep respect for women’s gifts and ministry.

In a sentence. He began speaking boldly in the synagogue, and when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him home and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

On a Tuesday. Correct privately and gently. And when corrected, receive it humbly, like Apollos.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.

And when he wished to cross to Achaia. Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

The brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. A letter of recommendation (2 Corinthians 3:1).

He greatly helped those who through grace had believed. Key words. “Through grace had believed”: faith itself is the gift of grace (Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 1:29). They believed because of grace. And Apollos “helped” believers: his gift watered what Paul planted (1 Corinthians 3:6).

For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Apologetics from Scripture. He answered objections publicly and powerfully.

In a sentence. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him, and when he arrived he was a great help to those who had believed by grace, for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

For worship. Your faith is a gift of grace. Thank God for it, and for those who help you grow in it.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is the climax of Paul’s free ministry. It was the capital of the province of Asia, a port of perhaps a quarter of a million people, home of the vast temple of Artemis and famous across the empire for magic. Paul stays nearly three years (20:31), longer than anywhere else. He first meets a dozen men who know only John’s baptism; taught about Jesus, they are baptised in his name and receive the Spirit. Three months in the synagogue are followed by two years of daily teaching in a hired hall, and the word spreads through the whole province: the churches of the Lycus valley and the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 probably date from these years.

The gospel then collides with the city’s religion. God works unusual miracles through Paul; seven Jewish exorcists who use Jesus’ name as a spell are overpowered; and new believers burn their magic books, worth a fortune. Paul plans to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome, the plan the rest of Acts follows. Finally the silversmith Demetrius, whose trade depends on the goddess, stirs up a riot that fills the great theatre for two hours, until the town clerk calms the crowd: the Christians have committed no crime, and the courts are open. Luke’s summary is the key: the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reaches Ephesus and finds about twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John pointed to Jesus; they are baptised in Jesus’ name, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes, with tongues and prophecy. Paul teaches in the synagogue for three months; when some harden and slander the Way, he moves the disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and teaches daily for two years, so that the whole province hears the word. God does unusual miracles through him. Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest, Sceva, try to drive out a spirit in the name of “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims”, and the possessed man overpowers them. Fear falls on the city, believers confess their practices, and magicians burn books worth fifty thousand silver coins. Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome. Demetrius the silversmith rallies the craftsmen whose shrines of Artemis are losing trade, and the city rushes into the theatre, dragging two of Paul’s companions. Paul is kept from going in. For two hours the crowd chants “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians”, until the town clerk quiets them, points out that these men have committed no crime, sends complaints to the courts or a lawful assembly, warns of Roman displeasure, and dismisses the crowd.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”

Meaning first. Acts 19 tells of Paul’s longest mission, nearly three years in Ephesus, the great city of Asia. Twelve disciples of John receive the Spirit; Paul teaches daily for two years, and the word spreads through the whole province; God works extraordinary miracles; magicians burn their books; and the silversmiths, whose trade depends on the goddess Artemis, start a riot. The chapter shows the power of the gospel against every rival power: incomplete religion, demons, magic, and the money-making idolatry of a whole city.

Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis, with perhaps 250,000 people. Paul had promised to return if God willed (18:21).

There he found some disciples. “Disciples” here means disciples of John the Baptist, as v. 3 shows. Like Apollos, they knew only John’s baptism.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? Key words. Paul senses something missing. Notice the assumption: the Spirit is received when one believes. Not later.

No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit. Not that they had never heard of the Spirit at all, since John spoke of him (Luke 3:16), but that they hadn’t heard the Spirit had been given, that Pentecost had happened.

In a sentence. While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul travelled through the interior and came to Ephesus, where he found some disciples and asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit when they believed, and they said they had not even heard that the Holy Spirit had come.

On a Tuesday. Every believer receives the Spirit at faith. If you believe in Christ, he is in you.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.”

Into what then were you baptized? Paul connects the Spirit with baptism in Jesus’ name.

Into John’s baptism. A baptism of preparation.

John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus. Key words. John’s baptism pointed forward. He himself said: believe in the one coming after me. John was the forerunner; Jesus is the fulfilment. These men had stopped at the signpost and never reached the destination.

In a sentence. Paul asked what baptism they had received, and they said John’s, and Paul explained that John’s was a baptism of repentance, telling people to believe in the one coming after him, Jesus.

For worship. Don’t stop at the signpost. Every preparation points to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Key words. The only case in the New Testament of people being baptised twice. Not because John’s baptism was invalid in its time, but because they had not yet believed in Jesus as the one who had come. Their first baptism was a preparation; this was Christian baptism, into Christ. Interestingly, there is no record that the apostles, who had John’s baptism, were rebaptised. They had received the Spirit at Pentecost.

Where Christians differ: rebaptism. Some use this to justify rebaptising those baptised as infants or in other churches. Verdict: this case was unique, as John’s baptism was not Christian baptism. Where someone was baptised before they truly believed, credobaptists rightly see believer’s baptism as the first true baptism, not a repetition. But those who were baptised as believers in the name of the Trinity should not be baptised again; there is one baptism (Ephesians 4:5).

In a sentence. When they heard this, they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you learn more truth, act on it at once, as these men did.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all.

And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them. Key words. As with the Samaritans (8:17), through an apostle’s hands. Why? Perhaps to bring this group of John’s followers fully into the one church, and to show that Paul’s apostleship equalled Peter’s.

And they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. Visible signs, as at Pentecost (chapter 2) and Caesarea (chapter 10), at a key point in the spread of the gospel. Luke records tongues only at these turning points: Jews, Samaritans (implied), Gentiles, and the disciples of John. They marked the gospel’s advance into new groups.

Where Christians differ: a pattern for today? Pentecostals see a second-blessing pattern here. Verdict: these men were not yet Christians in the full sense; they hadn’t believed in Jesus as having come. When they believed and were baptised, they received the Spirit at once. This is not a two-stage experience for Christians, but conversion. The tongues were a sign for a transitional moment in salvation history.

There were about twelve men in all. Perhaps a hint: the full number of a renewed Israel.

In a sentence. When Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied; there were about twelve men.

For worship. The Spirit unites all who believe into one church. Praise him for his work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus.

For three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. Three months, a longer time than usual in a synagogue. The kingdom of God: God’s reign in Christ (28:23, 31).

But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief. “Stubborn” (esklērynonto): hardened (Hebrews 3:8).

Speaking evil of the Way before the congregation. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith (9:2).

He withdrew from them and took the disciples with him. A separate congregation.

Reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. Key words. The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. One early manuscript adds “from the fifth to the tenth hour,” 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the hot hours of rest when the hall was free and workers could attend. Paul worked his trade in the mornings (20:34) and taught through the afternoon heat. Daily, for two years.

In a sentence. Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God, but when some hardened their hearts and slandered the Way publicly, he left them, took the disciples with him, and reasoned daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

On a Tuesday. Use the time you have. Paul taught in the midday heat while others rested.
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.

This continued for two years. Plus the three months, nearly three years in Ephesus (20:31).

So that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. Key words. Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis were probably founded in these years, through Paul’s co-workers like Epaphras (Colossians 1:7; 4:13). The seven churches of Revelation 2–3 were all in Asia. Paul trained others, who went out. Ephesus became a hub. Strategic ministry multiplies.

In a sentence. This went on for two years, so that everyone living in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.

For worship. Teach others who will teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). That is how the word spreads.
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.

And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul. Key words. “God was doing”: not Paul. “Extraordinary” (ou tas tychousas): not the ordinary kind, unusual even by apostolic standards. In a city famous for magic, God showed his superior power.

So that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick. The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used at work: sweatbands and work aprons from his tentmaking. Like Peter’s shadow (5:15).

And their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. God honoured their faith, even mixed with superstition.

Where Christians differ: prayer cloths. Some ministries today sell or send “anointed” cloths, promising healing or prosperity. Verdict: Luke calls these miracles extraordinary, done by God through an apostle at a unique time, to confirm the gospel in a city of magic. Nothing in Scripture tells believers to use objects for healing. Paul never sold anything. Seeking power through objects is close to the magic Ephesus was about to renounce (v. 19).

In a sentence. God did extraordinary miracles through Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and their illnesses were cured and evil spirits left them.

On a Tuesday. God’s power is not in objects but in himself. Pray to him directly.
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.

Some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists. Travelling exorcists, common in the ancient world.

Undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits. Key words. Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. Magical papyri from this period mix Jewish, Greek and Egyptian names. They added “Jesus” to their list, as a magic word.

I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims. Second-hand faith: not “my Lord Jesus,” but “the Jesus Paul preaches.” They didn’t know him.

Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva. No Sceva appears in the lists of high priests. He may have been from a high-priestly family, or claimed the title to impress.

In a sentence. Some Jews who went around driving out evil spirits tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over the possessed, saying, “I command you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches,” including seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest.

For worship. The name of Jesus is not a magic word. It belongs to a person you must know.
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you? Key words. Two different verbs: “know” (ginōskō) Jesus, “recognize” (epistamai) Paul. Demons know Jesus and tremble (James 2:19). They know his true servants. They don’t fear people who use his name without knowing him.

And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them. Seven against one, and the one won.

So that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. A humiliating, almost comic scene. Spiritual power is not a technique.

In a sentence. The evil spirit answered that it knew Jesus and recognised Paul, but who were they? and the possessed man jumped on them, overpowered them all, and they fled from the house naked and bleeding.

On a Tuesday. Don’t borrow someone else’s faith. Know Jesus for yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices.

And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Key words. The name they tried to use as magic was honoured as holy. God turned even the humiliation of false exorcists to his glory.

Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. Key words. Believers, who had kept up their magic secretly. “Divulging” (anangellontes): disclosing. Perhaps revealing their spells, which were thought to lose power when made public. Real repentance brings sins into the light (1 John 1:9; James 5:16).

In a sentence. This became known to all the Jews and Greeks in Ephesus, fear came over them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honour, and many believers came openly confessing what they had done.

For worship. Bring hidden sins into the light. Confession breaks their power.

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.

A number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. Key words. Ephesus was famous for magic spells, known as “Ephesian letters.” Scrolls of incantations, charms and spells. They didn’t sell them (which would pass the evil on), but burned them publicly. Repentance cost them.

And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, a day’s wage. Fifty thousand days’ wages: a fortune. True repentance is costly.

So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. Key words. Another progress report (6:7; 12:24). “Prevail” (ischyen): grew strong, overpowered. The word of the Lord overpowered the magic of Ephesus.

In a sentence. Many who had practised sorcery brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly, and when the value was counted it came to fifty thousand silver coins, and so the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to burn? Get rid of whatever ties you to sin, whatever it costs.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.

Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem. Key words. “In the Spirit”: perhaps his own spirit, or by the Holy Spirit. Probably both: a Spirit-led decision. He was collecting money from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

After I have been there, I must also see Rome. Key words. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. The rest of Acts follows this sentence: Jerusalem, then Rome. He would go, but in chains (23:11). Paul wrote to the Romans of this plan (Romans 1:13; 15:23–24).

Having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus. Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears in an inscription found there (Romans 16:23), the city treasurer who paved a square at his own expense.

He himself stayed in Asia for a while. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus during this time (1 Corinthians 16:8).

In a sentence. After this Paul decided in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, saying he must then also see Rome, and sent Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while he stayed a while in Asia.

For worship. Make your plans in the Spirit, and hold them open to God’s way of fulfilling them.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.

About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. Understatement.

A man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis. Key words. The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, four times the size of the Parthenon, with 127 columns. Artemis of Ephesus was not the Greek huntress, but a mother goddess of fertility, shown with many breasts or eggs. Pilgrims bought miniature silver shrines as souvenirs and charms.

Brought no little business to the craftsmen. Religion was big business.

In a sentence. About that time a great disturbance arose about the Way, for a silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought a great deal of business to the craftsmen.

On a Tuesday. Where idolatry makes money, the gospel will be opposed.
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth.

These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades. A trade union meeting.

Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. Key words. Honest, at least. The first argument is money. Religion was cover for profit. As in Philippi (16:19): the gospel threatens those who profit from falsehood.

In a sentence. He gathered them with other workers in related trades and said they all knew their wealth came from this business.

For worship. Don’t let money shape your beliefs. Let truth shape your use of money.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
