And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.

Not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people. A testimony from an enemy to the gospel’s success (v. 10).

Saying that gods made with hands are not gods. Key words. Paul’s message summed up by an opponent (17:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4). So many had turned from idols that sales were falling.

There is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing. Then he adds religious patriotism to the money argument. City pride, religion and profit were bound together.

She whom all Asia and the world worship. Within a few centuries, the temple lay in ruins and the goddess was forgotten. Today, a single column stands. The word of the Lord endures.

In a sentence. Demetrius said they could see and hear how Paul had persuaded many people in Ephesus and almost all of Asia that man-made gods are not gods, and so their trade was in danger of losing its good name, and the temple of the great goddess Artemis of being discredited, and she herself, worshipped by all Asia and the world, of being robbed of her majesty.

On a Tuesday. Every idol falls in the end. Only the living God remains. Trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel.

Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! A cry of civic and religious pride, used in Ephesian worship. Inscriptions confirm the title.

So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater. The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Its ruins still stand, and you can sit where the crowd sat.

Dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions. Aristarchus, from Thessalonica, later went with Paul to Rome and shared his imprisonment (27:2; Colossians 4:10).

In a sentence. Hearing this, they were furious and shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”, and the city was thrown into confusion as the people rushed into the theatre, dragging Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s Macedonian travel companions.

For worship. The crowd shouted for Artemis. We shout for the Lord Jesus, who is truly great.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.

But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. Brave Paul wanted to stand with his friends and speak. Wise disciples held him back.

And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his. Key words. The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the imperial cult and public games, appointed annually. And they were Paul’s friends. The gospel had reached the highest circles, or at least won their respect. Another sign for Theophilus: respectable Romans did not see Paul as a criminal.

Were urging him not to venture into the theater. Good advice. Courage needs wisdom.

In a sentence. Paul wanted to go into the crowd, but the disciples wouldn’t let him, and some of the officials of the province, who were his friends, sent word begging him not to go into the theatre.

On a Tuesday. Courage needs wise friends. Listen to them.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.

For the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Key words. Luke’s wry humour. A mob doesn’t think. Most didn’t know why they were there.

Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had nothing to do with Paul, since Jews also refused to worship idols.

And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. To distance the Jews from the Christians.

In a sentence. The assembly was in confusion, some shouting one thing and some another, and most did not even know why they were there, and the Jews pushed Alexander forward, and he motioned for silence to make a defence.

For worship. Don’t follow the crowd. Know why you believe what you believe.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

But when they recognized that he was a Jew. Anti-Jewish feeling. To the crowd, Jews and Christians were the same: both rejected Artemis.

For about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Key words. Two hours of chanting. Like the prophets of Baal crying from morning till noon (1 Kings 18:26). Repetition is not truth. Their goddess could not hear them.

In a sentence. When they realised he was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

On a Tuesday. Loud chanting doesn’t make something true. Truth is truth, however many shout against it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.

And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd. The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for order in the city.

The city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis. “Temple keeper” (neōkoron): a title of honour, confirmed by inscriptions.

And of the sacred stone that fell from the sky. Probably a meteorite, worshipped as an image of Artemis.

Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. His argument: Artemis is secure; why riot? The irony: what he thought could not be denied was denied, and his goddess is gone.

In a sentence. The town clerk quieted the crowd and said everyone knew Ephesus was the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image that fell from heaven, and since this was undeniable, they should calm down and do nothing rash.

For worship. What the world thinks undeniable often crumbles. God’s truth stands.
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.

For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. Key words. A civic official declares Paul’s companions innocent. “Sacrilegious” (hierosylous): temple-robbers. Paul didn’t attack temples or mock the goddess; he simply preached the truth. A model: Christians should not insult other religions, but proclaim Christ. The truth undermines idols without our ridicule.

The courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Go through proper channels.

In a sentence. He said they had brought these men, though they had neither robbed temples nor blasphemed the goddess, and if Demetrius and the craftsmen had a complaint, the courts were open and there were proconsuls; let them press charges.

On a Tuesday. Proclaim Christ without insulting others. Let the truth do its work.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.

But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. The lawful city assembly, which met on fixed days.

For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today. Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting, removing its privileges as a free city. The clerk was worried about Rome, not Artemis.

In a sentence. Anything further should be settled in a legal assembly, for they were in danger of being charged with rioting, with no reason they could give for this commotion.

For worship. God uses even worried officials to protect his people. Thank him for good order and law.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly. Key words. “Assembly” (ekklēsia): the same word as “church.” Luke may be drawing the contrast: the confused, idolatrous assembly of Ephesus is dismissed; the church of Christ, God’s true assembly, remains. Once again, a Roman official protects the gospel by keeping the peace. The word of the Lord continues to prevail.

In a sentence. After saying this, he dismissed the assembly.

On a Tuesday. The world’s assemblies come and go. Christ’s church remains. Belong to it.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth more than a century’s wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
After the riot Paul leaves Ephesus, strengthens the churches of Macedonia and spends three winter months in Corinth, where he almost certainly wrote Romans. A plot against him at sea makes him go back overland. He travels with representatives of the Gentile churches, who are carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and Luke rejoins him at Philippi (“we”). At Troas, at an evening gathering on the first day of the week, Paul teaches until midnight; a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-storey window and is picked up dead, and Paul restores him. The church breaks bread and talks until dawn.

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sails past Ephesus and summons its elders to Miletus. His farewell is the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders, and the nearest thing in Acts to one of his letters. He reviews his ministry: humble, tearful, open, teaching the whole counsel of God, supporting himself. He tells them he goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit and expecting chains, counting his life worth nothing beside finishing his course. He charges them to guard themselves and the flock that God bought with his own blood, warns of wolves from outside and false teachers from within, and commends them to God and the word of his grace. They kneel, pray, weep and see him to the ship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the uproar is over, Paul encourages the disciples and leaves for Macedonia, then spends three months in Greece. A plot by his opponents as he is about to sail for Syria makes him return through Macedonia. Seven companions from the churches go ahead to Troas, and after the Feast of Unleavened Bread Paul and Luke sail from Philippi to join them. On the first day of the week the church meets to break bread, and Paul, leaving the next day, talks until midnight in a lamp-lit upper room. Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into sleep and falls three storeys, and is picked up dead. Paul goes down, embraces him and says his life is in him. Back upstairs they break bread and talk till dawn, and the young man is taken home alive, to their great comfort. The party sails down the coast while Paul walks to Assos and joins them there; they pass Ephesus because Paul is hurrying to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — perhaps choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.

Meaning first. Acts 20 is a chapter of farewells. Paul revisits the churches of Macedonia and Greece, raises a young man who fell from a window during a long Sunday service, and then, at Miletus, gives his only recorded speech to Christian leaders: his farewell to the elders of Ephesus. It is the New Testament’s great charge to pastors. Paul reviews his own ministry, warns of wolves, and commits them to God and to the word of his grace. Then they kneel, weep and part.

After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell. He didn’t leave in a hurry, or in fear. He encouraged them first.

And departed for Macedonia. To Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea. He wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia at this time (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:5).

And had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

In a sentence. When the uproar ended, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye and left for Macedonia, and after travelling through that area encouraging the believers, he came to Greece.

On a Tuesday. Encourage before you leave. Paul never left a church without strengthening it.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.

There he spent three months. Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth, around AD 57, the greatest statement of the gospel ever written.

When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria. Perhaps to kill him on a pilgrim ship bound for Passover, where it would be easy to throw him overboard.

He decided to return through Macedonia. A longer route by land, to avoid the plot. Prudence is not lack of faith.

In a sentence. He spent three months there, and when the Jews plotted against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia.

For worship. Wisdom avoids needless danger. Trust God and use your head.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,

Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus... Aristarchus and Secundus... Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy... Tychicus and Trophimus. Key words. These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:3–4; 2 Corinthians 8:19–21). Representatives from Macedonia, Galatia and Asia, Gentile believers carrying their gift. Accountability in handling money. And a living picture of the Gentile church’s love for the Jewish church.

Trophimus. His presence in Jerusalem will spark Paul’s arrest (21:29).

These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas. “Us”: Luke is back.

In a sentence. Paul was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia, who went ahead and waited for the rest at Troas.

On a Tuesday. Handle money for God’s work with transparency and accountability. Paul did.
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days.

But we sailed away from Philippi. “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi, where he had stayed since chapter 16.

After the days of Unleavened Bread. Passover week, spring of AD 57. Paul kept the Jewish calendar as a time marker.

And in five days we came to them at Troas. The crossing had taken two days the other way (16:11). Contrary winds.

Where we stayed for seven days. Including a Sunday.

In a sentence. They sailed from Philippi after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, joined the others at Troas five days later, and stayed there seven days.

For worship. Paul waited seven days, perhaps to worship with the church on the Lord’s Day. Make time for it.
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.

On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread. Key words. The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, after work. One of the clearest New Testament glimpses of Christian worship: on Sunday, gathered, to break bread, the Lord’s Supper, with teaching. Sunday was the day of resurrection (Luke 24:1), and became the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and Sunday. Seventh-day Adventists and others hold that Christians must keep Saturday as the Sabbath; some Christians see no special day at all. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The church from the beginning gathered on the first day, the day of resurrection. The Lord’s Day is not a burdensome law but a privilege: a day to gather, worship, break bread, hear the word, rest and do good.

Paul talked with them... and he prolonged his speech until midnight. “Talked” (dielegeto): discussed, reasoned. A long session, with questions. His last chance with them.

There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. An eyewitness detail explaining what follows: hot, smoky air, a sleepy young man.

In a sentence. On the first day of the week, when they gathered to break bread, Paul talked with them until midnight, since he planned to leave the next day, in an upstairs room lit by many lamps.

On a Tuesday. Make the Lord’s Day a delight. Gather with God’s people, break bread, hear the word.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead.

And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window. Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room made the air heavy. He sat at the window for fresh air. Perhaps a slave who had worked all day.

Sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. A comfort to preachers whose hearers doze, and a warning to long-winded ones. Even Paul put someone to sleep.

He fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. Key words. “Taken up dead”: Luke the doctor says he was dead, not just apparently dead.

In a sentence. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, and overcome by sleep he fell from the third floor and was picked up dead.

For worship. God knows our weaknesses, even our sleepiness. He is gracious.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.

But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms. Like Elijah and Elisha, who stretched themselves on dead boys (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34).

Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him. Key words. Not that he was never dead, but that his life had returned. A resurrection, like Tabitha (9:40).

And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten. The Lord’s Supper, at last, after midnight.

He conversed with them a long while, until daybreak. All night. Not boring after all.

In a sentence. Paul went down, threw himself on him and took him in his arms, telling them not to be alarmed, for he was alive, and then went back upstairs, broke bread and ate, and talked with them until daybreak before leaving.

On a Tuesday. In the middle of worship, death came, and Christ’s power answered. He is Lord of life.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted.

And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. Key words. Understatement: greatly comforted. A Lord’s Day service that included teaching, the Supper, a death and a resurrection. The church went home with joy.

In a sentence. They took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.

For worship. The resurrection is the comfort of the church. Every Lord’s Day remembers it.

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.

Intending himself to go by land. About twenty miles on foot, perhaps for solitude and prayer before the journey to Jerusalem, or to visit believers on the way.

And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor. Mitylene was on the island of Lesbos.

In a sentence. The others went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, planning to take Paul aboard there, since he had arranged to walk, and when he met them at Assos they took him aboard and went to Mitylene.

For worship. Even busy servants of God need time alone with him. Find yours.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.

And the day after that we went to Miletus. Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus.

For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia. If he went to Ephesus, he would be delayed by many friends.

For he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover. With the collection, as a gift at the feast of firstfruits. Perhaps fitting: the Gentile firstfruits bringing their offering to Jerusalem (Romans 15:16).

In a sentence. Sailing on, they passed Chios, reached Samos, and the next day Miletus, for Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in Asia, hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost if possible.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes love means saying no to good things in order to do the best thing.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Miletus Paul calls the Ephesian elders. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord humbly, with tears and trials, holding back nothing helpful, teaching publicly and house to house, calling Jews and Greeks to repent and trust the Lord Jesus. Now the Spirit compels him to Jerusalem, and the Spirit warns him in every city of prison and hardship, but his life matters to him only so that he may finish the race and the task Jesus gave him, to testify to the gospel of God’s grace. They will not see him again, and he is clear of everyone’s blood, for he has declared the whole purpose of God. They must keep watch over themselves and the flock the Spirit has entrusted to them, shepherding God’s church, bought with his own blood. Savage wolves will come, and some of their own number will distort the truth to win followers, so they must stay alert, remembering his three years of tearful warning. He commits them to God and to the word of his grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance. He has wanted nobody’s money, but worked with his own hands to support himself and others, to show that the weak must be helped, remembering Jesus’ words that giving is more blessed than receiving. Then he kneels and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him and kiss him, grieving most that they will not see him again, and they go with him to the ship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the letter to Ephesus in Revelation (2:1–7) shows a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him.

He sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. Key words. “Elders” (presbyterous): plural, a group of leaders in one church (14:23). It would take a few days for them to come. What follows is Paul’s charge to them, a model for every pastor.

In a sentence. From Miletus Paul sent for the elders of the church in Ephesus.

For worship. Pray for your elders. They carry a heavy charge.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews;

You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time. Key words. Paul appeals to his life, not just his words. Ministry is first a life lived openly before people (1 Thessalonians 2:10; 2 Corinthians 1:12). Character before charisma.

Serving the Lord with all humility. “Serving” (douleuōn): serving as a slave. Humility, the first mark.

And with tears. Paul wept (v. 31; 2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18). Not a hard, professional minister, but a man who felt deeply.

And with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews. Suffering was part of it.

In a sentence. When they arrived, Paul reminded them how he had lived among them from the first day he came to Asia, serving the Lord humbly, with tears and through the trials caused by Jewish plots.

On a Tuesday. Pastors: serve humbly, with tears, through trials. Everyone: pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

How I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable. Key words. “Shrink” (hypesteilamēn): hold back, draw back, as a sail is lowered. Paul didn’t hold back anything they needed, even unpopular truths. A pastor must not keep back the hard parts.

And teaching you in public and from house to house. Public preaching, and private, personal ministry in homes. Both matter.

Testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The gospel in two words: repentance and faith. Turning from sin to God, and trusting Christ. They go together (Mark 1:15; Hebrews 6:1). The same message to everyone.

In a sentence. Paul reminded them that he had not held back from telling them anything helpful, teaching them publicly and from house to house, and testifying to Jews and Greeks about repentance towards God and faith in the Lord Jesus.

For worship. Repentance towards God and faith in Christ: the whole Christian life in two words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.

I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit. Key words. “Constrained” (dedemenos): bound. Bound by the Spirit before being bound by chains (21:33). Compelled.

Not knowing what will happen to me there. He walks by faith, not sight.

Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. Through prophets (21:4, 11). He goes knowing it will cost him.

In a sentence. Paul said he was going to Jerusalem compelled by the Spirit, not knowing what would happen there, except that in every city the Holy Spirit warned him that prison and hardships awaited him.

On a Tuesday. Following the Spirit doesn’t mean avoiding hardship. It may mean walking into it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.

But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself. Key words. Paul’s life was not his own (Philippians 1:21; 2 Corinthians 5:15). Not that life is worthless, but that finishing his task mattered more than his safety.

If only I may finish my course. “Course” (dromon): race. At the end of his life he could say: I have finished the race (2 Timothy 4:7).

And the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus. His ministry was given, not chosen (9:15; Galatians 1:1).

To testify to the gospel of the grace of God. Key words. The gospel is the good news of God’s grace: undeserved favour. Paul’s whole message in four words: the gospel of grace.

In a sentence. Paul said he did not consider his life worth anything to himself, if only he could finish his race and the task the Lord Jesus gave him, of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.

For worship. Make this your prayer: that you may finish your course and testify to the gospel of the grace of God.

parallels.desc: I have finished the race

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,

I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. A sad farewell. Paul may later have revisited the area after his first Roman imprisonment (1 Timothy 1:3), but he didn’t expect to.

Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all. Key words. The watchman’s words again (18:6; Ezekiel 33:1–9). Paul had warned everyone. If they perished, their blood was not on his hands. A solemn picture of a pastor’s accountability.

In a sentence. Paul said he knew none of them would see him again, and so he declared that he was innocent of the blood of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Have you warned those around you? Don’t let their blood be on your hands.

parallels.desc: the watchman

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.

For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Key words. “The whole counsel” (pasan tēn boulēn): God’s whole purpose, plan, will. Not selected favourite topics, not only the comfortable parts, but everything God has revealed: sin and grace, judgment and mercy, election and evangelism, doctrine and duty. This is why preaching through whole books of the Bible matters. A pastor who preaches only what people want to hear has blood on his hands.

In a sentence. For he had not held back from declaring to them the whole purpose of God.

For worship. Want the whole counsel of God, not just the parts you like.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;

Pay careful attention to yourselves. Key words. First, yourselves. A pastor who neglects his own soul can’t care for others (1 Timothy 4:16).

And to all the flock. All, not just favourites.

In which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Key words. Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers: two names for one office. “Overseers” (episkopous) gives us “bishops.” In the New Testament, elder, overseer and shepherd describe the same leaders (Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–2). And the Spirit appointed them. Church leadership is the Spirit’s gift.

To care for the church of God. “Care for” (poimainein): shepherd. Feed, lead, protect.

Which he obtained with his own blood. Key words. The church belongs to God, bought with a price. “His own blood”: God’s own blood. A striking phrase: the blood of Christ is the blood of God, because Christ is God. Some manuscripts read “the church of the Lord,” and some translate “with the blood of his own,” meaning his own Son. But the plain reading expresses what the church confessed: the one who died is God the Son (communication of attributes). Pastors care for people Christ died for. That is why they matter so much.

I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock. False teachers from outside. Jesus warned of wolves in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15).

In a sentence. Paul told them to watch over themselves and the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he bought with his own blood, for he knew savage wolves would come in after he left and not spare the flock.

On a Tuesday. The church was bought with God’s blood. Treat it, and its people, as precious.
verseByVerse.note: Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers — two names for one office. “With his own blood” — the blood of God’s own Son. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”; “his own blood” may also be rendered “the blood of his Own” (ESV notes).

parallels.desc: shepherds who feed themselves

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears.

And from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things. Key words. Not only wolves from outside, but false teachers from inside, even among the elders. “Twisted” (diestrammena): perverted, distorted truth. It happened: Paul later wrote to Timothy in Ephesus about false teachers there (1 Timothy 1:3–7, 19–20; 2 Timothy 2:17–18). And Jesus commended Ephesus for testing false apostles (Revelation 2:2).

To draw away the disciples after them. The mark of false teachers: drawing people to themselves rather than to Christ.

Therefore be alert. “Be alert” (grēgoreite): stay awake, watch. Shepherds keep watch at night.

Remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. Paul’s example. Every one, individually. Night and day. With tears.

In a sentence. Even from among them men would arise distorting the truth to draw disciples after them, so they must be on guard, remembering that for three years Paul never stopped warning each of them night and day with tears.

For worship. Watch for teachers who draw people to themselves. Follow those who point you to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel.

And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace. Key words. Paul’s last provision for them: not a successor, not a system, but God and his word. The word of grace is the gospel, now preserved in Scripture. That is the protection against wolves.

Which is able to build you up. The word builds up the church (Ephesians 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). It is enough.

And to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. The future hope, for all God’s holy people (26:18; Ephesians 1:14, 18).

I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. Key words. Paul’s integrity with money. Unlike false teachers, he wasn’t in it for gain (1 Thessalonians 2:5; 1 Timothy 6:5). In the ancient world, wealth was often stored as clothing.

In a sentence. Paul committed them to God and to the message of his grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance among all who are made holy, and said he had never wanted anyone’s silver, gold or clothing.

On a Tuesday. You have been commended to God and the word of his grace. They are enough. Open your Bible.

parallels.desc: whose ox have I taken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’

These hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. Paul may have held up his calloused tentmaker’s hands. He supported himself and his team.

By working hard in this way we must help the weak. Work, not only to support oneself, but to have something to give (Ephesians 4:28).

And remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” Key words. This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was passed down by those who heard him (John 21:25). The only saying of Jesus quoted in Acts. It sums up his life: he gave himself. Giving brings deeper joy than getting.

In a sentence. They knew Paul had worked with his own hands to supply his needs and his companions’, and showed them that by hard work we must help the weak, remembering the Lord Jesus’ words: it is more blessed to give than to receive.

For worship. It is more blessed to give than to receive. Give something today.
verseByVerse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was remembered and passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,

He knelt down and prayed with them all. Key words. He ended with prayer, on his knees, with them. Not standing, but kneeling, in humility. Paul’s ministry began, continued and ended in prayer.

And there was much weeping on the part of all. Grown men, church leaders, weeping. Deep love.

They embraced Paul and kissed him. “Embraced”: literally fell on his neck. The holy kiss of greeting and farewell (Romans 16:16).

In a sentence. When he had said this, he knelt and prayed with them all, and they all wept as they embraced and kissed him.

On a Tuesday. Christian love is not cold. It weeps, embraces, and prays together.

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.

Being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. The deepest grief: parting. But not for ever. Christians who part on earth will meet again (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

And they accompanied him to the ship. To the very end. A touching picture of love between a pastor and his people.

In a sentence. What grieved them most was his statement that they would never see him again, and they went with him to the ship.

For worship. Christians never say goodbye for the last time. We will see each other’s faces again in glory.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God and Pastoral Faithfulness. Acts 20:27 gives the church its standard for preaching: the whole counsel of God, without shrinking. This phrase has defined the Reformed tradition’s commitment to expository, systematic, comprehensive proclamation of Scripture — preaching through whole books, teaching the full range of doctrine, refusing to select only the comfortable and suppress the challenging. The shepherd who preaches the whole counsel will declare both the tenderness of the Father and the terror of the Judge, both the free grace of justification and the necessary fruit of sanctification, both the comfort of election and the urgency of repentance. Paul could stand before his people at Miletus and say “I am innocent of your blood” because he had given them everything. That is the standard every preacher must aspire to.
20.examples:
Then: A beach at Miletus, a group of weeping elders on their knees, a man who knew he was going to chains and possibly death — and who spent his last hours with these people not arranging his escape but commending them to God and declaring his conscience clear. The tears on the beach are the overflow of three years of tears in the houses of Ephesus. Ministry that produces this kind of grief at parting has been ministry that produced this kind of love in the doing.

Now: Paul’s farewell is the standard against which every pastoral ministry will be measured. Did we shrink? Did we select? Did we give them the comfortable Christ without the demanding Lord, the free grace without the costly discipleship, the promise without the warning? The whole counsel of God. Nothing less. The flock that has been given the whole counsel will be able to stand when the wolves come — because they will recognise the deviation when they hear it.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed <sup>6</sup>and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>9</sup>He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>16</sup>And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law, <sup>21</sup>And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. <sup>22</sup>What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. <sup>23</sup>Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; <sup>24</sup>take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. <sup>25</sup>But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>29</sup>For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>34</sup>Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. <sup>35</sup>And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, <sup>36</sup>for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” <sup>37</sup>As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? <sup>38</sup>Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” <sup>39</sup>Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” <sup>40</sup>And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
21.overview:
Paul’s road to Jerusalem deliberately echoes Jesus’ own (Luke 9:51). At Tyre, disciples moved by the Spirit urge him not to go; at Caesarea, in the house of Philip the evangelist, the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will hand Paul over to the Gentiles. The church weeps and pleads; Paul answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they say, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul and praise God for the Gentile mission, but warn him that thousands of zealous Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To show the rumour is false, he joins four men completing a vow and pays their temple costs. Near the end of the week, Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing a Gentile inside, and the city erupts. The Roman tribune rescues Paul from a beating, chains him, and mistakes him for an Egyptian rebel; Paul replies in polished Greek that he is a citizen of Tarsus, and asks to address the crowd. The prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: bound, and in Gentile hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, Paul’s party sails by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, then crosses on a larger ship to Tyre. There they find the disciples and stay a week; prompted by the Spirit, these believers urge Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When the week is over the whole church, wives and children too, walks them to the shore, where they kneel and pray before parting. From Ptolemais they reach Caesarea and stay with Philip the evangelist, whose four unmarried daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus arrives from Judea, ties his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt, and announces that the Spirit says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go. He asks why they are weeping and breaking his heart; he is ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. When he cannot be persuaded, they give up, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” They go up to Jerusalem with some Caesarean disciples, who take them to lodge with Mnason of Cyprus, a believer from the early days.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guidance, and the Difference Between a Revelation and an Inference

This passage is the clearest case in Scripture of sincere, Spirit-filled Christians getting guidance wrong, and it is wonderfully instructive because nobody in it is a villain. The Spirit really did reveal what was waiting in Jerusalem; he revealed it at Tyre, at Caesarea, and in every city (20:23). What the Spirit did not say was do not go. That was added by people who loved Paul and could not bear the arithmetic. Agabus, a true prophet, models the discipline exactly: he announces the outcome and issues no instruction.

The Reformed doctrine of providence is what makes the distinction bearable. Because God ordains the end and the means together, a warning of suffering is not a detour sign; it is often the itinerary. Paul is not being tricked into a cell — he is being told the cost in advance so that he can pay it with his eyes open. And when the church cannot change his mind, its submission is not fatalism but faith with a name attached: not the will of fate, but the will of the Lord, prayed by people who know whose will it is because they have watched him keep his promises for years. It is Gethsemane repeated in a front room, and it is the sentence every Christian eventually needs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A whole congregation at Tyre — men, women, children — walking a man they had known for seven days out of the city gate and kneeling in the wet sand of a working harbour to pray for him, in public, in front of dockers. Then going home to supper while he sailed toward chains. Their names are not recorded. Nothing they said survives. It is in the Bible anyway.

Now: Most of us are Tyre. The great work of God in our generation will pass through our town for about a week, and our share in it will be a spare bed, a meal, and a prayer on the way out — and that is not the reduced version of the Christian life, it is the thing itself. And when someone we love is walking toward a costly obedience we cannot talk them out of, we will need what that church found on the beach: the grace to stop arguing without going cold, to lose the argument and keep the love, and to say with them, let the will of the Lord be done.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.

Meaning first. Acts 21 tells of Paul’s last journey to Jerusalem and his arrest there. All along the way, believers warn him by the Spirit that chains await him, and beg him not to go. Paul goes anyway, ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. In Jerusalem he tries to calm Jewish believers’ fears by joining a temple ceremony, but a false rumour sets off a riot, and he is rescued from the mob by Roman soldiers. Like his Lord, he goes up to Jerusalem knowing what awaits him, and is handed over to the Gentiles.

When we had parted from them. “Parted” (apospasthentas): literally tore ourselves away. A painful farewell (20:37–38).

We came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. Cos, Rhodes and Patara were ports along the south-west coast of Asia Minor. Luke records the route like a ship’s log.

Having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. A larger ship for the open sea crossing.

In a sentence. After tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, they sailed straight to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, then Patara, where they found a ship crossing to Phoenicia and boarded it.

On a Tuesday. Partings in Christ are painful, because love is real. That is a good thing.
verseByVerse.note: Cos, Rhodes and Patara were ports along the south-west coast of Asia Minor; from Patara they crossed the open sea east toward Phoenicia.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.

When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left. Passing south of Cyprus, where Paul’s first journey began. Memories.

We sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre. Tyre was a major port of Phoenicia, north of Galilee. Jesus had visited the region (Mark 7:24).

For there the ship was to unload its cargo. A week’s stop.

In a sentence. Sighting Cyprus and passing it to the south, they sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload.

For worship. God uses even cargo schedules to bring his servants where he wants them.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a major port of Phoenicia, north of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed

And having sought out the disciples. They found the believers. A church Paul didn’t found, probably from the scattering after Stephen (11:19).

And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. Key words. The Spirit revealed the danger ahead; the disciples concluded he should not go. Was Paul disobeying the Spirit? No. The Spirit showed them that suffering awaited him (20:23); the conclusion “don’t go” was their loving inference. The Spirit himself was leading Paul to Jerusalem (20:22; 19:21).

Where Christians differ: can prophecy be mistaken? Some cite this to argue that New Testament prophecy was fallible, mixing God’s revelation with human interpretation. Verdict: what the Spirit revealed was true: chains awaited Paul. What the disciples drew from it, that he should avoid them, was their own conclusion. Revelation must be distinguished from our application of it. The Spirit’s word is never mistaken; our inferences can be.

They all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. Whole families came to see him off.

And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed. A beautiful scene: a prayer meeting on the beach.

In a sentence. They found the disciples and stayed seven days, and through the Spirit these disciples urged Paul not to go to Jerusalem, but when the time came they left, and everyone, with wives and children, went with them out of the city, and they knelt on the beach and prayed.

On a Tuesday. Distinguish between what God says and what you conclude from it. Test your conclusions by his clear will.
verseByVerse.note: The Spirit revealed the danger ahead; the disciples concluded that he should not go.

verseByVerse.quote: "and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home.

And said farewell to one another. Another tearful parting.

Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. Simple, poignant.

In a sentence. They said goodbye to each other, boarded the ship, and the believers went home.

For worship. Pray with others before journeys and partings. It strengthens both.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.

We arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers. Ptolemais is modern Acre. Believers everywhere along the coast.

And we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven. Key words. Philip was one of the seven chosen to serve tables (6:5), who preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian (chapter 8), and settled in Caesarea (8:40). About twenty years later, still serving. “Evangelist”: a gospel preacher, a recognised gift (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 4:5). Here, two men who had once been on opposite sides: Philip, whose friend Stephen died; and Paul, who approved it. Now brothers under one roof. Luke probably gathered some of his information here.

In a sentence. Finishing their voyage from Tyre at Ptolemais, they greeted the believers and stayed a day, then went on to Caesarea, staying at the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven.

For worship. The gospel makes enemies into family. Philip welcomed the man who persecuted his friends.
verseByVerse.note: Ptolemais is modern Acre. Philip was one of the seven chosen in Acts 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied.

He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. Key words. Joel’s promise fulfilled: your daughters shall prophesy (2:17). Women received and exercised the gift of prophecy in the early church (1 Corinthians 11:5). Early church tradition remembered Philip’s daughters as important sources of information about the apostolic age.

Where Christians differ: prophesying women and church leadership. Some argue that because women prophesied, they may also hold the office of elder or pastor. Verdict: prophecy and the office of elder are different things. Women prophesied, prayed and served in the apostolic church, and are honoured for it. The office of elder and authoritative teaching in the gathered church Scripture gives to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:6). The complementarian view honours both truths: the full dignity and gifts of women, and the order God has given for the church.

In a sentence. He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

On a Tuesday. Fathers, raise daughters who know and speak God’s word.

parallels.desc: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

verseByVerse.quote: "While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul's belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit, "This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”

A prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. The same Agabus who foretold the famine (11:28). A proven prophet.

He took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands. Key words. Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did: Isaiah walking barefoot (Isaiah 20), Jeremiah’s loincloth and yoke (Jeremiah 13; 27), Ezekiel’s brick (Ezekiel 4). The belt: a long cloth wrapped round the waist.

Thus says the Holy Spirit. The Old Testament formula: thus says the LORD. The Spirit is God.

This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. Key words. The same words used of Jesus: handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32). Paul will follow his Lord’s path. It came true: the Jews seized him, the Romans bound him (21:30–33).

In a sentence. During their many days there, a prophet named Agabus came from Judea, took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said the Holy Spirit declared that the Jews in Jerusalem would bind the owner of this belt like this and hand him over to the Gentiles.

For worship. Paul walked the road his Master walked. Be willing to walk it too.
verseByVerse.note: Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Key words. “We”: even Luke begged him. Love wanted to protect him. Like Peter trying to stop Jesus going to the cross (Matthew 16:22). Natural, loving, and wrong.
