verseByVerse.quote: "And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks.

The tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them. The highest court of Israel nearly tearing a man apart. The tribune was getting nowhere.

Commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. Rescued a second time by Rome.

In a sentence. When the dispute turned violent, the commander, afraid Paul would be torn apart, ordered soldiers to take him from them by force and bring him back to the barracks.

For worship. God protected Paul again and again. He is faithful to his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.' When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.

The following night the Lord stood by him. Key words. Paul was probably discouraged: rejected by his people, nearly killed twice, his testimony in Jerusalem apparently a failure. And the Lord stood by him. Jesus himself (2 Timothy 4:17). The Lord stood by him in the dark, in the barracks.

Take courage. “Take courage” (tharsei): the word Jesus used to the paralysed man, the sick woman, the disciples in the storm (Matthew 9:2, 22; 14:27).

For as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome. Key words. Jesus calls his Jerusalem testimony a success: you have testified. Faithfulness, not results. And a promise: “must” (dei), you will get to Rome. Paul’s desire (19:21; Romans 1:10–11) will be fulfilled. This promise held him through two years in prison, shipwreck and snakebite.

When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. A curse on themselves (anathematisan). A hunger strike for murder.

In a sentence. The next night the Lord stood by Paul and told him to take courage, for as he had testified about him in Jerusalem, he must testify also in Rome, and when day came the Jews formed a plot and swore not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.

On a Tuesday. In your darkest night, the Lord stands by you. Take courage; his promises hold.

verseByVerse.quote: "There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, 'We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.

There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. A serious threat. Forty against one.

They went to the chief priests and elders. Key words. Religious leaders agreeing to murder. The same men who plotted against Jesus. The rabbis allowed vows to be released if they became impossible to keep; presumably they didn’t starve.

In a sentence. More than forty men were in this plot, and they went to the chief priests and elders and told them they had sworn a solemn oath not to eat until they had killed Paul.

For worship. Forty men vowed to kill Paul; one promise from Christ kept him alive. Count God’s promises bigger than your threats.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul.

Give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. A trap, using a fake legal hearing.

And we are ready to kill him before he comes near. An ambush in the narrow streets between the fortress and the council chamber.

Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush. Key words. This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem. We know nothing else about his sister or nephew. Perhaps his family hadn’t disowned him (Philippians 3:8). God used a boy who happened to overhear. Nothing happens by chance.

So he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. Brave: he risked the conspirators’ anger.

In a sentence. The plotters asked the council to request the commander to bring Paul down, pretending to examine his case more carefully, while they waited to kill him on the way, but Paul’s nephew heard of the ambush, went into the barracks and told Paul.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary people, even young ones, to fulfil his promises. Be ready to be used.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.”

Paul called one of the centurions. Key words. Paul trusts God’s promise, and uses ordinary means. Faith in God’s sovereignty doesn’t mean doing nothing. God promised Rome; Paul still acted wisely.

Paul the prisoner. Paul later called himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1). Not Rome’s prisoner, but Christ’s.

In a sentence. Paul called a centurion and asked him to take the young man to the commander, since he had something to tell him, and the centurion did, saying Paul the prisoner had asked him to bring the young man.

For worship. Trusting God and acting wisely go together. Use the means he gives.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately. Key words. A kind, almost fatherly touch. The young man may have been a boy. The tribune handled it wisely and discreetly.

The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow. He tells the plan.

In a sentence. The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside and asked privately what he had to say, and he said the Jews had agreed to ask him to bring Paul before the council tomorrow, pretending to look into his case more carefully.

On a Tuesday. Kindness from unexpected people is God’s grace too. Thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.”

But do not be persuaded by them. Bold advice from a young man to a Roman officer.

And now they are ready, waiting for your consent. Urgent: it was planned for tomorrow.

Tell no one that you have informed me of these things. Protecting the boy, and the secret.

In a sentence. He urged the commander not to agree, since more than forty men were waiting in ambush, sworn not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul, and were ready, awaiting his consent, and the commander sent him away, telling him not to tell anyone he had reported this.

For worship. Plots against God’s people often fail through small, hidden means. God is never outwitted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commander calls two centurions and orders two hundred soldiers, seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen to be ready to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, with horses for Paul, to bring him safely to Governor Felix. He writes a letter: Claudius Lysias greets His Excellency Felix. The Jews had seized this man and were about to kill him when he rescued him with his troops, having learned he was a Roman. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found it concerned disputes about their law, nothing deserving death or prison. Told of a plot against the man, he has sent him at once and instructed his accusers to bring their case to Felix. The soldiers take Paul overnight as far as Antipatris; next day the cavalry go on with him while the rest return. In Caesarea they deliver the letter and hand Paul over. Felix reads it, asks his province, and on hearing Cilicia says he will hear the case when the accusers arrive. He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the theological point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses a boy's ears, an officer's fear of a court-martial, a standard troop deployment, and a piece of self-serving correspondence. Scripture is entirely comfortable with both, and Christians who will only recognise God's hand in the spectacular will miss most of what he does.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. First, providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Lysias's falsified report is a lie, and Luke's silence is not approval. Second, providence does not promise comfort. This chapter's happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor angling for a bribe. God's certain purposes and a believer's real losses run down the same road, at the same time, and Scripture never asks anyone to pretend otherwise.

The pattern is Joseph's: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The forty men were, without knowing it, working for the One they were trying to thwart — and so was the empire, which spent a great deal of money that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune's letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He did not invent a single fact. He moved one clause — putting the discovery of Paul's citizenship before the rescue instead of after it — and let his superior draw a generous conclusion. Luke set the letter down beside the events of the previous chapter and left it there.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode — why the job ended, why the friendship cooled, how the argument went. You have told it enough times that it runs smoothly now. Every detail in it probably happened. Then lay it beside a transcript, the way Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask the narrower question: is the sequence right, and is the motive you imply the motive you actually had? Most of us are not liars. Most of us are editors, and the edit is nearly always in our own favour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. Key words. 470 soldiers to protect one prisoner from forty assassins. Nearly half the Jerusalem garrison. Rome took the protection of a citizen seriously, and the tribune wasn’t taking chances. God’s promise kept Paul; Rome supplied the escort.

To go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Under cover of darkness.

Also provide mounts for Paul to ride. More than one: perhaps for changes of horse, or for his companions.

And bring him safely to Felix the governor. Felix, governor of Judea about AD 52–59. A former slave, freed by the emperor’s family. The historian Tacitus said he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave.

In a sentence. Then he called two centurions and ordered them to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, and to provide horses for Paul and take him safely to Governor Felix.

On a Tuesday. God sent 470 soldiers to escort one apostle. He can protect you too.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he wrote a letter to this effect: “Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.

And he wrote a letter to this effect. “To this effect”: Luke gives the substance, perhaps from a copy read at the trial.

Claudius Lysias. Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship (22:28). Lysias was his Greek name.

To his Excellency the governor Felix. “Excellency” (kratistō): the same title Luke uses for Theophilus (Luke 1:3). A formal Roman letter.

In a sentence. He wrote a letter: Claudius Lysias to His Excellency Governor Felix, greetings.

For worship. God’s plans unfold even through official letters and bureaucracy. He is Lord of the paperwork too.
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him. True.

Having learned that he was a Roman citizen. Key words. Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen, and implies he rescued Paul because he was a citizen. In fact he only learned it later (22:25–29). A small, self-serving twist of the facts. Luke, the careful historian, preserves both versions honestly.

In a sentence. He wrote that this man had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed when he came with soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

On a Tuesday. It’s tempting to tell the story so we look good. Tell the truth, even when it’s unflattering.
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.

I found that he was being accused about questions of their law. Religious disputes, as Gallio said (18:15).

But charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Key words. A Roman official declares Paul innocent. Luke records such verdicts repeatedly (25:25; 26:31–32): Paul, like Jesus, was innocent under Roman law. Important for Theophilus, and for the church’s standing in the empire.

In a sentence. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found that the accusation concerned questions of their law, with no charge deserving death or imprisonment.

For worship. Christians should live so that even unbelieving authorities find no fault in them (1 Peter 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.

When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once. Passing the problem upwards.

Ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him. A proper Roman trial would follow.

In a sentence. When he learned of a plot against the man, he sent him at once to Felix, and ordered his accusers to present their case before him.

On a Tuesday. God uses governments to provide due process. Pray for just courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him.

Brought him by night to Antipatris. Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond ran through open, mostly Gentile country, safer from ambush. A forced march through the night.

And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. The foot soldiers went back; the cavalry took him the last 25 miles.

In a sentence. The soldiers followed orders, took Paul by night to Antipatris, and the next day returned to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to go on with him.

For worship. God’s escort brought Paul safely through the night. He brings his people through every dark road.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him.

When they had come to Caesarea. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. Paul would be held here for two years (24:27). And from here, he would sail for Rome.

They presented Paul also before him. One step closer to Rome.

In a sentence. When they reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.

On a Tuesday. Each step, even into custody, brought Paul closer to God’s purpose. So with you.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.

He asked what province he was from. To decide whether he had jurisdiction. Cilicia was then under the governor of Syria, Felix’s superior, so Felix could hear the case.

I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive. Roman law required the accused to face his accusers (25:16).

And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium. Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, now the governor’s residence. Paul was a prisoner in a palace.

In a sentence. Felix read the letter, asked what province Paul came from, and learning he was from Cilicia, said he would hear his case when his accusers arrived, and ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s palace.

For worship. Whether in a palace or a prison, Paul was in God’s hands. So are you.
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the council he once served. The hearing is a disaster as a trial and a triumph of providence. The high priest Ananias, a notoriously greedy and violent man, has Paul struck for claiming a clear conscience; Paul flares up, then apologises when told who gave the order, citing the law. Seeing the council split between Sadducees and Pharisees, he declares that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council dissolves into a shouting match, some Pharisees even defending him. The tribune has to rescue him a second time.

That night the Lord stands by Paul: he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. Next morning more than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed him, but Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and warns him, and the tribune sends Paul by night under an escort of 470 soldiers to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that states Paul has done nothing deserving death or chains. God’s promise is kept through a boy’s ears, a centurion’s errand and a Roman army. Paul is now in Roman custody, which will last more than four years and bring him, as promised, to Rome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five days later the high priest comes down with elders and a lawyer, Tertullus. After flattering Felix, Tertullus charges Paul with being a troublemaker who stirs up Jews everywhere, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and one who tried to desecrate the temple. The Jews back him up. Paul replies calmly: he went up to worship only twelve days ago and started no disturbance anywhere, and they cannot prove their claims. He admits that he worships the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and sharing their hope that God will raise both righteous and wicked; so he strives for a clear conscience. He came bringing gifts for the poor and was found in the temple ritually pure; the Asian Jews who caused the trouble are not even here, and the council found nothing except his cry about the resurrection. Felix, who knows about the Way, adjourns the case and keeps Paul under guard with some freedom. Later he and his wife Drusilla hear Paul on faith in Christ; when Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment, Felix grows afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. Hoping for a bribe, he often sends for him. After two years Festus succeeds Felix, who leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is the most quietly terrifying figure in Acts, because nothing about him is dramatic. He does not oppose the gospel. He is interested in it. He understands it accurately (v. 22), he sends for the preacher repeatedly (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him badly enough to end the meeting. He is the nearest thing in this book to a man under conviction — and he dies outside of Christ, so far as Scripture records, with nothing standing between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2). The reason is visible in this very chapter: Felix felt more at the first conversation than at any of the many that followed. Repeated exposure without submission does not keep the heart tender; it callouses it. The second hearing of a truth is always easier to survive than the first.

This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that conviction is not conversion. Felix's fear was real and it was the Spirit's work on his conscience — and a frightened conscience saves nobody. What God requires is not to be moved but to be surrendered. Grace is sovereign and grace is free, and the same doctrine that says no one comes unless the Father draws him says also that whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to act on it while you can still feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter's argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and settled to the point of cheerfulness (v. 10). One postpones; the other has already been told he must testify at Rome and simply waits. Circumstance is a poor guide to who in a room is actually at liberty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul was asked, by the man who could have freed him with a sentence, to speak about faith in Christ Jesus. He was a prisoner, entirely in that man's power, and the governor's known weaknesses were a court that could be bought and a wife he had taken from another man. Paul chose righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment. He did not trim one of the three, and he stayed in prison for two more years.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and nearly all of us will at some point have something true to say to somebody who holds an advantage over us — an employer, a relative whose goodwill we need, a friend whose reaction we fear. The pressure is not usually to lie. It is to select: to say the two things that will land well and leave out the third, and to call the omission tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and then ask why it is always the same one. Paul's three subjects took ten seconds to choose and cost him two years, and Luke thought them worth recording precisely because he did not shorten the list to two.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,

Meaning first. Acts 24 is Paul’s trial before the Roman governor Felix. A professional lawyer accuses him of being a plague and a ringleader of the Nazarenes. Paul answers calmly with facts: he caused no riot, he worships the God of his fathers, believes the Law and the Prophets, and hopes in the resurrection of the just and the unjust. Felix delays the verdict. Later, Paul speaks to Felix and his wife about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and Felix trembles, but sends him away to wait for a convenient time, which never comes. Paul stays in prison for two years.

The high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case in Roman legal style. Perhaps a Hellenistic Jew, or a Roman.

Since through you we enjoy much peace. Key words. Flattery, the customary opening of a speech to a governor (captatio benevolentiae). And mostly false: Felix had crushed rebels brutally, but his rule provoked more unrest. Tacitus and Josephus describe him as cruel and corrupt. The Jews later complained of him to Rome.

In a sentence. Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented their case against Paul to the governor, beginning with flattery about the peace and reforms Felix had brought.

On a Tuesday. Beware flattery, in giving and receiving it. Honest words are better than smooth ones (Proverbs 28:23).
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.

In every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. More flattery.

But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. “Kindness” (epieikeia): gentleness, clemency. Ironic, of Felix.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they gratefully welcomed this in every way and everywhere, and asked Felix kindly to hear them briefly so as not to weary him.

For worship. Truth needs no flattery. Speak plainly and honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.

For we have found this man a plague. Key words. “Plague” (loimon): pest, pestilence. A personal attack.

One who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. The political charge: sedition. The most serious accusation before a Roman governor, under an emperor nervous of Jewish unrest.

And is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. “Nazarenes”: followers of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish name for Christians, still used for them in Hebrew and Arabic. “Sect” (hairesis): party, school, like Pharisees or Sadducees (5:17; 15:5). Not yet “heresy” in the later sense.

He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. The religious charge, false (21:28–29). “We seized him”: they were trying to kill him.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verses 7–8 that they would have judged him by their own law, but Lysias took him away with violence. It is probably a later addition, shifting the blame onto Lysias.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they had found Paul a troublemaker who stirred up riots among the Jews all over the world, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, who even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him.

For worship. Followers of Jesus may be called a plague. Let your life prove the charge false.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.

By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him. Confident, but empty. They offered no witnesses. Roman law required evidence.

In a sentence. Tertullus said that by examining Paul himself, Felix could learn the truth of all their charges.

On a Tuesday. Accusations without evidence are cheap. Don’t believe everything you hear.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so.

The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. The delegation backed Tertullus. Many voices don’t make a lie true.

In a sentence. The Jews joined in, affirming that all this was true.

For worship. Jesus was accused by many voices too. He knows how it feels.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,

Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. Key words. Felix had been in office for several years, about six. Paul’s opening is respectful and true, without flattery. He is glad to answer to someone who knows Jewish affairs. “Cheerfully” (euthymōs): confidently.

You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem. Key words. Facts that can be checked. Not much time to start a world-wide riot. And “to worship”: not to cause trouble.

In a sentence. When Felix nodded for him to speak, Paul said that knowing Felix had been judge over this nation for many years, he gladly made his defence, and Felix could check that it was no more than twelve days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship.

On a Tuesday. When defending your faith, be calm, respectful and factual.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.

They did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd. Point by point, Paul denies the sedition charge.

Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. Key words. No evidence. Under Roman law, the burden of proof was on the accusers.

In a sentence. No one had found him arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd in the temple, the synagogues or the city, and they could not prove their charges.

For worship. Live so that no charge against you can be proved.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.

But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers. Key words. Paul admits one thing: he follows the Way. Not a new religion, but the fulfilment of the old. The same God.

Believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets. Key words. Everything. Paul held to the whole Old Testament (Romans 3:31). The Christian faith is the true reading of the Old Testament, which points to Christ.

Having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept. The Pharisees did, at least.

That there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. Key words. A clear statement of the general resurrection (Daniel 12:2; John 5:28–29). Everyone will be raised: the righteous to life, the wicked to judgment.

Where Christians differ: the resurrection of the unjust. Some teach that the wicked will simply cease to exist (annihilationism), or never be raised. Verdict: Paul says both the just and the unjust will rise. Jesus says some to eternal life, and some to eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 5:29). The wicked are raised to stand before God and face conscious, eternal judgment. This is the historic Christian teaching, sobering and true.

In a sentence. Paul confessed that he worshipped the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, which they called a sect, believing everything in the Law and the Prophets, and hoping in God, as they did, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

On a Tuesday. Everyone will rise. Are you ready to rise to life?

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,

So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Key words. “So”: because of the coming resurrection and judgment. “Take pains” (askō): train, exercise, work hard at. The hope of judgment shapes how we live. A clear conscience towards God and people (23:1).

Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28). Paul came with gifts, not trouble. The only time Acts mentions it.

In a sentence. Because of this hope, Paul said, he always tried to keep a clear conscience before God and people, and after several years away he had come to bring gifts for the poor of his nation and to offer sacrifices.

For worship. The coming judgment should make you careful with your conscience. Keep short accounts with God.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.

They found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. Ritually pure, not profaning the temple.

But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation. Key words. Roman law expected accusers to appear in person. Where were the Asian Jews who started it? Absent. A legal weakness in the prosecution.

In a sentence. They found him ritually purified in the temple, with no crowd or disturbance, but the Jews from Asia, who should be present to accuse him if they had anything against him, were not there.

On a Tuesday. Those who accuse should be willing to face the accused. Follow Matthew 18 in your disputes.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’

Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council. Ask the council: they found nothing.

Other than this one thing that I cried out... “It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” Key words. The one real issue: the resurrection. Paul keeps bringing it back to the centre (23:6; 26:8). If Jesus rose, everything changes. That is a theological question, not a crime.

In a sentence. Otherwise, let these men say what crime they found when he stood before the council, apart from his one statement that he was on trial over the resurrection of the dead.

For worship. Keep the resurrection at the centre. It is what Christianity stands or falls on.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs.

Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way. Key words. He knew more than they thought: perhaps from his Jewish wife, or from Christians in Caesarea (Philip and Cornelius lived there). He knew Paul was innocent.

Put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” A delaying tactic. Lysias never came, as far as we know. Felix didn’t want to offend the Jews by releasing Paul, nor break Roman law by condemning him.

He should be kept in custody but have some liberty. Light custody.

And that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. Prisoners relied on friends for food and care. Luke and others probably visited. Some think Luke gathered material for his Gospel during these two years.

In a sentence. Felix, who knew the Way well, adjourned the case, saying he would decide when Lysias came, and ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard but give him some freedom and let his friends take care of his needs.

On a Tuesday. Knowing the truth and delaying a decision is a dangerous place to be. Don’t be a Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.”

Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I (chapter 12); she had left her husband, the king of Emesa, to marry Felix, who was her third husband (Josephus). She was about twenty. A marriage built on adultery.

And heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. Curiosity, perhaps.

And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment. Key words. Paul didn’t soften his message for the powerful. Righteousness: to a corrupt, unjust governor. Self-control: to a couple in an adulterous marriage. The coming judgment: to a man who judged others. The gospel addresses the conscience, and calls for repentance. Paul preached to Felix’s life, not just his mind.

Felix was alarmed. “Alarmed” (emphobos): terrified. The Spirit was convicting him (John 16:8).

Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you. Key words. The most dangerous words a person can say to the gospel. “A convenient time” (as older translations put it). There is no record that he ever repented. The opportunity was then. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

In a sentence. Some days later Felix came with his Jewish wife Drusilla, sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus, but as Paul talked about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “That’s enough for now; when I find it convenient I will send for you.”

On a Tuesday. If God is speaking to your conscience, don’t say, “Later.” Respond today.
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. Key words. A bribe. Felix had heard of the collection (v. 17), and perhaps thought Paul had wealthy friends. Taking bribes for releasing prisoners was illegal but common. Paul never paid.

So he sent for him often and conversed with him. Many conversations, no conversion. Felix heard the gospel many times and was hardened, not softened. Hearing without heeding hardens.

When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in office about two years later. Felix was recalled to Rome after violent clashes in Caesarea.

And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison. Key words. Political convenience over justice. Two years in prison, unjustly. Yet these years weren’t wasted: perhaps Luke wrote his Gospel, and Paul prayed and wrote. And God was keeping him safe for Rome.

In a sentence. Felix also hoped Paul would offer him a bribe, so he sent for him often and talked with him, and when two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, but wanting to please the Jews, he left Paul in prison.

For worship. God can use years of unjust waiting. Trust him in yours.
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
24.overview:
Five days after Paul reaches Caesarea, the high priest arrives with elders and a hired advocate, Tertullus, who opens with lavish flattery of Felix and then brings three charges: Paul is a public menace who stirs up Jews across the empire, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a would-be desecrator of the temple. Paul answers calmly, point by point. He went to Jerusalem to worship only twelve days ago and caused no disturbance anywhere; the accusers cannot prove their claims. He admits only that he worships the God of the fathers according to the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and hoping, as they do, for the resurrection of both righteous and wicked. He came bringing alms, was found ritually pure in the temple, and the Asian Jews who started the trouble are not even present.

Felix, who knows a good deal about the Way, adjourns the case. Over the following two years he and his Jewish wife Drusilla summon Paul repeatedly. When Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment to come, the governor, notorious for cruelty and for taking another man’s wife, becomes afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. He also hopes for a bribe. When he is recalled, he leaves Paul in prison to please the Jewish leaders. The chapter is a portrait of a man who heard the gospel often and put it off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days after arriving in his province, Festus goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. The chief priests and Jewish leaders present their charges against Paul and press him, as a favour, to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning to kill him on the way. Festus answers that Paul is held at Caesarea and he himself will soon return there; their leaders can come and accuse him if he has done wrong. After about ten days he goes back, takes his seat in court the next day and has Paul brought in. The Jews from Jerusalem surround him with many serious charges they cannot prove. Paul declares he has done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks Paul whether he will go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul answers that he is standing before Caesar’s court, where he should be tried, and he has done the Jews no wrong, as Festus well knows. If he deserves death he will not refuse to die, but if the charges are empty, no one may hand him over to them: he appeals to Caesar. After consulting his advisers, Festus replies that to Caesar he shall go. Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrive to welcome Festus, who tells the king about the prisoner Felix left behind. The Jewish leaders wanted him condemned, but Roman custom requires that the accused face his accusers and defend himself. When they came, their charges were not the crimes he expected, but disputes about their religion and about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Unsure how to investigate, Festus offered a trial in Jerusalem, but Paul appealed to the emperor. Agrippa says he would like to hear the man, and Festus promises he shall, tomorrow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

Paul's appeal to Caesar settles a question Christians still raise: may a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had a promise from the risen Christ that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a statutory right to get there. Faith in the promise did not make the appeal unnecessary; it made the appeal obvious. The same man who was told every soul aboard the ship would survive still warned that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31).

Providence does not bypass means. It employs them, and it is content to employ thoroughly unspiritual ones — a citizenship registry, a governor's ambition, an emperor's court, and a bureaucrat's need to fill in a form correctly. God ordains the end and he ordains the road, and the road here runs through Roman administrative procedure.

Two guards. First, the lawfulness of the means does not sanctify the motives of those who supply them: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did, and Luke uses the identical phrase so the reader will not miss it. Second, God's certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime and Paul stays in chains. Scripture never asks anyone to pretend that the second fact is softened by the first. They are simply both true, and the Christian lives in the overlap.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment — a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. He had identified the hinge of the entire religion. He could have passed an examination on it. And it never crossed his mind that if it were true it might concern him personally; it was a fact about somebody else's people.

Now: This is the particular danger of a life spent near the things of God. Anyone raised in a believing home, or twenty years in a pew, or halfway through a theology course, can state the resurrection more accurately than Festus did. The question the governor puts to such a reader is not whether the doctrine is held correctly. It is whether it has ever once been allowed to be about him. Say the sentence out loud — a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive — and notice honestly whether anything in you moves. Festus said it in passing and moved on.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,

Meaning first. Acts 25 brings a new governor, Festus, and the same old plot. The Jewish leaders want Paul brought to Jerusalem to ambush him. Festus refuses, holds a hearing in Caesarea, and then, wanting to please the Jews, suggests a trial in Jerusalem. Paul, knowing what that means, uses his right as a Roman citizen: I appeal to Caesar. And so the Lord’s promise begins to be fulfilled: he will testify in Rome. Then King Agrippa arrives, and Festus, who finds Paul’s case about “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive,” asks the king to hear him.

Three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem. A new governor visiting the religious centre, to meet the leaders. Wise politics.

And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul. Two years later, they still hadn’t forgotten. Hatred keeps long accounts.

In a sentence. Three days after arriving in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, where the chief priests and Jewish leaders presented their case against Paul and pressed him...

On a Tuesday. Hatred doesn’t forget. But neither does God forget his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way.

Asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem. A favour to start the new governor’s term well.

Because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. Key words. The same plan as two years before (23:12–15). Religious leaders still planning murder.

In a sentence. They asked him, as a favour, to have Paul transferred to Jerusalem, for they were planning to ambush and kill him on the way.

For worship. Men plot, but God overrules. Their ambush never happened.

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. “So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.”

Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea. Key words. Festus refused. Perhaps from Roman procedure; but behind it, God’s protection.

Let the men of authority among you go down with me. Come to Caesarea and make your case.

And if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him. A fair procedure.

In a sentence. Festus answered that Paul was being held at Caesarea and he himself was going there soon, so their leaders should come with him and bring charges if the man had done anything wrong.

On a Tuesday. God works through fair procedures and sensible officials. Pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove.

The next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. No delay, unlike Felix.

The Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him. Surrounding him, intimidating.

Bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. Key words. Many, serious, unproven. The same as before (24:13). Two years, and still no evidence.

In a sentence. After eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea, and the next day convened the court and had Paul brought in, and the Jews from Jerusalem stood around him bringing many serious charges they could not prove.

For worship. Many charges can’t make a lie true. Rest in your innocence before God through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.”

Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense. Key words. Three charges, three denials. Law, temple, Caesar: religious and political. Paul had kept the law, honoured the temple, respected Caesar. The same charges were brought against Jesus (Luke 23:2), and against Stephen (6:13).

In a sentence. Paul defended himself, saying he had done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Christians should be good citizens, honouring God and the authorities. Give no one a just charge against you.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor. Key words. Like Felix (24:27), and Pilate (Mark 15:15). Politics over justice. A new governor wanting a good start with the people he must govern.

Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me? Before Festus, in Jerusalem. But Paul knew the ambush awaited, and that in Jerusalem the Sanhedrin would effectively decide.

I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. Festus represented Caesar. Paul was a Roman citizen, in a Roman court.

To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. Key words. Bold: you know I’m innocent.

In a sentence. Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asked Paul if he would go to Jerusalem to be tried before him there, but Paul said he was standing before Caesar’s court, where he should be tried, and he had done the Jews no wrong, as Festus knew very well.

For worship. Speak truth to those in power, respectfully and plainly, as Paul did.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”

If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. Key words. Paul accepts the state’s right to punish real crime, even with death. He is not trying to escape justice.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong. Verdict: Paul here accepts that some crimes deserve death and that the state may impose it, as he teaches in Romans 13:4 (the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain), grounded in Genesis 9:6. The state has the God-given right to punish grave crimes, including with death, though it must do so justly, with due process and certain guilt. Christians may disagree on when it is wise to use it.

But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. Not even the governor, as a favour.

I appeal to Caesar. Key words. A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself (the right of provocatio). Once made, the appeal could not be refused. The emperor was Nero, then in his early, better years. Paul used his rights wisely, and God used it to send him to Rome, at the state’s expense, under guard, as Jesus promised (23:11).

To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go. Festus may have been relieved.

In a sentence. Paul said that if he had done anything deserving death, he would not refuse to die, but if the charges were empty, no one could hand him over to them, and he appealed to Caesar, and Festus, after conferring with his advisers, said, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”

On a Tuesday. Use your legal rights wisely. God can use them to further his purposes.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix,

Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea. Key words. King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I (chapter 12), great-grandson of Herod the Great. He ruled territories north and east of Galilee and had the right to appoint the high priest. The last of the Herods. Bernice was his sister; rumours of incest followed them (Josephus, Juvenal). She later became the mistress of the Roman general Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem. They came to welcome the new governor.

Festus laid Paul’s case before the king. Agrippa was an expert in Jewish affairs (26:3). Festus wanted help.

There is a man left prisoner by Felix. Felix’s unfinished business.

In a sentence. Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus, and as they stayed many days, Festus discussed Paul’s case with the king, saying Felix had left a prisoner there.

For worship. God was fulfilling his promise that Paul would carry his name before kings (9:15). He is never late.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.

Asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. Without a trial.

It was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense. Key words. Roman justice at its best: the right to face your accusers and answer. Christian legal traditions drew on this and on Scripture (Deuteronomy 19:15–19; John 7:51). Festus presents himself well.

In a sentence. In Jerusalem the chief priests and elders had pressed charges and asked for his condemnation, but Festus told them it was not Roman custom to hand anyone over before he faced his accusers and had a chance to defend himself.

On a Tuesday. Give everyone a fair hearing before you judge. It is justice, and love.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.

I made no delay. Festus presents himself as efficient, unlike Felix.

But on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. True (v. 6).

In a sentence. When they came, he did not delay, but the next day convened the court and had the man brought in.

For worship. Justice delayed is justice denied. Don’t delay doing right.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.

When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. No real crimes.

Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion. “Religion” (deisidaimonias): could mean superstition. Festus speaking to a Jewish king, he chooses a neutral word.

And about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. Key words. A pagan’s summary of the gospel, and it’s exactly right. The whole case comes down to this: Jesus died, and Paul says he is alive. That is the heart of Christianity. If it’s true, everything changes; if not, nothing matters (1 Corinthians 15:14–17). Festus said it dismissively. It is the most important fact in history.

In a sentence. When the accusers spoke, they did not charge him with the crimes Festus expected, but had disputes with him about their religion and about a certain Jesus, who had died, but whom Paul claimed was alive.

On a Tuesday. A certain Jesus, who was dead, is alive. Believe it, and tell it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.

Being at a loss how to investigate these questions. Honest. Festus didn’t understand Jewish religious disputes, or how to judge whether a dead man was alive.

I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem. He omits that it was to please the Jews.

For the decision of the emperor. “The emperor” (tou Sebastou): the Augustus, the revered one, a title of the emperor. Nero.

In a sentence. At a loss how to investigate such questions, he asked if Paul would go to Jerusalem to be tried there, but Paul appealed to be held for the emperor’s decision, so he ordered him held until he could send him to Caesar.

For worship. Even confused rulers serve God’s plans. Nothing is outside his control.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
