Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.”

I would like to hear the man myself. Key words. Curiosity, like his great-uncle Herod Antipas who wanted to see Jesus (Luke 23:8). Agrippa had probably heard of Paul for years.

Tomorrow you will hear him. And Paul would preach the gospel to a king.

In a sentence. Agrippa told Festus he would like to hear the man himself, and Festus said he would hear him tomorrow.

On a Tuesday. Curiosity about Christ can be a door. Pray for curious people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great ceremony and enter the audience hall with the senior officers and leading citizens, and Paul is brought in. Festus introduces him: the whole Jewish community, in Jerusalem and here, has petitioned against this man, crying that he must not live. But Festus has found that he has done nothing deserving death, and since Paul has appealed to the emperor, he has decided to send him. The trouble is that he has nothing definite to write to his lord. So he has brought Paul before them, and above all before King Agrippa, so that after this hearing he may have something to write; it seems absurd to send a prisoner without stating the charges.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus told his disciples that they would be dragged before kings and governors for his name's sake, and then said something startling about it: this will be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). Not your ordeal — your opportunity. Acts 25 is that promise arriving in a form nobody would have designed. The hostility of the Sanhedrin, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king, and an administrative problem with a covering letter combine to assemble the entire ruling class of a Roman province in one room and sit them down in front of a preacher.

Note who did the assembling. Not the church, which had no power to convene such a gathering and no money to hire the hall. The opposition built the platform, paid for it, filled it with the most important people available, and then handed the prisoner the floor.

The Reformed instinct here is neither triumphalism nor passivity. God is not obliged to use worldly power, and he frequently works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he does use the machinery of the age, he does not ask its permission and he does not need its cooperation to be willing. Festus wanted a charge sheet. What he arranged was an evangelistic meeting for the aristocracy of Judea.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. The king had the title, Bernice had the jewels, the tribunes had the swords, the leading men had the money, and Festus had the authority to decide what happened next. Paul had a chain and the floor. Within a day the man with the chain had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to deflect him with a joke.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and the principle does not require it. It shows up in smaller rooms — the meeting where you are plainly the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the eccentric position, the conversation where everyone else has the confidence and the vocabulary and the standing. The instinct is to wait for a better platform, one where you are taken more seriously. Paul never got a better platform than the one his enemies built for him, and he did not ask for one. He used the floor he was given, in the clothes he was wearing, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp. Key words. “Pomp” (phantasias): display, show, the word gives us “fantasy.” Robes, attendants, ceremony. In contrast, Paul in chains. Which was truly great? The kings of this world come with pomp that fades; the servant of the King of kings stood in chains, and his words endure.

They entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Five tribunes, each commanding a thousand, and the city’s leaders. The most distinguished audience Paul had ever addressed.

You see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me... shouting that he ought not to live any longer. An exaggeration.

In a sentence. The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great ceremony into the audience hall with the military commanders and leading men of the city, and at Festus’s command Paul was brought in, and Festus said this was the man the whole Jewish community had petitioned him about in Jerusalem and Caesarea, shouting that he should not live.

For worship. Earthly pomp fades. The glory of Christ’s servants is in their message.

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.

But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. Key words. Another declaration of Paul’s innocence by a Roman official (23:29; 26:31). Like Pilate of Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. “My lord” (tō kyriō): the emperor. A title that Christians would give only to Jesus. Festus had a problem: sending a prisoner to the emperor with no charge would look foolish.

So that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. Agrippa could help him frame a charge.

In a sentence. Festus said he had found that Paul had done nothing deserving death, but since he had appealed to the emperor, he decided to send him, though he had nothing definite to write to his lord, so he had brought him before them all, especially King Agrippa, so that after examining him he would have something to write.

On a Tuesday. Even Paul’s enemies couldn’t find a crime. Let your life be like that.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.

For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him. Key words. The absurdity of the situation: a prisoner with no charge. Paul was in chains for preaching that Jesus is alive. Festus’s honesty shows that Christianity was persecuted not for crimes, but for its message.

In a sentence. He thought it unreasonable to send a prisoner without stating the charges against him.

For worship. Many Christians today are imprisoned for no crime but their faith. Pray for them.

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”
25.overview:
A new governor, Porcius Festus, arrives about AD 59. Within days the Jerusalem leaders ask him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, intending to ambush him on the road, as their predecessors had tried two years earlier. Festus insists they come to Caesarea instead. They bring many serious charges they cannot prove, and Paul denies any offence against the law, the temple or Caesar. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul sees the danger and uses his right as a citizen: “I appeal to Caesar.” Festus has no choice but to send him to Nero.

The appeal leaves Festus with a problem: he must send a report to the emperor, and he can find no crime. When King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice pay a courtesy visit, Festus explains the case: the dispute concerned the Jews’ religion and “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.” Agrippa wants to hear Paul, and the next day, in a hall full of pomp, Festus presents the prisoner. Jesus had promised that his followers would stand before kings and governors for his name’s sake (Luke 21:12); this chapter sets the scene for the greatest of Paul’s defences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Given leave to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa he is glad to defend himself before one who knows Jewish customs so well. All his people know he lived as a strict Pharisee; now he is on trial for hoping in God’s promise to the fathers, the hope that God raises the dead. Once he was sure he must oppose Jesus’ name: he jailed believers, voted for their deaths and hunted them abroad. On the way to Damascus at noon a light brighter than the sun struck him and his companions down, and a voice in Aramaic asked why he persecuted him: it was hard to kick against the goads. It was Jesus, who appointed him servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, to receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith. Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere; for this he was seized and nearly killed, but God has helped him. He says only what Moses and the prophets foretold: the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus shouts that Paul’s learning has made him mad. Paul answers that he speaks sober truth: the king knows, for this was not done in a corner. Does Agrippa believe the prophets? Agrippa asks if Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly. Paul replies that he prays all his hearers may become as he is, apart from the chains. Leaving, the officials agree he has done nothing deserving death or prison; he could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The theological spine of this speech is that Christianity is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the one question that would settle it — do you believe the prophets? The charge is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room and his accusers have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isa. 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Dan. 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isa. 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish settlement; that is precisely what his opponents wanted, and precisely what he would not give them.

Underneath it lies the doctrine this whole chapter is a case study in: grace that is entirely from God's side. Nothing in Paul's account belongs to Paul. He was not seeking, dissatisfied, or badly taught; he was convinced, exactingly trained, and in a raging fury, riding hard in the opposite direction — and he was stopped, blinded, named, and commissioned. He did not find Christ. Christ appeared to him. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness in the same breath. Repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20). The works are never the root; they are the fruit, exactly as Paul argued at length elsewhere (Eph. 2:8–10). A sovereign work of grace produces a visibly different life, and a life with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the finest presentation of the gospel any ruler in the New Testament ever received, delivered by the ablest preacher of the age, in his own theological vocabulary, by a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not argue with it. He did not refute a single point. He made a joke, stood up, walked out, and remarked in the corridor that the prisoner had done nothing wrong.

Now: Notice how the refusal was actually shaped, because almost nobody declines Christ the way we imagine. There was no debate, no crisis, no considered rejection. There was wit, and then there was standing up, and the standing up was the answer. That is how it usually goes — a subject changed with a light remark, an evening that ran late, a genuine intention to come back to it. If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa had none worth stating. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way five or six times, and whether anything is actually going to be different about the sixth. Paul's one request at the start of the speech was that the king would not become impatient before he had finished. It is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: “I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,

Meaning first. Acts 26 is Paul’s greatest defence, before King Agrippa, Bernice, Festus, and the leading men of Caesarea. This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts. Paul tells how he, a strict Pharisee who hoped in the resurrection, persecuted Jesus’ followers until Jesus met him and sent him to open the eyes of the Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God. He insists that he says nothing but what Moses and the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer and rise. Festus calls him mad; Agrippa deflects; Paul wishes they were all like him, except for the chains. And the rulers agree: this man has done nothing wrong.

Then Paul stretched out his hand. The orator’s gesture, with a chained hand.

I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa. Key words. Not flattery, but genuine: at last a judge who understands Jewish matters. And Jesus’ promise fulfilled: before kings (9:15).

In a sentence. Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak, and Paul stretched out his hand and began his defence, saying he considered himself fortunate to make his defence against the Jews’ accusations before King Agrippa.

On a Tuesday. Every opportunity to speak of Christ, even under pressure, is a good fortune. Use it.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.

Especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Agrippa knew Judaism well. He oversaw the temple and appointed high priests.

Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. A long speech was coming.

In a sentence. Agrippa knew all the Jewish customs and disputes, so Paul asked him to listen patiently.

For worship. Ask people to listen patiently to the story of Christ. It is worth their time.

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.

My manner of life from my youth... is known by all the Jews. His past was public.

According to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. Key words. “Strictest” (akribestatēn): most exact. The Pharisees were the most precise in keeping the law. Paul was no lax, half-hearted Jew. His conversion wasn’t from irreligion to religion, but from the best religion without Christ to Christ.

In a sentence. All the Jews knew how he had lived from his youth among his people and in Jerusalem, and could testify, if they would, that he lived as a Pharisee, the strictest party of their religion.

On a Tuesday. Even the strictest religion can’t save without Christ. Paul learned that.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!

And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers. Key words. The promise: the Messiah and the resurrection. Paul is on trial for being a faithful Jew who believes God’s promise has been kept.

To which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. “Twelve tribes”: all Israel, as one people. Their worship was hope, waiting for God to act.

And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! The irony: Jews accuse a Jew for believing the Jewish hope.

In a sentence. Paul said he was on trial because of his hope in what God promised their fathers, the promise the twelve tribes hoped to see fulfilled as they worshipped God day and night, and it was for this hope that the Jews accused him.

For worship. The hope of Israel is fulfilled in Jesus. Your hope rests on God’s oldest promises.

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? Key words. The central question. “Any of you”: Paul turns to the whole audience, Jews and Gentiles. If God is God, the Creator who gives life to all (17:25), why is it incredible that he raises the dead? The question is not whether resurrection is possible, but whether God is God.

I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Key words. Paul admits he once thought it incredible too, at least of Jesus. “Ought”: he thought it his duty. Sincere, and wrong.

In a sentence. Paul asked why any of them should think it incredible that God raises the dead, and said he himself had been convinced he ought to do all he could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

On a Tuesday. If God made the universe, raising the dead is not too hard for him. Believe it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.

I not only locked up many of the saints in prison. Key words. “Saints”: now Paul calls them saints, God’s holy people. Then he called them heretics.

But when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply gave his approval. Literally “I cast my pebble”: a black pebble for condemnation. Stephen, and others.

And tried to make them blaspheme. Key words. Tried to force them to curse Jesus. The worst kind of persecution: attacking the soul.

And in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. “Raging fury” (perissōs emmainomenos): exceedingly mad. Paul is honest about the depth of his sin. The greatest sinner (1 Timothy 1:15), and the greatest trophy of grace.

In a sentence. In Jerusalem, with authority from the chief priests, he imprisoned many saints, voted for their deaths, punished them often in the synagogues trying to force them to blaspheme, and in his rage pursued them even to foreign cities.

For worship. If grace could save Paul, it can save anyone. Praise God for it.
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.

With the authority and commission of the chief priests. Official authority. Then he met a higher authority.

At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun. Key words. The middle-eastern noon sun is blinding. This light was brighter. The glory of the risen Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

That shone around me and those who journeyed with me. Witnesses.

In a sentence. On one such journey to Damascus, with the authority of the chief priests, at noon he saw on the road a light from heaven brighter than the sun shining around him and his companions.

On a Tuesday. The glory of Christ outshines the sun. Let it fill your vision today.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language. Aramaic. A new detail, for Agrippa.

It is hard for you to kick against the goads. Key words. A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. A Greek proverb for resisting the gods. Was God already pricking Paul’s conscience: Stephen’s face, the believers’ courage, the Scriptures he knew? Resisting God only hurts yourself. And God’s goad would win.

Effectual grace. The picture is of a resistance that God overcomes. Paul kicked, and Christ conquered him. God’s grace is not forceful against our will, but it is effectual: it changes the will, and brings us willingly (Philippians 2:13).

In a sentence. They all fell to the ground, and he heard a voice in Aramaic saying, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.”

For worship. Stop kicking against God’s goads. Surrender is freedom.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,

I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. As before.

But rise and stand upon your feet. Key words. As God told Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:1). The commission of a prophet.

For I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness. “Servant” (hypēretēn): an assistant, an under-rower in a ship. “Witness” (martyra): one who testifies. Both humble and solemn. In this account, Paul compresses Ananias’s words into Jesus’ own, since they came from Jesus.

To the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you. More revelations to come (18:9; 22:17; 23:11; 2 Corinthians 12:1–4).

In a sentence. He asked who it was, and the Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting; now get up, for I have appeared to you to appoint you as my servant and witness to what you have seen and what I will show you.”

On a Tuesday. Christ appoints his people as servants and witnesses. That is your calling too.

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.

Delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles. Protection, as Jeremiah was promised (Jeremiah 1:8).

To whom I am sending you to open their eyes. Key words. Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant, who would open blind eyes and be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6–7, 16). Paul, struck blind, was sent to open eyes.

So that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God. Key words. Salvation in four contrasts. Darkness to light: ignorance and sin to truth and holiness. The power of Satan to God: a change of kingdom (Colossians 1:13). Conversion is a transfer of allegiance.

That they may receive forgiveness of sins. The first gift.

And a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me. Key words. “A place” (klēron): inheritance, a share. “Sanctified”: set apart as God’s holy people. By faith in Christ. Not by works or law, but by faith. A summary of the gospel from the lips of Jesus himself.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would rescue Paul from his own people and the Gentiles, to whom he was sending him to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so that they would receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those made holy by faith in him.

For worship. You have been turned from darkness to light, forgiven and set apart by faith in Christ. Live as a child of light.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.

I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. Key words. Paul obeyed. A vision without obedience is useless. And grace makes obedience possible.

But declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles. The pattern of 1:8.

That they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. Key words. The message: repent, turn, and show it by your deeds. As John the Baptist preached (Luke 3:8). Deeds don’t save; they show that repentance is real.

Where Christians differ: faith and works. Some think Paul and James contradict each other on faith and works. Verdict: Paul teaches that we are justified by faith alone (Romans 3:28), and here, that true repentance produces fitting deeds. Works are not the root but the fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:18). Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

In a sentence. So Paul did not disobey the heavenly vision, but preached first in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and all Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent, turn to God, and show their repentance by their deeds.

On a Tuesday. Has your repentance shown up in your deeds? Ask God to make it visible.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:

For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. Because he preached to Gentiles.

To this day I have had the help that comes from God. Key words. God’s help, through every danger. The secret of Paul’s survival.

And so I stand here testifying both to small and great. To slaves and kings alike. Today, great: a king.

Saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass. Key words. Paul’s gospel was not new, but the fulfilment of the Old Testament. Christianity is not a break from Moses, but his goal.

In a sentence. That is why the Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him, but God had helped him to this day, so he stood testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen.

For worship. God’s help is enough, to this day and every day. Testify to small and great.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.”

That the Christ must suffer. Key words. The Scriptures foretold a suffering Messiah (Isaiah 53; Psalm 22; Luke 24:26, 46).

And that, by being the first to rise from the dead. The firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23; Colossians 1:18). Others were raised, but died again; Jesus was the first to rise to eternal resurrection life.

He would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles. The risen Christ proclaims light, through his messengers (Isaiah 49:6).

Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind. Key words. Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd (17:32). Festus interrupts loudly. A compliment and an insult: you’re too clever for your own good. Jesus too was called mad (John 10:20; Mark 3:21).

In a sentence. Paul said the prophets foretold that the Messiah would suffer and, as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles, and at this point Festus shouted that Paul was out of his mind, his great learning driving him mad.

On a Tuesday. If you are called foolish for believing the resurrection, you are in good company.
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.

I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus. Calm and courteous. Not offended.

But I am speaking true and rational words. Key words. “True” (alētheias): factually true. “Rational” (sōphrosynēs): sober, sound-minded. Christianity is not madness but sober truth. Faith is reasonable.

For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. Agrippa knew the facts.

For this has not been done in a corner. Key words. A famous phrase. The life, death and resurrection of Jesus were public events, in a known place and time, witnessed by many. Not a secret cult’s private visions. Christianity invites investigation. Its claims can be tested in history.

In a sentence. Paul answered that he was not mad, but speaking true and sensible words, for the king knew about these things and he could speak freely to him, being sure none of it had escaped his notice, since it was not done in a corner.

For worship. The gospel happened in public history. Your faith rests on facts, not feelings.

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?”

King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe. Key words. Paul turns from defence to evangelism. A direct, personal question to a king. If Agrippa believed the prophets, he must believe in Jesus, who fulfilled them. He is in a corner. If he says no, he loses his standing with the Jews. If yes, he must accept Jesus.

In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian? Key words. The ESV notes that the question can also be read: “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” Probably ironic or evasive: do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly? The old translation, “almost thou persuadest me,” became a famous hymn and sermon, but probably misreads him. “Christian”: only the second use of the word in the New Testament (11:26; 1 Peter 4:16), probably said with a sneer.

In a sentence. Paul asked King Agrippa if he believed the prophets, saying he knew he did, and Agrippa replied, “Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me to be a Christian?”

On a Tuesday. Don’t deflect the gospel’s personal questions. Answer them honestly.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.” Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them.

Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am. Key words. A heart for the lost. Paul doesn’t care how long it takes; he wants them all saved. A prisoner wishing a king were like him. He was richer than all of them: forgiven, free in soul, a child of God.

Except for these chains. Key words. A touch of grace and wit. He lifts his chained hands. He wishes them his faith, not his suffering. Love for his judges.

Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. The king had heard enough. He ended the hearing. We know of no response of faith. He heard the gospel from the greatest apostle, and walked away.

In a sentence. Paul replied that, short time or long, he prayed to God that not only the king but all who heard him that day would become what he was, except for these chains, and then the king rose, with the governor, Bernice and those sitting with them.

For worship. Pray that everyone you know would become a Christian, whether in a short time or long.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment. Key words. Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent: Gallio (18:14–15), Lysias (23:29), Festus (25:25), and now Agrippa and Festus together. Like Jesus before Pilate and Herod (Luke 23:14–15). Christianity is no threat to lawful government.

This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar. Key words. The irony: his appeal kept him a prisoner. But it was God’s way to send him to Rome (23:11). Paul’s chains carried the gospel to the capital of the world, and the emperor’s court (Philippians 1:12–13).

In a sentence. As they left, they agreed that this man was doing nothing that deserved death or imprisonment, and Agrippa told Festus he could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.

On a Tuesday. What seems a mistake may be God’s way. Paul’s appeal took him exactly where God wanted.
verseByVerse.note: Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent.

26.title: Paul Before Agrippa
26.text: <sup>1</sup>So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: <sup>2</sup>“I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews, <sup>3</sup>especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. <sup>4</sup>My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. <sup>5</sup>They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. <sup>6</sup>And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, <sup>7</sup>to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! <sup>8</sup>Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? <sup>9</sup>I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <sup>10</sup>And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. <sup>11</sup>And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. <sup>12</sup>In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. <sup>13</sup>At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me. <sup>14</sup>And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ <sup>15</sup>And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. <sup>16</sup>But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you, <sup>17</sup>delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles—to whom I am sending you <sup>18</sup>to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, <sup>20</sup>but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. <sup>21</sup>For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. <sup>22</sup>To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: <sup>23</sup>that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” <sup>24</sup>And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” <sup>25</sup>But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. <sup>26</sup>For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner. <sup>27</sup>King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” <sup>28</sup>And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” <sup>29</sup>And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.” <sup>30</sup>Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. <sup>31</sup>And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” <sup>32</sup>And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
26.overview:
This is Paul’s fullest and most polished defence, given before King Agrippa II, Bernice, the governor Festus and the leading men of Caesarea. It is the third account of his conversion in Acts, now shaped for an audience that includes a Jewish king expert in the Scriptures. Paul presents his whole life as one story of Israel’s hope. He was a strict Pharisee; he is on trial for believing God’s promise to the fathers, the hope of resurrection. He once thought he must oppose Jesus’ name with all his strength, imprisoning and voting against believers. Then on the Damascus road, at noon, a light brighter than the sun stopped him, and the risen Jesus commissioned him as servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, that they might receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith in him.

Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere, and he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus interrupts, shouting that Paul’s learning has driven him mad. Paul replies that his words are true and sober, and appeals directly to the king: do you believe the prophets? Agrippa deflects with a wry question; Paul answers that he wishes everyone listening would become what he is, except for the chains. The officials agree that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. In Luke’s design, the gospel has now been heard before a king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Setting Sail and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and other prisoners are handed to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, and sail with Luke and Aristarchus on a coastal ship. At Sidon Julius kindly lets Paul see friends. Contrary winds take them past Cyprus to Myra, where they board an Alexandrian grain ship for Italy. Progress is slow, and they reach Fair Havens on Crete. It is now after the autumn Fast, and sailing is dangerous; Paul warns of disaster. But the centurion follows the pilot and the owner, and the majority vote to try for a better winter harbour at Phoenix. A gentle south wind tempts them out, then a violent northeaster rushes down from the island and drives them helplessly before it. Behind the island of Cauda they haul in the boat, brace the hull with cables, and, fearing the Syrtis sandbanks, lower the sea anchor. They throw cargo and tackle overboard. For many days there is no sun or stars, and all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up: they should have listened, but now they must take heart. An angel of the God he belongs to and serves has told him that he must stand before Caesar, and that God has given him the lives of all on board. They will lose only the ship and must run aground on an island.
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Actually Promised

The theology of this section turns on a distinction most Christians need more than they need another verse about victory: the difference between what God promises and what we assume he promises.

The angel's word was precise, and it had two halves. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22), and then we must run aground on some island (v. 26). God guaranteed every person. He explicitly did not guarantee the vessel, the cargo, the owner's fortune, the crew's wages, or a safe arrival at a chosen port — and he said so in advance. Every one of those was lost, and the promise was kept in full.

That is the pattern of the promises Scripture actually makes. Nothing will separate his people from his love (Rom. 8:38–39); he works all things together for their good (Rom. 8:28); he will never leave them (Heb. 13:5). Read the list and notice what is not on it. Comfort is not on it. Property is not on it. The preservation of your circumstances is not on it. A believer standing in the surf watching his ship break up is not watching God fail; he may well be watching God keep his word exactly as given.

Alongside that runs the chapter's second theme: providence works through means, and never around them. God decreed that all 276 would live, and he decreed the whole chain that delivered it — the frapping cables, the four stern anchors, the sailors kept aboard, the meal at dawn, the swimmers going first. Paul's absolute confidence in the angel's word and his urgent practical interventions are not in tension; they are the same faith, and the sharpest expression of it is his own sentence at v. 31: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.

And note the instruments God employs. Not one of them is a believer. A centurion's professional kindness, a crew's seamanship, an officer's fear for his own career — the Lord uses them all, unimproved and unconsulted, and they go off duty with no idea what they have been part of.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The disaster began with a harbour that was perfectly safe and thoroughly boring. Fair Havens would have kept 276 people alive all winter. It was small, it sat beside an unremarkable village, it had no facilities, and staying there meant four idle months with a valuable cargo earning nothing. So the professionals took a vote and ran for somewhere better, forty miles down the coast, on one day's easy sail — and a gentle south wind came up that morning and seemed to confirm it.

Now: Most people can spot the obviously ruinous choice and avoid it. Far fewer notice the other moment — when something safe and unglamorous was working, and the only real argument against it was that it was dull. The job that was steady. The church that was ordinary. The routine that was quietly keeping you upright. The stretch of life that felt like stagnation and was actually shelter. And when you moved, the circumstances seemed to agree with you, because a following wind on the morning of a decision feels overwhelmingly like a green light and is very often just the weather. Before the northeaster, every soul on that ship would have told you they had made a sensible call. Afterwards, every one of them would have given everything they owned to be back in the boring harbour.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica.

Meaning first. Acts 27 is one of the most detailed accounts of a sea voyage from the ancient world, and an eyewitness story of shipwreck. Paul, a prisoner, sails for Rome. He warns against sailing late in the season and is ignored; a hurricane drives the ship for two weeks; all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up and says: an angel of the God I belong to has promised that not one life will be lost. He encourages them, gives thanks for bread, and every one of the 276 reaches land. The prisoner becomes the leader. God’s promise is kept, through storm, sailors and planks.

And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy. “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. His seamanship details are remarkably accurate, as studies by sailors have shown.

A centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. An imperial regiment. Julius treats Paul well throughout.

Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor; the ship would hug the coast, where they could find a ship for Italy.

Accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. A faithful companion (19:29; 20:4), later Paul’s fellow prisoner in Rome (Colossians 4:10). Luke and Aristarchus may have travelled as Paul’s servants, which prisoners of status were allowed.

In a sentence. When it was decided they would sail for Italy, Paul and other prisoners were handed over to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, and they boarded a ship from Adramyttium bound for ports along the coast of Asia, with Aristarchus from Thessalonica.

On a Tuesday. Friends who stay with you in hard times are a gift from God. Be one.
verseByVerse.note: “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. Aristarchus later shared Paul’s imprisonment.

parallels.desc: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner

verseByVerse.quote: "The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.

The next day we put in at Sidon. Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre, about seventy miles from Caesarea.

And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. Key words. Kindness from a Roman officer. “His friends”: the believers in Sidon, probably under guard. The church cared for Paul.

We sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. “Under the lee” means on the sheltered side, out of the wind. The prevailing westerly winds in late summer forced them to go north of Cyprus.

In a sentence. The next day they landed at Sidon, where Julius kindly allowed Paul to visit his friends and receive their care, and from there they sailed along the sheltered side of Cyprus because the winds were against them.

For worship. God gives his servants favour with unexpected people. Pray for kindness from those in authority over you.
verseByVerse.note: Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre. “Under the lee” means sheltered from the wind by the island.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia.

Along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia. Past Paul’s home province.

We came to Myra in Lycia. Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt. Later the home of Bishop Nicholas, the original Saint Nicholas.

In a sentence. Crossing the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, they landed at Myra in Lycia.

On a Tuesday. Every port on the way was in God’s plan. So is every stage of your journey.
verseByVerse.note: Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone.

There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy. Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Large ships, up to 180 feet long, under imperial contract.

We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus. Cnidus, on the south-west tip of Asia Minor. Slow going against the wind.

As the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. They turned south to shelter behind Crete.

In a sentence. There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy and put them aboard, and they made slow progress for many days, reaching Cnidus with difficulty, and since the wind prevented them from going on, they sailed along the sheltered side of Crete, past Salmone.

For worship. Slow progress and contrary winds are not outside God’s control. Keep going.
verseByVerse.note: Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Cnidus lay at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; they turned south to shelter behind Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens. Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete. It still bears the name (Kaloi Limenes). Not well protected for winter.

Near which was the city of Lasea. Ruins have been found nearby.

In a sentence. Struggling along the coast, they came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.

On a Tuesday. A place can be called fair and still not be a safe place to stay. Choose your harbours wisely.
verseByVerse.note: Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, 'Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”

Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous. Sailing in the Mediterranean was considered dangerous from mid-September, and stopped altogether from mid-November to March.

Because even the Fast was already over. “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. In AD 59 it fell on 5 October. A Jewish writer dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar.

Paul advised them. Key words. A prisoner giving advice. Paul was an experienced traveller: he had been shipwrecked three times already (2 Corinthians 11:25).

I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives. Common sense from experience, not yet a revelation. (Later God reveals that no lives will be lost, v. 22.)

In a sentence. Since much time had been lost and sailing had become dangerous, the Day of Atonement having passed, Paul warned them that he could see the voyage would bring disaster and heavy loss of cargo, ship and lives.

For worship. Christians can give wise, practical advice in ordinary matters. Speak up when you see danger.
verseByVerse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether in winter.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there.

But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. Understandable: the experts against a prisoner. But the experts were wrong. Expertise and profit can blind.

Because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in. Fair Havens was exposed.

The majority decided to put out to sea from there. Key words. The majority. But the majority was wrong. Truth is not decided by vote.

Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest. Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete, about forty miles.

In a sentence. But the centurion listened to the pilot and the ship’s owner rather than to Paul, and since the harbour was unsuitable for winter, most decided to sail on, hoping to reach Phoenix, a Cretan harbour facing south-west and north-west, and winter there.

On a Tuesday. The experts and the majority can be wrong. Listen to wise voices, even unexpected ones.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land.

Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose. Key words. “Supposing.” A gentle breeze, and false confidence. Pleasant conditions can lure us into danger.

But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from Crete’s mountains, a typhoon (typhōnikos), hurricane-force. Without warning.

In a sentence. When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had what they wanted, weighed anchor and sailed close along Crete, but soon a hurricane-force wind called the Northeaster swept down from the island.

For worship. Life’s storms come suddenly. Build on the rock before they come (Matthew 7:24–25).
verseByVerse.note: The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from the mountains of Crete.

parallels.desc: he raised the stormy wind

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.

When the ship was caught and could not face the wind. “Face” (antophthalmein): literally look in the eye. Ancient ships had eyes painted on the bow. The ship couldn’t look the wind in the eye.

We gave way to it and were driven along. Helpless. They let the storm carry them.

In a sentence. The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind, so they gave way and let it drive them along.

On a Tuesday. When you can’t steer, remember who rules the wind (Mark 4:41).

verseByVerse.quote: "Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along.

Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda. About twenty-three miles south of Crete. A few minutes’ shelter.

We managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind; in the storm it filled with water. “We”: Luke helped haul it in.

They used supports to undergird the ship. Cables were passed under the hull to hold the timbers together, as the strain could split the ship apart.

Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of Libya, notorious for wrecking ships. The wind was driving them south-west.

They lowered the gear. Probably the sea anchor, to slow their drift, or the mainsail.

In a sentence. Passing to the lee of a small island called Cauda, they barely managed to secure the lifeboat, hoisted it aboard, ran ropes under the ship to hold it together, and fearing the sandbanks of Syrtis, lowered the sea anchor and let the ship drift.

For worship. Do what you can in the storm, and trust God for what you can’t.
verseByVerse.note: The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind. Cables were passed under the hull to hold it together. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

They began the next day to jettison the cargo. Lightening the ship, as Jonah’s sailors did (Jonah 1:5). Some of the grain.

And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. “With their own hands”: desperate. Spare rigging, perhaps the main yard. Everything that could go, went.

In a sentence. So violently were they battered that the next day they began throwing cargo overboard, and on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

On a Tuesday. In storms, we learn what really matters. Possessions can go; people and souls matter.

parallels.desc: the mariners hurled the cargo into the sea

verseByVerse.quote: "When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, 'Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.

When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days. Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate. They had no idea where they were.

All hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Key words. Total despair. “Saved” (sōzesthai): rescued, the word for salvation. Hopelessness, before God acts.

Since they had been without food for a long time. Seasickness, despair, and wet food.

Paul stood up among them. The prisoner takes charge.

Men, you should have listened to me. Not “I told you so” for its own sake, but to establish his credibility for what comes next. If he was right before, they should listen now.

In a sentence. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm raged on, they finally gave up all hope of being saved, and after they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up and said they should have listened to him and not sailed from Crete, avoiding this damage and loss.

For worship. When all hope is gone, God is still there. He speaks in the darkness.
verseByVerse.note: Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,

Yet now I urge you to take heart. Key words. “Take heart” (euthymein): be cheerful, take courage. A prisoner encouraging the crew.

For there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. A promise of God, now revealed.

For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship. Key words. “To whom I belong and whom I worship”: Paul’s identity in a phrase. Belonging and serving. Not a god among many, but the God who owns him. In a ship full of pagans, Paul bears witness.

In a sentence. But now Paul urged them to take courage, for none of them would be lost, only the ship, since that night an angel of the God he belonged to and served had stood beside him.

On a Tuesday. You belong to God. That is your security in every storm.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and he said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.

Do not be afraid, Paul. Paul was afraid too.

You must stand before Caesar. Key words. “Must” (dei): God’s purpose. Paul couldn’t die at sea, because God had promised Rome (23:11). God’s plan for him guaranteed his survival.

And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you. Key words. “Granted” (kecharistai): given as a gift of grace. Perhaps Paul had been praying for them. For Paul’s sake, God spared 275 others. The presence of a righteous man can bless those around him (Genesis 18:32; 39:5).

So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. Key words. Faith is believing God will do what he said. Not wishful thinking, but trust in a promise.

In a sentence. The angel told him not to be afraid, for he must stand before Caesar, and God had graciously given him the lives of all who sailed with him, so Paul told them to take courage, for he had faith in God that it would happen just as he had been told.

For worship. Faith is trusting that God will do exactly what he said. Trust his promises today.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we must run aground on some island.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we must run aground on some island.

But we must run aground on some island. Key words. “Must”: God’s plan included the shipwreck. Not rescue from the storm, but through it. Safety, not comfort. The ship would be lost; the lives saved.

In a sentence. But they would have to run aground on some island.

On a Tuesday. God doesn’t always spare us the wreck. But he brings us through it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic, the sailors sense land near. Soundings show the water growing shallower, so they drop four anchors from the stern and pray for daylight. When the sailors try to escape in the boat, pretending to lay anchors from the bow, Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay, the rest cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. Before dawn Paul urges everyone to eat after two weeks of fasting: they need strength, and not a hair of their heads will be lost. He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it and eats, and they are all encouraged and eat. There are 276 on board. After eating they lighten the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. At daybreak they see an unfamiliar coast with a beach and decide to run the ship ashore. They cut the anchors, loosen the steering oars, raise the foresail and head for the beach, but strike a sandbar. The bow sticks fast and the stern is broken up by the waves. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners to prevent escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. He orders those who can swim to jump first and the rest to follow on planks and wreckage. And so everyone reaches land safely.
verseByVerse.theology:
Certainty and Effort Are the Same Faith

Verse 31 is the hinge, and it is one of the clearest answers in Scripture to the oldest bad question about providence: if God has already decided, why bother?

Nine verses after announcing an unconditional promise — not one life will be lost — Paul says something that sounds like its opposite: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Both are true, because God does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means that bring them about. The sailors staying aboard was not an alternative to the promise. It was the promise arriving. The same logic governs the meal at dawn: eat, because God has guaranteed you will live and you will need the strength.

So Paul's serenity and Paul's urgency are not in tension. A man who thinks everything hangs on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well; a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither, and the doctrine he lived by he also wrote down: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13). The for in that sentence carries the whole argument.

The section also shows how God's promises are typically fulfilled — not by suspending the ordinary world but by working through the wreckage of it. There is no calmed sea here, no parting of the waters, no angel carrying anyone ashore. There are exhausted people swimming, and non-swimmers clinging to splintered planks off the ship that has just been destroyed beneath them. The debris of the disaster is the means of the rescue, and the promise is kept down to the last person on the roll.

And one thing more, quietly at the centre: the prisoners live because the centurion wanted Paul. Condemned men, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. Luke does not press the point. He does not have to.
verseByVerse.examples:
