Then: An hour before the ship broke apart, with an unknown shore ahead and no boat left, Paul took a piece of bread and thanked God for it out loud where everyone could hear. He had nothing. He had not eaten in two weeks, he was in chains, the vessel was doomed, and he was about to swim for his life. And a shipful of frightened people watched a man be visibly grateful to God, and something in them changed — Luke says they were encouraged, and they ate.

Now: Notice what actually moved that ship's company. Not Paul's argument; he had made his case at Fair Havens and been outvoted. Not his warning; they had ignored it. What reached them was watching one man's confidence in God hold steady when there was no visible reason for it, and do something ordinary and cheerful in front of them. People around you are far better at reading that than at following reasoning. They will discount what you say about God when things are going well, and they will not forget what you did with a piece of bread on the worst morning of your life. Courage is contagious in a way that argument is not — and the place it becomes contagious is almost always the small, practical, unembarrassed act done in front of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms.

When the fourteenth night had come. Two weeks of storm.

As we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea. In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily.

About midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. Perhaps they heard breakers. Modern sailors calculate that a ship drifting from Cauda at this rate would reach Malta in about fourteen days. Luke’s account fits exactly.

They took a sounding and found twenty fathoms... fifteen fathoms. A fathom was about six feet. 120 feet, then 90. Shallowing quickly. The soundings match the approach to St Paul’s Bay in Malta.

In a sentence. On the fourteenth night, as they were still being driven across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land, and took soundings, finding twenty fathoms, and a little later fifteen.

For worship. God knew exactly where the ship was, even when no one else did. He knows where you are.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily. The ESV notes that twenty fathoms is about 120 feet and fifteen about 90 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship's boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,

They let down four anchors from the stern. Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready to beach the ship at dawn. Nelson was said to have read this chapter before the Battle of Copenhagen.

And prayed for day to come. Key words. Even pagan sailors prayed. Literally “wished.” The longest night.

The sailors were seeking to escape from the ship. Selfish. Abandoning the passengers.

Under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow. A lie.

In a sentence. Afraid of hitting rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight, while the sailors tried to escape from the ship, lowering the lifeboat as if to put out anchors from the bow.

On a Tuesday. In a crisis, some look after themselves. Be the one who stays and helps.
verseByVerse.note: Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready for beaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.' Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go.

Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Key words. God had promised all would be saved (v. 24). Yet Paul says: unless they stay, you cannot be saved. Both true. God’s promise is fulfilled through means. The sailors were needed to beach the ship.

Divine sovereignty and human means. Some say that if God has determined something, our actions don’t matter. Verdict: this verse refutes it. God had decreed the end (all saved) and the means (sailors staying, eating, swimming, planks). God’s sovereignty doesn’t make human action pointless; it makes it meaningful. As with salvation: God has chosen his people, and calls them through preaching (Romans 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:10). The decree includes the means.

Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. Now the centurion listened to Paul.

In a sentence. Paul told the centurion and soldiers that unless these men stayed with the ship, they could not be saved, so the soldiers cut the ropes of the lifeboat and let it drift away.

For worship. God’s promises don’t make your obedience unnecessary. They make it certain to succeed.

verseByVerse.quote: "As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, 'Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.”

Paul urged them all to take some food. Key words. Practical care. The apostle was also a sensible man: you need strength for the swim. Spiritual and physical care together.

Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food. Too anxious or sick to eat properly.

For it will give you strength. “Strength” (sōtērias): literally salvation, safety. Eating is part of their rescue.

For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you. A proverb of complete safety (Luke 21:18; 1 Samuel 14:45).

In a sentence. Just before dawn Paul urged them all to eat, saying that for fourteen days they had been in constant suspense without food, and they should eat for their survival, since not one of them would lose a hair from his head.

On a Tuesday. Care for people’s bodies as well as their souls. Paul fed a hungry crew.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves.

He took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Key words. Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before meals. In the presence of all: a public witness on a sinking ship. The words echo the Last Supper (Luke 22:19), but this was not the Lord’s Supper; it was a meal for pagans, with thanks to God. Still, it shows the habit of a man who gave thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. Courage is contagious. One man’s faith lifted 275 people.

In a sentence. After saying this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it and began to eat, and they were all encouraged and ate too.

For worship. Give thanks before meals, even in public, even in storms. It is a witness.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: "(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.

We were in all 276 persons in the ship. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred; Josephus sailed in one with 600. Perhaps counted for the food rations. Every one of them would be saved.

And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. The rest of the grain cargo, so the ship would ride higher and run further onto the beach.

In a sentence. There were 276 people on board, and after they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.

On a Tuesday. God counts every person. None is forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach.

Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land. The traditional St Paul’s Bay in Malta, off the main shipping route.

But they noticed a bay with a beach. A place to run aground.

Loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern, lashed up during the storm.

Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. Skilled seamanship. Luke records each step.

In a sentence. At daybreak they did not recognise the land, but saw a bay with a beach where they decided to run the ship aground if they could, so they cut loose the anchors, untied the ropes holding the rudders, hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach.

For worship. God gives skill to sailors and doctors and workers. Thank him for those who use their skills for others.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf.

But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas,” a sandbar or a channel where two currents meet. Such a place exists in St Paul’s Bay, between the mainland and a small island.

The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. The ship broke apart, as Paul said (v. 22). The ship was lost; the lives were not.

In a sentence. But they struck a sandbar and ran the ship aground, the bow stuck fast and wouldn’t move, and the stern was being smashed by the pounding surf.

On a Tuesday. God’s word came true: the ship was lost, but not one life. Trust his word in every detail.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,

The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment (12:19; 16:27). Brutal logic.

But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. Key words. Julius had come to respect Paul. Because of Paul, all the prisoners were spared. God’s promise kept, through a centurion’s will.

He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land. Orderly evacuation.

In a sentence. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to stop any from swimming away and escaping, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stopped them, and ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land.

For worship. One faithful Christian’s presence can save others. Your faithfulness matters to those around you.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.

And the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. Non-swimmers clinging to wreckage.

And so it was that all were brought safely to land. Key words. All 276. Not one lost. “Brought safely” (diasōthēnai): saved through, rescued completely. Exactly as God promised. Some have seen a picture of salvation: the ship of this world breaks apart, but all whom God has given to Christ are brought safely home, some swimming, some clinging to planks, but all safe (John 6:39).

In a sentence. The rest followed on planks or pieces of the ship, and so everyone reached land safely.

On a Tuesday. God keeps every promise to the last soul. All whom he has promised to save will be brought safely home.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.
27.overview:
Luke’s account of the voyage to Rome is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring that survives. In 1848 James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman who sailed these waters, showed that its winds, depths, distances and manoeuvres fit the conditions exactly: this is the log of an eyewitness. Paul, a prisoner under the centurion Julius, sails with Luke and Aristarchus up the coast to Myra, then on an Alexandrian grain ship towards Italy. Late in the season, against Paul’s warning, the ship leaves Fair Havens on Crete for a better harbour, and is caught by a violent north-easterly gale. For two weeks it is driven helplessly west, without sun or stars, cargo and tackle thrown overboard, until all hope is gone.

Then the prisoner takes charge. An angel has told Paul that he must stand before Caesar and that God has given him the lives of everyone aboard; they will lose the ship but not one life. When land is near, Paul stops the sailors abandoning ship, urges everyone to eat, gives thanks and breaks bread. At dawn they run the ship onto a sandbar off Malta; the stern breaks up, the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them, and all 276 reach land. The chapter is a parable of providence: God’s promise is certain, and he keeps it through ordinary means, sailors, anchors, food, a centurion’s decision, and planks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Safe ashore, the travellers learn the island is Malta. The islanders show unusual kindness, lighting a fire and welcoming everyone, for it is raining and cold. As Paul puts a bundle of sticks on the fire, a viper driven out by the heat fastens on his hand. The islanders conclude he must be a murderer whom Justice will not let live, even though he escaped the sea. But Paul shakes the snake into the fire and is unharmed. They wait for him to swell up or drop dead, and when nothing happens, they change their minds and say he is a god. Publius, the island’s chief official, has an estate nearby and welcomes them generously for three days. His father is ill with fever and dysentery; Paul visits him, prays, lays hands on him and heals him. Then the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured. The islanders honour them in many ways and, when they sail, supply what they need. After three months they leave on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there, with the twin gods as its emblem. They stop at Syracuse for three days, then Rhegium, and with a south wind reach Puteoli, where they find believers and stay a week. And so they come to Rome. Believers there hear of them and travel out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet them; seeing them, Paul thanks God and is encouraged. In Rome Paul is allowed to live on his own, with a soldier guarding him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it comes from a believer. A fire lit by islanders who worship other gods. Three days' hospitality from a Roman official. A winter's provisions loaded aboard by people who thought Paul was a deity. A ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux. A favourable wind. God furnishes the last stage of his apostle's journey almost entirely out of pagan hands, and not one of those hands knows what it is doing.

That is the same doctrine the storm chapter taught, arriving now in a gentler key. There God used a centurion's fear and a crew's seamanship; here he uses simple human decency. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes is not an abstraction in Acts — it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and drew a confident conclusion about his standing with God, and they were as wrong as it is possible to be — twice, in opposite directions, within one evening. Scripture is consistent about this: you cannot read a person's standing before God off the surface of their life. Job's friends could not, the disciples could not at the blind man (John 9:2–3), and neither can we, in a sickroom or anywhere else.

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15. Paul took courage, which means he needed to. God's provision for a discouraged apostle was not an angel — he had used angels earlier and would again — but a handful of ordinary Christians who walked two days out along a road to be standing there when he passed. The means God most often uses to keep his servants going is other believers turning up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Believers in Rome heard that a prisoner they had never met was on the road. They had one letter from him, written three years earlier. So they walked — thirty-three miles to Three Taverns, forty-three to the Forum of Appius — stood at the side of the Appian Way, and waited. They did not free him, feed him, or improve his legal position by a single clause. They just turned up. And the apostle to the Gentiles looked at them, thanked God, and found he could go on.

Now: Two things follow, and both cut. The first is that the strong Christian you know is more likely to need this than to say so. Paul had faced down a mob, survived a shipwreck and shaken off a snake, and he still arrived on that road with his courage low. The assumption that mature believers are past needing encouragement is one of the loneliest lies in the church. The second is that showing up almost never feels worth the trip. It accomplishes nothing you can point to, it costs a day you did not have, and you will usually never learn whether it mattered. Luke thought it mattered enough to record, in a book with no room to spare, in the sentence immediately before Paul walks into Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold.

Meaning first. Acts 28 brings Paul to Rome at last. On Malta he survives a viper’s bite and heals the sick. In spring he sails for Italy, is met by believers on the road, and enters Rome as a prisoner. He meets the Jewish leaders, explains the hope of Israel from Moses and the Prophets, and when many reject it, quotes Isaiah and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. The book ends with Paul under house arrest for two years, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The gospel has reached the capital of the world. The story of Acts ends, but the story of the word goes on.

We then learned that the island was called Malta. Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect. Luke calls them barbaroi, meaning non-Greek-speaking, not savage.

The native people showed us unusual kindness. Key words. “Kindness” (philanthrōpian): love for people, humanity. Pagans showing kindness to 276 shipwrecked strangers. God’s common grace in unbelievers.

For they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. Wet, cold, exhausted survivors in late October or November.

In a sentence. Once safely ashore, they found the island was called Malta, and the islanders showed them extraordinary kindness, building a fire and welcoming them all because it was raining and cold.

On a Tuesday. Show kindness to strangers in need. It reflects God’s kindness to us.
verseByVerse.note: Malta lies south of Sicily. The islanders spoke a Phoenician dialect, not Greek — hence “native people.”

verseByVerse.quote: "When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, 'No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”

When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire. Key words. The great apostle gathering firewood. No task beneath him. A servant to the end.

A viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. A snake, sluggish from the cold, woken by the heat. There are no venomous snakes on Malta today, but the islanders clearly believed it was deadly, and the island was more forested then.

No doubt this man is a murderer. They saw his chains. A prisoner bitten by a snake after surviving the sea: divine justice.

Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live. “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty (Dikē). Popular religion assumed that suffering proves guilt, as Job’s friends did. Jesus rejected that link (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5).

In a sentence. When Paul gathered a pile of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened on his hand, and when the islanders saw it hanging from his hand, they said he must be a murderer, for though he escaped the sea, Justice would not let him live.

For worship. Suffering doesn’t prove guilt. Don’t judge others by their misfortunes.
verseByVerse.note: “Justice” was a goddess who was believed to pursue the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. Key words. God’s protection. Paul must stand before Caesar (27:24). No snake could stop that. Jesus had promised the apostles protection (Luke 10:19).

They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. Luke the doctor uses medical terms: swelling, inflammation.

They changed their minds and said that he was a god. From murderer to god: as at Lystra (14:11), but in reverse. Popular opinion swings wildly. Paul was neither.

Where Christians differ: snake-handling. Some groups handle venomous snakes in worship, citing this and Mark 16:18. Verdict: Paul didn’t pick up the snake on purpose; it bit him by accident, and God protected him. Mark 16:9–20 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and is not a command. Deliberately testing God this way is forbidden (Matthew 4:7). God protects his servants in their work; he doesn’t ask us to court danger.

In a sentence. But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no harm, and they waited for him to swell up or drop dead, but after a long time when nothing happened, they changed their minds and said he was a god.

On a Tuesday. Don’t test God by courting danger. But trust him in the dangers you meet.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him.

The chief man of the island, named Publius. “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman governor of Malta; inscriptions found on the island confirm the title. Another precise detail.

Who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. Kindness from the top.

The father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. Key words. Luke the doctor’s precise diagnosis. Perhaps Malta fever, caused by goat’s milk, common on the island until the twentieth century.

And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. Prayer first: the power was God’s. Paul repays kindness with kindness.

In a sentence. Nearby was an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island, who welcomed them and entertained them generously for three days, and his father was ill with fever and dysentery, so Paul went in, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.

For worship. Repay kindness with kindness, and with prayer.
verseByVerse.note: “Chief man” (literally “first man”) was the title of the Roman official on Malta, found in inscriptions there. Luke, a doctor, names the illness precisely.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured.

The rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. Key words. A healing ministry for three months. “Cured” (etherapeuonto): treated, healed. Some suggest Luke the doctor also treated them medically. Either way, God’s kindness came to Malta. And surely Paul preached Christ there; a church has existed on Malta from early times.

In a sentence. After this, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured.

On a Tuesday. God’s goodness spreads through his servants wherever they are washed up. Bloom where you’re planted.

verseByVerse.quote: "They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead.

They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. They had lost everything in the wreck. God provided through the islanders.

After three months we set sail. Early in the spring, around February, when sailing resumed.

A ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. Key words. The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus, protectors of sailors. A touch of irony: the true God had protected them, not the twin gods. Luke notes it, perhaps with a smile.

In a sentence. They honoured them in many ways and, when they were ready to sail, supplied whatever they needed, and after three months they set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, with the twin gods Castor and Pollux as its figurehead.

For worship. The true God protects, not the gods of the sailors. Trust him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the figurehead was the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, twin sons of Zeus and protectors of sailors.

verseByVerse.quote: "Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.

Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily.

And arrived at Rhegium. Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy.

And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the Alexandrian grain ships, 170 miles from Rome. A good wind at last.

In a sentence. They put in at Syracuse for three days, sailed on to Rhegium, and after a day, with a south wind, reached Puteoli the following day.

On a Tuesday. After the storm, God sends good winds. Wait for them.
verseByVerse.note: Syracuse was the chief city of Sicily; Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy; Puteoli, near Naples, was the main port for the grain ships.

verseByVerse.quote: "There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.

There we found brothers. Key words. Christians in Puteoli, before Paul ever came. The gospel had spread without him. The church is bigger than any apostle.

And were invited to stay with them for seven days. Julius allowed it, a sign of his respect for Paul. A Sunday together.

And so we came to Rome. Key words. Five words, a long-awaited moment. From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way. Paul’s great desire (19:21; Romans 1:10–15), Jesus’ promise (23:11), finally fulfilled. Not as he had planned, but as God had promised.

In a sentence. There they found believers who invited them to stay a week, and so they came to Rome.

For worship. God’s promises are fulfilled, in his time and in his way. And so we came to Rome.
verseByVerse.note: From Puteoli the journey to Rome continued by road, the Appian Way.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him.

And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. Key words. The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, about forty and thirty miles from Rome. The Roman Christians walked a day or two to welcome him, like citizens going out to meet a dignitary. Paul had written them his greatest letter three years earlier. Now they met face to face.

On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. Key words. Even Paul needed courage. He had arrived in chains, uncertain of his trial. His fellow believers strengthened him. Christian fellowship is God’s gift for weary souls.

Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. House arrest, chained to a soldier. Probably a rented apartment. A mild form of custody, perhaps on the strength of Festus’s letter and Julius’s report.

In a sentence. The believers in Rome heard they were coming and travelled to the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet them, and when Paul saw them he thanked God and was encouraged, and in Rome he was allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him.

On a Tuesday. Go and meet those who are weary. Your presence can give them courage.
verseByVerse.note: The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stops on the Appian Way, roughly 40 and 30 miles from Rome. Paul was kept under house arrest, chained to a soldier.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later Paul calls together the Jewish leaders in Rome. He tells them that although he has done nothing against their people or ancestral customs, he was arrested in Jerusalem and handed to the Romans. They examined him and wanted to release him, finding nothing deserving death, but when the Jews objected he had to appeal to Caesar, not to accuse his own nation. He has asked to see them because it is for the hope of Israel that he wears this chain. They reply that they have received no letters about him from Judea and no visitor has reported anything bad, but they want to hear his views, since people everywhere speak against this sect. On an agreed day many more come to his lodging. From morning till evening he explains and testifies about the kingdom of God, seeking to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded, others refuse to believe. As they leave, disagreeing among themselves, Paul makes one last statement: the Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah to their fathers about a people who listen without understanding and look without seeing, whose hearts have grown dull, who have closed their eyes and ears so as not to turn and be healed. So they should know that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen. For two whole years Paul stays in his own rented house and welcomes everyone who comes to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without hindrance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Book Has No Ending

The abrupt close of Acts is a decision, not an accident. Luke had written the death of Stephen and the death of James; he could have written the death of Paul. Instead he stops with his hero alive, chained, and preaching.

The reason is that Luke's subject was announced in his first chapter and it was never Paul: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1:8). That programme is now complete. The word has travelled from an upper room in Jerusalem to rented lodgings in Rome, and it is being preached in the capital of the world without restriction. There is nothing left to report.

Hence the final word, akolytos — unhindered — the last word of the Greek text and Luke's verdict on everything that came before it. The Sanhedrin ordered the message silenced; it spread. Stephen was stoned; it spread. Herod killed James and jailed Peter; the door opened. It was flogged out of Philippi, mocked in Athens, rioted against in Ephesus, tried in four courts, sworn against by forty men, driven into a fortnight's storm, wrecked on Malta, and bitten by a snake. At the end, the emperor's soldiers have the preacher chained by the wrist — and the word walks in and out of that room for two years and nobody can touch it.

Two guards keep this from becoming triumphalism. First, unhindered does not mean unopposed; every hindrance in the list was real and several were lethal, and Paul himself would die under Nero within a few years. Second, the man is still in chains as the book closes. Luke's claim is not that the church wins its comfort, but that the word of God cannot be stopped — which is a very different and much sturdier promise, and the only one he offers.

As for Paul himself: early tradition outside Scripture, and therefore to be held loosely, says he was released, travelled again — perhaps to Spain as he had hoped (Rom. 15:24) — was re-arrested and executed at Rome. The Pastoral Epistles read like letters from that later period. Luke declines to tell us, and his silence is the point.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The last thing Luke shows us is a prisoner in a rented room, chained by the wrist to a soldier who changed shift every few hours, unable to leave the building. He could not travel to a single one of the churches he had planted. And out of that room, on the traditional reckoning, came Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon — letters that have reached further than all his journeys put together — while the guard rotation carried the gospel through the imperial barracks until there were believers in Caesar's own household.

Now: The circumstance that looks like the end of a person's usefulness is very often the beginning of the part that outlasts them. Illness that stops a working life. A redundancy. A move to somewhere with no ministry to speak of. Children, or care of a parent, that shrinks the world to a few rooms for a decade. Every one of those feels like being taken off the field, and every one of them puts you in a room with a small number of people who cannot easily get away from you. Paul's chain did not interrupt his ministry; it relocated it, narrowed it, and made it permanent. He did not know that at the time either. He simply welcomed whoever came through the door, every day, for two years — and that is the last thing the book of Acts records anybody doing.

verseByVerse.quote: "After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, 'Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case.

After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews. Key words. To the Jew first, even in Rome, even in chains (Romans 1:16). Paul couldn’t go to the synagogue, so he invited them. Jews had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion (18:2).

Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers. Still “brothers.” Paul never stopped loving his people (Romans 9:1–5).

Yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. Like Jesus (Luke 24:7).

When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty. The Romans found him innocent.

In a sentence. Three days later Paul called together the leaders of the Jews, and told them that though he had done nothing against their people or ancestral customs, he had been handed over as a prisoner in Jerusalem to the Romans, who examined him and wanted to release him, since he had done nothing deserving death.

For worship. Love your people, even when they have wronged you. Paul still called them brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar — though I had no charge to bring against my nation.

But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar. Forced to appeal.

Though I had no charge to bring against my nation. Key words. Paul wasn’t in Rome to accuse the Jews before Caesar. No bitterness, no revenge. He had come to defend himself, not attack them.

In a sentence. But when the Jews objected, he had been forced to appeal to Caesar, though not to bring any charge against his own people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t seek revenge on those who wronged you. Leave it to God (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.' And they said to him, 'We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you.

It is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain. Key words. “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection (23:6; 24:15; 26:6–7). Paul held up his chain: I wear this for Israel’s hope. Christianity is the fulfilment of Israel’s hope, not its rejection.

We have received no letters from Judea about you. Perhaps the Jerusalem leaders had given up, or their letters hadn’t arrived, or they didn’t want to pursue a case they couldn’t win in Rome.

And none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. No prejudice. An open door.

In a sentence. That was why he had asked to see them, for it was because of the hope of Israel that he wore this chain, and they replied that they had received no letters from Judea about him, nor had any visiting Jews reported anything bad.

For worship. The hope of Israel is your hope too: the risen Messiah. Hold it up proudly.
verseByVerse.note: “The hope of Israel” is the promised Messiah and the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.

But we desire to hear from you what your views are. Openness.

For with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against. Key words. “Spoken against” everywhere: as Simeon foretold of Jesus, a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34). Christianity was already notorious, about thirty years after the cross. Within five years, Nero would blame Christians for the fire of Rome. The Roman historian Tacitus called it a deadly superstition.

In a sentence. But they wanted to hear his views, for they knew that people everywhere were speaking against this sect.

On a Tuesday. If the faith is spoken against, don’t be surprised. It always has been. Speak for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved.

They came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. A house meeting.

From morning till evening he expounded to them. Key words. A whole day of Bible teaching. “Expounded” (exetitheto): explained, set out.

Testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus. The two great themes of Acts, together (v. 31; 1:3).

Both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. Key words. As Jesus did on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27, 44). The whole Old Testament points to Jesus. Paul’s method to the end: Scripture.

And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. The same result as always. The gospel divides.

In a sentence. They arranged a day and came in even larger numbers to his lodging, and from morning till evening he explained and testified to the kingdom of God, trying to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, and some were convinced, while others refused to believe.

For worship. Open the Scriptures and show people Jesus. Some will believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: 'The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: "Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: ‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.’

And disagreeing among themselves, they departed. Divided.

The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet. Key words. Again, the Spirit speaking through the prophet. Scripture’s divine author. “Your fathers”: Paul identifies them with their unbelieving ancestors.

You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. Isaiah 6:9–10, the hardening passage quoted by Jesus (Matthew 13:14–15), John (John 12:40), and now Paul. The New Testament’s explanation of Israel’s unbelief: foretold, and God’s judgment on hardened hearts. Acts ends with it, as the Gospels do.

In a sentence. They left, disagreeing among themselves, after Paul made one last statement, that the Holy Spirit spoke rightly to their ancestors through Isaiah: go and tell this people they will keep hearing but never understand, and keep seeing but never perceive.

On a Tuesday. Hearing without understanding is a judgment. Ask God for an open heart when you read his word.

parallels.desc: keep on hearing, but do not understand

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.

For this people’s heart has grown dull. Key words. “Grown dull” (epachynthē): grown fat, insensitive, like thick skin. The heart hardens over time.

And their eyes they have closed. They closed them. Responsibility. Hardening is both their choice and God’s judgment (Romans 1:24; 11:7–8).

Lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them. Key words. The tragedy: healing was available, if they would turn. God longs to heal (Ezekiel 33:11). But hardened hearts refuse.

Israel’s future. This is not the end of Israel. Paul, writing to Rome a few years earlier, said the hardening is partial and temporary: until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). There is hope.

In a sentence. For this people’s heart has become calloused, they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, so that they might not see, hear, understand with their hearts and turn, and God would heal them.

For worship. Don’t let your heart grow dull. Keep it soft before God by daily repentance and his word.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.

Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. Key words. The third and final turning to the Gentiles in Acts (13:46; 18:6). In Asia, Greece, and now Rome. The pattern is complete: to the Jew first, then the Gentile.

They will listen. Key words. A prophecy, fulfilled through the centuries: Gentiles in their millions have listened and believed. Most Christians reading this are Gentiles who listened.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: that when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves. Probably added later from v. 25.

In a sentence. Paul declared that they should know that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.

On a Tuesday. If you are a Gentile believer, you are the fulfilment of this verse. You listened. Praise God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 29: “And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.”

parallels.desc: your saving power among all nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

He lived there two whole years at his own expense. Key words. AD 60–62. “At his own expense”: in rented lodgings, paying his own way, perhaps with gifts from churches (Philippians 4:10–18). Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment, the Prison Letters. Chained, he wrote words that have fed the church ever since.

And welcomed all who came to him. All: Jews, Gentiles, soldiers, slaves like Onesimus (Philemon 10). The gospel spread through the praetorian guard and Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:13; 4:22).

Proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The two themes of Acts, from the first chapter (1:3) to the last. The kingdom of God, which has come in Jesus; and Jesus himself, Lord and Christ.

With all boldness and without hindrance. Key words. The last words of Acts. In Greek, the last word is akōlytōs, unhindered. Paul was in chains; the word was not (2 Timothy 2:9). Acts doesn’t tell us how Paul’s trial ended. Early tradition says he was released, travelled again, was re-arrested, and was beheaded under Nero around AD 67. But Luke’s story isn’t about Paul; it is about the word of God, which runs on, unhindered, from Jerusalem to Rome, and to the ends of the earth. The book is unfinished because the story is unfinished. We are in it.

In a sentence. For two whole years Paul stayed in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

For worship. The story of Acts continues through you. Proclaim the kingdom and teach about the Lord Jesus Christ, boldly. The word is unhindered.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon during this imprisonment. Luke ends with the gospel preached “without hindrance” at the heart of the empire.

parallels.desc: the word of God is not bound

28.title: Rome at Last
28.text: <sup>1</sup>After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta. <sup>2</sup>The native people showed us unusual kindness, for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because it had begun to rain and was cold. <sup>3</sup>When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <sup>4</sup>When the native people saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” <sup>5</sup>He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <sup>6</sup>They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <sup>7</sup>Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <sup>8</sup>It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery. And Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <sup>9</sup>And when this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <sup>10</sup>They also honored us greatly, and when we were about to sail, they put on board whatever we needed. <sup>11</sup>After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the twin gods as a figurehead. <sup>12</sup>Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. <sup>13</sup>And from there we made a circuit and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <sup>14</sup>There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome. <sup>15</sup>And the brothers there, when they heard about us, came as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. On seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage. <sup>16</sup>And when we came into Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. <sup>17</sup>After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews, and when they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <sup>18</sup>When they had examined me, they wished to set me at liberty, because there was no reason for the death penalty in my case. <sup>19</sup>But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—though I had no charge to bring against my nation. <sup>20</sup>For this reason, therefore, I have asked to see you and speak with you, since it is because of the hope of Israel that I am wearing this chain.” <sup>21</sup>And they said to him, “We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of the brothers coming here has reported or spoken any evil about you. <sup>22</sup>But we desire to hear from you what your views are, for with regard to this sect we know that everywhere it is spoken against.” <sup>23</sup>When they had appointed a day for him, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. From morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus both from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. <sup>24</sup>And some were convinced by what he said, but others disbelieved. <sup>25</sup>And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: “The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: <sup>26</sup>‘Go to this people, and say, You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. <sup>27</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed; lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>28</sup>Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen.” <sup>30</sup>He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, <sup>31</sup>proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
28.overview:
The book ends where Jesus’ commission pointed: the word has reached the capital of the world (1:8). On Malta the shipwrecked party is welcomed by the islanders. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand; the locals assume divine justice has caught a murderer, then, when he is unharmed, decide he is a god. Paul heals the father of Publius, the island’s chief official, and many others. After three months they sail on a ship with the twin gods as its figurehead, land at Puteoli, and walk the Appian Way to Rome, where believers come out to meet them and Paul takes courage.

Under house arrest, chained to a soldier, Paul calls the leaders of Rome’s Jewish community. He explains that he is innocent and bound “because of the hope of Israel.” They have heard nothing against him but know the sect is everywhere opposed. On an appointed day he explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the Prophets about Jesus from morning until evening. Some are persuaded; others refuse. Paul quotes Isaiah 6 on hearing without understanding and announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles: they will listen. Luke closes with Paul spending two years in his rented house, welcoming all, preaching the kingdom and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. The prisoner is chained; the word is not (2 Timothy 2:9).
